sources.news_title: Netanyahu rejects US-led Gaza plan
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday rejected a US-led Gaza plan endorsed by Hamas, putting distance between himself and US President Donald Trump as he tries to shore up his base ahead of close elections.
After more than a week of gradually escalating criticism of the plan, and despite receiving assurances that Israel would not need to start withdrawing in Gaza immediately, Netanyahu explicitly opposed the deal following pushback from his right-wing allies.
“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said, referring to the plan Hamas agreed to late last month.
Photo: AFP
The Israeli military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed, and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens,” he told a Cabinet meeting.
Netanyahu described Trump, who had hailed the Gaza deal as a milestone for peace, as “our greatest friend in the White House,” but quickly made it clear he was willing to challenge him, saying Israel was raising its objections with the US.
“They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters,” he said.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader, is running even or trailing in some polls ahead of Oct. 27 elections, the country’s first since the devastating Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas that sparked the Gaza war.
Polls show that the Gaza plan is unpopular with Netanyahu’s right-wing base, and far-right members of his Cabinet have urged him to kill it.

“The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again,” Nickolay Mladenov, the board’s high representative for Gaza, told Israel’s Channel 12 television.
He said he hoped for a “positive outcome” from follow-up discussions with Israel, and characterized the latest stage of the deal as a commitment involving the US, Hamas and the Board of Peace — notably leaving out Israel.

sources.news_title: Israel's Netanyahu rejects Gaza plan in new break from Trump
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a US-backed Gaza plan endorsed by Hamas, putting him at odds with President Donald Trump.
Image: Chip Somodevilla / AFP
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday rejected a US-led Gaza plan endorsed by Hamas, putting distance between himself and President Donald Trump as he tries to shore up his base ahead of close elections.
After more than a week of gradually escalating criticism of the plan, and despite receiving assurances that Israel would not need to start withdrawing in Gaza immediately, Netanyahu explicitly opposed the deal following pushback from his right-wing allies.
"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said, referring to the plan Hamas agreed to in late July.
The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed, and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he told a cabinet meeting.
Netanyahu described Trump, who had hailed the Gaza deal as a milestone for peace, as "our greatest friend in the White House" - but quickly made clear he was willing to challenge him, saying Israel was raising its objections with the United States.
"They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader, is running even or trailing in some polls ahead of October 27 elections, the country's first since the devastating October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas that sparked the Gaza war.
Polls show that the Gaza plan is unpopular with Netanyahu's right-wing base, and far-right members of his cabinet have urged him to kill it.
'Only way forward'
The head of Trump's body implementing the plan, dubbed the Board of Peace, defended the plan as a way to prevent a repeat of October 7.
"The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again," Nickolay Mladenov, the board's high representative for Gaza, told Israel's Channel 12 television.
He said he hoped for a "positive outcome" from follow-up discussions with Israel, and characterised the latest stage of the deal as a commitment involving the United States, Hamas and the Board of Peace - notably leaving out Israel.
Mladenov again promised that Israel would not face any obligations until Hamas gave up all its weapons, down to Kalashnikov rifles - but said Israel would eventually need to pull out.
Hamas, which publicly backed the plan days after selecting a new leader, Khalil al-Hayya, called on Washington to push Netanyahu.
"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap, and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," Bassem Naim, a member of Hamas's political bureau, told AFP.
Hamas in a statement said it was still committed to the plan.
Friction with Trump
Netanyahu until recently campaigned on the strength of his relationship with Trump, who has taken unprecedented steps to back Israel, including moving the US embassy to Jerusalem.
Trump joined Netanyahu in late February in launching a war against Iran, but the two diverged when Trump sought a ceasefire and subsequent settlement to the conflict as it sapped his popularity and sent oil prices soaring.
Netanyahu told his cabinet that "with an agreement or without an agreement, as long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons", a goal he has long alleged Tehran is pursuing.
Netanyahu last week also ordered fresh strikes on Lebanon in response to what Israel called a ceasefire violation by Iran-backed Hezbollah, just as Israel and Lebanon were holding US-mediated talks.
The Gaza plan was the latest stage in a US-brokered ceasefire announced in October that has reduced, but not ended, Israeli operations there.
Despite Netanyahu's stance, Israel appears to have decreased operations in Gaza since the deal was announced, without halting them completely.
Israeli gunfire on Sunday injured several people including a child who was taken to hospital in Khan Yunis, civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal told AFP.
Israeli operations in Gaza have killed 1,258 Palestinians since the ceasefire, according to the territory's health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
The Israeli army has reported five deaths in its ranks during the same period.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu REJECTS Trump's Gaza peace plan: 'They have ideas'
sources.text:
L/R: Ronen Zvulun/POOL/AFP/Getty Images; Aaron Schwartz/AFP/Getty Images
    
© 2026 Blaze Media LLC. All rights reserved.
Days after Trump announced a 'historic agreement,' the Israeli leader decided to throw a wrench in the gears.
President Donald Trump announced on July 30 that his Board of Peace had "reached a HISTORIC agreement" in Gaza that would bring an end to a conflict that has claimed well over 70,000 lives.
While the president characterized his proposed resolution as a major win for the Palestinian people and for Israel alike, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is evidently of a different mind.
'President Trump will be very, very disappointed.'
Netanyahu — whom Trump has rebuked repeatedly in recent months for undermining his initiatives in the region — rejected the Board of Peace's 15-point peace plan on Sunday, telling his cabinet that some of its terms are unacceptable.
Peace proposal
The peace plan released by Trump's Board of Peace, which would be undertaken in stages, requires, among other things, that:
- Israel, Hamas, and "other Palestinian factions" suspend military operations in Gaza;
- Hamas and other factions in Gaza agree not only that all civilian governance and security functions in Gaza will be taken over by the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, but that the committee can carry out its responsibilities independently;
- the NCAG will oversee the disarmament process;
- Gaza will be "governed according to the principle of One Authority, One Law, One Weapon";
- Israeli forces — who presently occupy more than half of Gaza — will execute a phased withdrawal from Gaza; and
- the International Stabilization Force will separate Israeli forces from NCAG-controlled areas during the withdrawal.
"This agreement is a critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the Board of Peace to help the Palestinian people," Trump said in a statement. "At the same time, Israel will have the security it deserves, with Gaza no longer used as a base for terror attacks."
RELATED: It’s the economy, stupid — again
Khan Yunis in the southern Gazan Strip on July 31, 2026. Bashar Taleb/AFP/Getty Images.
"The threat that emerged from Gaza on October 7 will NOT be allowed to rebuild!" continued the president. "Under this agreement, Gaza will finally be in the hands of a new Palestinian government that serves its PEOPLE."
After announcing the deal, which Hamas accepted through Egyptian mediators, Trump told reporters that "Israel is very happy."
While the Israeli security cabinet initially approved of having the International Stabilization Force enter Gaza to aid in the disarmament of Hamas and the transition, top officials called on Netanyahu to reject the plan, reported the Times of Israel.
Rejection
Netanyahu, who facing both a tough re-election battle and an ongoing corruption trial, told his cabinet on Sunday, "Israel rejects the 15-point document."
"The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed," continued Netanyahu. "And when I say Hamas must be disarmed, I mean the heavy weapons, the less-heavy weapons, all weapons. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not a fictitious one."
The Israeli leader — whose nation is the "largest cumulative recipient of U.S. foreign assistance since World War II" — noted that his government has raised its reservations over the peace deal with Washington.
"They have ideas," said Netanyahu, apparently referring to the Americans behind the peace deal. "Some of them are acceptable to us and some are unacceptable to us, and we know how to stand up to these things. We have proven this in the past, and we are proving it today as well. In addition, the IDF will continue to thwart threats against our forces and against our citizens."
The White House did not immediately respond to Blaze News' request for comment.
While flatly rejecting Trump's peace plan, Netanyahu nevertheless spoke warmly of the American president.
"I have great appreciation for President Trump," said the foreign leader. "He is a great friend of ours in the White House. I greatly appreciate the historic partnership with the United States against Iran's attempts to acquire nuclear weapons. And I want to emphasize again: With an agreement or without an agreement, as long as I am prime minister, Iran will not possess nuclear weapons."
"Unlike all those who preach to us, we are doing what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground even against our very best friends when necessary," added Netanyahu.
In addition to rejecting the peace deal, Netanyahu rejected the possibility of a Palestinian state in Gaza.
The prime minister's remarks were welcomed by various Israeli officials, including finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, the leader of the Religious Zionist Party.
"We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas," said Smotrich, in a statement reported by the Times of Israel. "The (military) cannot withdraw even a millimeter from the Gaza Strip. The Gaza Strip cannot begin any process of reconstruction before the complete dismantling and demobilization of Hamas and the Gaza Strip."
Hamas, on the other hand, remains supportive of Trump's plan and has asked Washington to pressure Israel to get on board.
According to an X.com translation of the original Arabic, Basem Naim, a member of Hamas' politburo, stated on Sunday, "We are committed to the roadmap reached with the representatives of the Peace Council in Cairo just days ago, and our agreement, despite all the challenges, reflected a commitment to the interests of our Palestinian people."
"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to press Netanyahu and his government to compel him to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the path for internal political and electoral reasons," added Naim.
After Trump first announced the deal, a U.S. official told the Washington Post, "We're not asking Israel to do anything other than agree to the 20-point plan that they agreed to initially, and so we're very confident they will adhere to it. If they don't, obviously, President Trump will be very, very disappointed."

sources.news_title: Netanyahu spokesman: Hamas must disarm before Gaza pullout
sources.text:
Israel will unequivocally reject any Gaza Strip ceasefire framework that fails to require the total disarmament of Hamas, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's new international spokesperson said on Monday, warning that the terrorist group must be completely stripped of its arsenal before Israel considers withdrawing it troops.
"The prime minister is not going to do anything that is going to put the Israeli people at risk," Doron Spielman told JNS, emphasizing that Netanyahu is "aware of Hamas's intentions" and that the group is "just as committed to terrorism today" as it was when it led the Palestinian massacre of Israelis on Oct. 7, 2023. "The only thing they're lacking is the ability" to carry out another atrocity, he added.
Netanyahu insists the terrorist group must "truly disarm" before any agreement moves forward, the spokesperson said. "By truly disarming, I mean all of their weapons are going to be handed over and removed from the area, from Gaza," Spielman said the premier told him.
Netanyahu on Sunday announced that Jerusalem rejects the roadmap on Hamas disarmament announced by U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace on July 30.
If all of the weapons are not removed, it "would enable Hamas to reconstitute itself," Spielman, appointed to the position on July 1, said in a phone interview from Ma'ale Adumim. "And therefore the 15-point plan is not accepted by Israel because it removes the teeth from the 20-point plan, which is that Hamas has to disarm before anything moves forward."
Trump introduced the 20-point plan to end the Israel-Hamas war in September of last year, requiring Hamas to lay down its arms, and Jerusalem accepted the framework. The recent 15-point plan was reached with Hamas terrorists through Qatar, Turkey and Egypt, and Jerusalem is not a party to it.
Shift in national security doctrine
Spielman outlined a historic pivot in Jerusalem's approach to the northern front in Lebanon, returning to the defense principles of Israel's founding prime minister, David Ben-Gurion. To protect its citizens, the military is holding a critical buffer zone and engaging Hezbollah threats preemptively rather than waiting for attacks on Israeli soil.
"Ben-Gurion specifically said that Israel should not be fighting wars in its own territory. It should be fighting wars in the enemy's territory," Spielman said. "It is a fundamental shift in Israel's security outlook, which is Israel is not responsive. Israel at this point is very much willing to initiate in order to protect Israeli citizens."
Tehran only respects threat of force
Regarding the Iranian threat, Spielman pointed out that Tehran deepened its ties with Turkey and Pakistan over the last month, a dynamic that tested the trilateral Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Ankara, Islamabad and Riyadh on Aug. 7.
He noted that after Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthis fired missiles at Saudi Arabia over the weekend, the regime in Tehran would see any lack of a military response from Riyadh as a sign of weakness.
By contrast, Spielman said the Jewish state maintains its security through overwhelming deterrence and a clear willingness to act against the Islamic Republic.
"There's only one country that Iran's not shooting against, which is Israel," he said. "Why aren't they shooting against Israel? Because they know, as the prime minister said, we will deal them a blow that they will never forget."
He praised the unique relationship between Jerusalem and Washington, noting that both nations have demonstrated the necessary resolve to respond forcefully to regional aggression.
"Iran understands one thing. One thing. The threat of force," Spielman said. "And that is what's keeping Israel safe."
Warnings on Saudi nuclear program
Addressing broader Middle East developments, the spokesperson expressed grave concern over Saudi Arabia's push for a civilian nuclear program. He confirmed that Netanyahu has discussed this issue directly with Trump, stressing the danger such a program could pose to regional stability.
"Every military nuclear program began with a civilian nuclear program. Every one," Spielman said. "There have to be safeguards and guardrails in place that have to be clarified."
Challenge to NATO regarding Turkey
Spielman delivered a sharp rebuke of Ankara, condemning Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan's "duplicitous" foreign policy and regional expansionism. He noted that Turkey has taken over an enormous swath of territory in Syria and continues to occupy more than a third of Cyprus while concurrently deepening its alliance with the Iranian regime.
"They support terrorism, they fund terrorism, they fund extremism," Spielman said. "You can't be duplicitous and on one hand turn to the West and say you're a member of NATO, and on the other hand turn to Iran and continue supporting terror. ... I would leave the question at NATO's doorstep."
Resilience of the Abraham Accords
Despite the ongoing multi-front war and hostility from nations such as Pakistan, Spielman said there are "serious prospects" for expanding the Abraham Accords. He emphasized that existing normalization agreements have endured what he called "the most trying time the Middle East has faced, perhaps ever."
"It shows that these are not just on paper. These are real agreements that have practical implications, security implications, intelligence implications," Spielman said. "It's a very positive thing and we look forward to expanding it."

sources.news_title: Netanyahu Rejects Trump’s 15-Point Gaza Plan as U.S. ‘Semi-Negotiates’ With Iran
sources.text:
Israeli prime minister refuses Gaza withdrawal until Hamas is fully disarmed as Washington confronts simultaneous crises involving Iran, the Strait of Hormuz and renewed Houthi attacks
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly rejected President Donald Trump’s 15-point Gaza peace proposal Sunday, opening a rare and potentially consequential disagreement between two leaders who have otherwise remained closely aligned throughout the widening Middle East conflict.
“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu told his Cabinet, according to the Associated Press, while making clear that Israeli forces will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas has been fully disarmed.
The rejection puts Netanyahu directly at odds with a central provision of the Trump administration’s latest Gaza proposal, which calls for a phased Israeli withdrawal alongside the dismantling of Hamas’ military capabilities and a transition to a new Palestinian governing structure backed by international security forces.
Netanyahu’s objection appears to center largely on sequencing.
Trump’s proposal envisions Israeli forces pulling back as Hamas disarms. Netanyahu is insisting that Hamas must first be completely and verifiably stripped of its weapons before Israeli troops surrender additional territory.
The Israeli prime minister said the military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.”
Despite rejecting the document, Netanyahu said Israel remains in discussions with Washington over Gaza, suggesting that the disagreement has not yet amounted to a complete breakdown in negotiations.
The White House did not immediately respond publicly to Netanyahu’s announcement Sunday, according to the Associated Press.
Hamas, meanwhile, says it remains committed to the broader roadmap and is calling on the Trump administration and other mediators to pressure Netanyahu to move forward.
“We remain committed to the road map,” Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim said Sunday.
The confrontation comes at a politically sensitive moment for Netanyahu, with Israeli elections scheduled for Oct. 27 and members of his right-wing coalition pressing him to resist concessions involving Israeli security control or Palestinian statehood.
Netanyahu has also repeatedly opposed the creation of a Palestinian state, describing such a state as a security threat to Israel.
Trump Takes ‘Low-Key’ Approach to Iran
The Gaza disagreement comes as Trump attempts to manage another potentially explosive front: Iran.
Trump told Axios over the weekend that his administration is deliberately taking a restrained approach toward Tehran rather than immediately returning to large-scale military action.
“We are low-keying it,” Trump said, describing the United States as “only semi-negotiating” with Iran while allowing sanctions and other economic pressures to bear down on the Iranian government.
The approach represents an effort by the White House to use economic and military pressure without immediately triggering another major round of combat.
Iranian officials, however, dispute the suggestion that formal negotiations have resumed.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said messages are being exchanged through intermediaries and that negotiations cannot fully resume until Tehran’s conditions are addressed.
Those conditions are extensive.
Iran’s Supreme National Security Council has demanded a permanent end to the war, the removal of the U.S. naval blockade on Iranian ports, the withdrawal of American military forces from the region, the lifting of sanctions, the release of frozen Iranian assets and compensation for damage caused during the war.
The demands illustrate just how far Washington and Tehran remain from a comprehensive settlement despite Trump’s suggestion that some form of limited communication is underway.
Iran Shakes Up National Security Leadership
Iran is also reorganizing its senior security leadership as the standoff continues.
Iranian state media reported Sunday that Mohsen Rezaei, a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and military adviser to Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, has been named to lead the country’s powerful Supreme National Security Council.
The appointment represents another major personnel change inside an Iranian government that has lost several senior political and military figures during the conflict.
Rezaei is a longtime figure inside Iran’s military and political establishment, and his elevation places a former Revolutionary Guard commander at the center of Tehran’s response to the United States, Israel and the continuing Strait of Hormuz crisis.
Strait of Hormuz Remains at Center of Crisis
One of the biggest unresolved issues is the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and one of the world’s most strategically important energy corridors.
Iran and Oman are reportedly close to finalizing a temporary maritime arrangement that could allow ships to resume movement through portions of the strait.
Under the proposal, vessels would enter near Iran and exit near Oman without paying fees or tolls during the interim period. The tentative arrangement has reportedly received support from Gulf Cooperation Council nations and could eventually be announced jointly by Iran, Oman, the United States and the United Nations’ International Maritime Organization.
But Iranian officials are warning that such an agreement would not necessarily amount to the unrestricted reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Araghchi said discussions with Oman over “new maritime routes” were nearing completion but stressed that the arrangement does not mean the strait itself will fully reopen.
The continued uncertainty has kept global energy markets on edge, although crude prices have fallen substantially from their wartime peaks earlier this year.
Brent crude was trading around $83.50 per barrel Monday, according to Reuters, significantly below the levels above $110 seen during the height of the Hormuz disruption this spring.
Houthis Launch New Attacks
While Washington, Jerusalem and Tehran maneuver diplomatically, the danger of the conflict spreading through Iranian-aligned proxy forces remains significant.
Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen carried out another wave of drone and missile attacks over the weekend, targeting both Yemen’s Red Sea coast and Saudi Arabia.
The Houthis attacked the government-held port city of Mocha, also known as al-Makha, in repeated strikes Sunday.
Yemeni government-aligned forces said four troops and three civilians were killed in one of the attacks, with additional civilians wounded.
The Houthis also claimed responsibility for a drone attack targeting an Aramco refinery in Jazan, Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry confirmed that a fire occurred at a facility connected to the refinery but reported no casualties and did not immediately attribute the fire to the Houthi strike.
The attacks underscore the fragile state of a region where several interconnected conflicts are now unfolding simultaneously.
For Trump, the diplomatic challenge is increasingly complicated.
His administration is trying to prevent renewed full-scale fighting with Iran, restore commercial traffic through one of the world’s most important shipping corridors and advance a Gaza agreement, all while one of America’s closest allies in the region has now publicly rejected a centerpiece of the president’s peace proposal.
Netanyahu, however, appears unwilling to compromise on what he views as Israel’s most fundamental security condition.
Before Israeli troops leave Gaza, he says, Hamas must first give up its guns.
For now, that disagreement leaves Trump’s Gaza plan stalled, and another major Middle East negotiation hanging in the balance.

sources.news_title: Israel’s Netanyahu formally rejects Trump’s Gaza peace plan
Israeli PM Netanyahu rejects 15-point, U.S.-backed Gaza plan, demands full Hamas disarmament
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu officially rejected a 15-point U.S.-backed Gaza proposal on Sunday, asserting that Israeli forces will not retreat from the enclave until Hamas completely surrenders its arsenal. Speaking at a cabinet meeting, Netanyahu stated that “Israel rejects the 15-point document” and emphasized that the military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens”.
The initiative, championed by President Trump, outlined a phased framework in which Israeli forces would pull back in conjunction with the gradual disarmament of militant factions in Gaza. However, Israeli leadership has firmly opposed any simultaneous timeline, insisting that the complete dismantlement of Hamas’s weapons must precede any military pullout or regional reconstruction. Clarifying the government’s stance, Netanyahu added, “When I say Hamas must be disarmed, I mean heavy weapons, lighter weapons, all weaponry. We are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament”.
In response, Hamas representatives maintained that any negotiations regarding its weapons remain contingent on an immediate cessation of Israeli strikes and a complete troop retreat. The militant group indicated it had agreed to transfer arms to a transitional Palestinian governing body under international oversight, but stressed that execution depends on Israel fulfilling earlier obligations. Calling on Washington to intervene, Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim stated, “We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons”.
The public disagreement underscores widening policy friction between Washington and Jerusalem ahead of Israel’s upcoming parliamentary elections. Facing political pressure from coalition partners who strongly reject concessions or a pathway toward Palestinian sovereignty, Netanyahu reaffirmed his opposition, stating that “as long as I am Prime Minister, there will be no Palestinian State”. While affirming ongoing diplomatic talks with American counterparts, the prime minister emphasized that Israel remains prepared to stand firm on its core security requirements regardless of external expectations.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu rejects Trump’s plan for disarming Hamas
sources.text:
Netanyahu rejects Trump’s plan for disarming Hamas
TEL AVIV, Israel — The Israeli government has rejected a 15-point plan backed by the Trump administration aimed at disarming the Palestinian militant group Hamas in the Gaza Strip, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday.
It appeared to be an unusually public break with President Donald Trump, whose relationship with Netanyahu has had a dizzying and often unpredictable arc. The two leaders launched the war against Iran together in late February. But they have since clashed over how to end it, as well as over the future of Israel’s military campaigns in Gaza and Lebanon.
Trump announced the agreement between his Board of Peace and Hamas late last month, lauding it as a major breakthrough. Netanyahu’s office had initially expressed reservations, saying that the framework did “not reflect Israel’s positions,” but stopped short of rejecting it outright.
The U.S.-backed proposal envisions a phased process in which Hamas would hand over its weapons in stages to a new Palestinian administration in Gaza. In exchange, Israel would gradually withdraw from the more than half of Gaza that it has controlled since the ceasefire in October.
On Sunday, Netanyahu openly dismissed the plan, saying that Israeli forces “would not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed.” He said that meant “heavy weapons, lighter weapons, all weapons,” adding, “We are talking about real disarmament.”
At a Cabinet meeting of government ministers, Netanyahu said, “I want to be clear here: Israel is ruling out the 15-point document.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Trump administration officials had hoped the deal could break nearly a year of deadlock in the devastated Gaza Strip. Despite last year’s ceasefire, many of Gaza’s 2 million residents are still living in sprawling tent camps, as Israel has said there will be no wide-scale reconstruction before Hamas disarms.
Israelis are skeptical that Hamas intends to follow through on its commitments, as the Palestinian militants see armed struggle as part of the group’s raison d’être. And for Netanyahu, any potential concessions in Gaza would come at a politically delicate moment.
He faces an uphill election campaign this fall — the first national vote since Hamas’ deadly attack of Oct. 7, 2023, ignited the devastating war in Gaza. Despite Netanyahu’s repeated pledges to secure “absolute victory,” Hamas still controls parts of Gaza nearly three years later.
The deal with Hamas followed months of delicate talks between its leaders in exile and officials from Trump’s Board of Peace, a new body established to oversee the Gaza ceasefire. The board includes heads of state, including Netanyahu, and is headed by Trump.
In practice, however, a small number of Trump appointees led the negotiations, including Nickolay Mladenov, a former U.N. Mideast envoy. The U.S.-backed negotiators sought to find a formula that would relieve Hamas of its weapons but that the militant group would still accept.
A Board of Peace official said that despite Netanyahu’s comments, the board was still seeing Israeli cooperation on the ground in Gaza, such as Israel’s easing of near-daily strikes in Gaza. The official requested anonymity to speak candidly.
On Sunday, Husam Badran, a senior Hamas official, argued that Netanyahu’s refusal to move ahead with the 15-point plan showed that Israel, rather than the Palestinian group, was the main obstacle to advancing it.
According to the text of the accord, Israel would first have to fulfill several outstanding conditions from the initial ceasefire with Hamas in October which ended the two-year war in Gaza, including a “cessation of military operations.”
Despite the ceasefire, Israel has continued attacks in Gaza, killing more than 1,000 people since October, according to Palestinian health officials. Those killed have included senior Hamas officials, but also civilians, including children.
Israeli bombardment intensified the weekend after the deal was concluded, with at least 20 people killed, Gaza health officials said.
But those attacks largely ceased after Mladenov met with Netanyahu last Monday. Mladenov had criticized the strikes, which he said had “killed civilians and destroyed medical supplies that people depend on.”
Under the Trump plan, an international committee was supposed to verify Israel’s compliance with the ceasefire reached in October. Hamas would then “decommission and store” heavy weapons as part of a process overseen by a group of U.S.-backed Palestinian technocrats.
Israel would gradually withdraw from Gaza, and Palestinian militias armed by Israel to fight Hamas would similarly give up their weapons.
The timeline, along with other details, has yet to be negotiated. The 15-point agreement specifies that the timetable for disarmament ought to be concluded within 14 days after all parties approve the deal. It is unclear whether that can be realized given the doubts hanging over the deal.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu says Trump’s new Gaza plan is unacceptable
sources.text:
Netanyahu says Trump’s new Gaza plan is unacceptable
JERUSALEM/CAIRO — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu restated his rejection of Donald Trump’s latest Gaza plan in televised remarks to his right-wing government on Sunday, even as Israel’s military has effectively halted attacks in the territory under pressure from the U.S. President.
Netanyahu is struggling in the polls as he seeks re-election at a vote due on October 27 but is caught between far-right ministers angered by concessions in Gaza and his key military backer, Trump, who wants progress toward ending the conflict there with a new 15-point roadmap.
ADVERTISING
Israel has scaled back attacks in Gaza since Monday, when Nikolay Mladenov, the Gaza envoy for Trump’s Board of Peace that oversees the ceasefire, met with Netanyahu.
A source familiar with Israel’s position said it had agreed that the military would only act against what it perceives as immediate threats in Gaza and no longer carry out targeted assassinations as it had been doing on a near-daily basis.
Mladenov said on Sunday that discussions on the new roadmap were ongoing.
Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough in his plan to end the war, to which both Israel and Hamas agreed, with Israeli forces withdrawing as Hamas disarms and an International Stabilization Force working with a new Palestinian police force to secure the enclave.
But complications have swiftly emerged with questions over the plan’s timeline. “Israel does not accept the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at the start of a meeting with cabinet ministers. The military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed … it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry.
Netanyahu made similar remarks in a social media post on Tuesday and Israeli officials have said reservations have been shared with Washington.
He added that Israel was in talks with the United States on the plan. “They (the U.S.) have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us and we know how to stand firm against these things,” Netanyahu said.
In an interview with Israeli N12 News, Mladenov said Israel would be required to withdraw “sector by sector” once weapons have been taken from Hamas and rendered unusable.
Basem Naim, a senior Hamas official, told Reuters on Sunday that the group remained committed to the roadmap agreed in Cairo 10 days ago.
“We expect the mediators and the U.S. guarantor to press Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons,” he said.
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich praised Netanyahu. “We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas,” he said in a statement. “The (military) cannot withdraw even a millimeter from the Gaza Strip.”
Trump said last month that Iran-backed Hamas, which ruled Gaza for nearly two decades before carrying out the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel that triggered the Gaza war, had agreed to lay down its weapons.
Hamas avoids the use of the term “disarmament” and said the group agreed to hand over weapons to be stored under a U.S.-backed Palestinian technocrat administration that would run the affairs in Gaza under the supervision of Trump’s Board of Peace.
Hamas said it agreed to the plan to avoid a resumption of war, but it added that the implementation of the deal would depend on Israel first meeting its own commitments, including withdrawal and halting attacks.
Israel had vowed to hunt down militants who had taken part in the October 2023 attack before halting the targeted attacks on Monday.
Since the U.S.-mediated ceasefire reached in October 2025, more than 1,250 people have been killed in the Israeli attacks, most of them civilians, according to Gaza health officials. Hamas has not disclosed the number of its fighters killed. Four Israeli soldiers have been killed in this time in Gaza.
Israeli troops have occupied and depopulated two-thirds of the enclave, leaving nearly all its more than 2 million residents confined to a tiny strip of land under Hamas control along the coast, most in makeshift tents or damaged buildings.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu Rejects Gaza Board of Peace Plan: 'No Withdrawal Unless Hamas is Disarmed'
sources.text:
Netanyahu Rejects Gaza Board of Peace Plan: 'No Withdrawal Unless Hamas is Disarmed'
JERUSALEM, Israel – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the 15-point plan outlined by President Trump's Gaza Board of Peace intended to create conditions for a full Israeli withdrawal and disarm Hamas.
Netanyahu announced on Sunday, "The IDF (Israel Defense Forces) will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say disarming Hamas, it means the heavy weapons, the less heavy weapons, and the light weapons, all the weapons, and we are talking about real disarmament, not a fictitious disarmament."
The prime minister added, "Additionally, the IDF will continue to thwart threats against our forces and citizens. Because once again, the existence of Israel and the security of all Israeli citizens is not up for negotiation."
The White House is reported not to be worried about Netanyahu's refusal. In an interview with Israel's Channel 12, Gaza Board of Peace representative Nickolay Mladenov noted, "Nobody is required to do anything, last of all, Israel, before we actually have verified steps on the ground."
Hamas claims that is never going to happen.
Ten days ago, a Hamas representative in Iran, Khaled Qaddoumi, was asked on Iranian television if the group would disarm, In a response translated and posted by MEMRI, he replied, "Never. Armed resistance is considered legitimate under international law, because we are living under occupation."

Regarding Iran, Netanyahu indicated that he appreciates President Trump, but insisted that Israel will take care of Iran's nuclear threat on its own, if need be.
He stated, "And I want to emphasize once again: with or without an agreement, as long as I am Prime Minister, Iran will not possess nuclear weapons."
Iran's Supreme National Security Council and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) set preconditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, including full compensation for war damages, lifting all sanctions, releasing frozen assets, and withdrawing U.S. forces from the region..
They also demand that the U.S.
- ["N]ever threaten nor insult Iran in any language."
- "[P]ermanently end the war against Iran and Iran's allies in Lebanon, Gaza, Yemen, and Iraq."
- Lift the naval blockade and withdraw military forces from the surroundings of Iran.
In an ABC interview with George Stephanopolous, former Defense Secretary Mark Esper says Iran's demands show they believe they have the upper hand.
"They are emboldened and it shows what we're up against after five and a half months of conflict."
At the same time, Iran facing 88 percent inflation. President trump observed in an interview with Axios, "We are low-keying it with Iran."
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed a defense pact on Friday, essentially agreeing to band together if any one of them is attacked. Shortly thereafter, Pakistan's defense minister told a local news outlet that "Israel is a threat to the entire Muslim world."
He called for a "united military front" against the Jewish state.
Analyst Jonathan Conricus from the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies told CBN News that the alliance calls into question Turkey's loyalty to NATO and whether the U.S. should supply Ankara with advanced American weaponry.
"I think it’s a worrying sign, three countries that allegedly are aligned with the U.S. but are breaking out and deciding to form a separate military strategic alliance. For me, it makes me question their loyalty toward the United States of America."
Conricus added, "And I wonder why Turkey, a significant and lauded NATO member, needs to be in yet another military alliance."

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump’s peace plan for Gaza, says PM Netanyahu
sources.text:
Israel rejects Trump’s peace plan for Gaza, says PM Netanyahu
Tel Aviv would not withdraw its forces from the territory until Hamas is ‘genuinely’ disarmed, the prime minister said.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday reiterated his rejection of United States President Donald Trump’s peace plan for Gaza, saying that Tel Aviv would not withdraw its forces from the territory until Hamas is “genuinely” disarmed, Reuters reported.
His remarks came even as the Israeli military has largely halted attacks in Gaza under pressure from Trump. Nikolay Mladenov, the Gaza envoy for Trump’s Board of Peace, said on Sunday that talks on the new roadmap to ending the conflict were still ongoing after meeting Netanyahu on Monday.
On July 30, Trump announced that the so-called Board of Peace had arrived at an agreement for the “complete disarmament” of Palestinian militant group Hamas and “all other armed” organisations operating in Gaza.
A day later, Hamas had said that it had agreed to the proposal, which would entail the group handing over its weapons and Israeli forces gradually withdrawing from the Gaza Strip.
The disarmament of Hamas had been among the sticking points in the peace deal moving forward.
The agreement will be carried out in phases, Trump said. “As disarmament is completed, Israeli forces will withdraw, and the International Stabilization Force will work with a new Palestinian police force to take responsibility for Gaza being safe for its residents and its neighbours,” he added.
Israel’s military offensive in Gaza began in October 2023 after Hamas killed 1,200 persons during its incursion into southern Israel and took hostages. Israel has been carrying out unprecedented air and ground strikes on Gaza since then, leaving more than 73,300 persons dead.
In September, the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry said that Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
In June, commission said that the Israeli military had deliberately targeted and killed Palestinian children to commit a genocide. The Israeli forces have killed more than 20,000 children and injured 44,000 since October 2023, the panel said.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump Gaza plan, demands Hamas disarmament
sources.text:
Gaza Strip: Israel on Sunday, August 9, rejected a Gaza deal announced by US President Donald Trump, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu saying Israeli forces will not withdraw from the Palestinian enclave until Hamas is “genuinely disarmed”.
Netanyahu told a Cabinet meeting that “Israel rejects the 15-point document”, while stressing that discussions with Washington on plans for Gaza would continue.
“Israel’s military will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed,” Netanyahu said.
Trump had proposed an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza linked to the completion of Hamas’ disarmament. Israeli forces currently control more than half of the Palestinian enclave, which has a population of around 2 million and has suffered widespread destruction during the war.
There was no immediate response from the White House to Netanyahu’s latest comments.
A member of the Hamas political bureau, Bassem Naim, said the group remained committed to the proposed roadmap.
“We remain committed to the road map,” Naim said, adding that Hamas expects mediators and the US to put pressure on Netanyahu.
Netanyahu is also facing domestic political pressure as he seeks to maintain his coalition ahead of Israel’s next elections, scheduled for October 27.
The Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, triggered the Gaza war. A fragile ceasefire remains in place, while negotiations continue over the enclave’s future and the conditions for a lasting settlement.

sources.news_title: No pull out from Gaza before Hamas disarms: Netanyahu
sources.text:
Tel Aviv - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday restated his rejection of Donald Trump’s latest Gaza plan in televised remarks to his right-wing government, even as Israel’s military has effectively halted attacks in the territory under pressure from the US president.
Netanyahu is in campaign mode as he seeks re-election at a vote due on October 27 but is caught between far-right ministers angered by concessions in Gaza and his key military backer, Trump, who wants progress toward ending the conflict there with a new 15-point peace plan.
Israel has scaled back attacks in Gaza since Monday, when Nikolay Mladenov, the Gaza envoy for Trump’s Board of Peace that oversees the Gaza ceasefire, met with Netanyahu. A source familiar with Israel’s position said it had agreed that the military would only act against what it perceives as immediate threats in Gaza and no longer carry out targeted assassinations as it had been doing on a near-daily basis.
Israel and Hamas disagree over timings in Trump’s plan
Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough in his plan to end the war, to which both Israel and Hamas agreed, with Israeli forces withdrawing as Hamas disarms and an International Stabilisation Force working with a new Palestinian police force to secure the enclave. But complications have swiftly emerged. Israel has said that Israeli troops in Gaza would not move before Hamas disarms. Hamas has insisted that Israel halt attacks before it begins implementing the part of the agreement dealing with its arms.
“Israel does not accept the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at the start of a meeting with cabinet ministers. The military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed ... it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry.
“And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament,” he said, noting that Israel is in talks with the United States on the plan. Netanyahu made similar remarks in a social media post on Tuesday. “They (the US) have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us,” Netanyahu said without elaborating. Basem Naim, a senior Hamas official, told news wire on Sunday that the group remained committed to the roadmap agreed with mediators in Cairo 10 days ago. “We expect the mediators and the US guarantor to press Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons, while continuing to jeopardise the region’s security and stability.”
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich praised Netanyahu.
“We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas,” he said in a statement. “The (military) cannot withdraw even a milimetre from the Gaza Strip. The Gaza Strip cannot begin any process of reconstruction before the complete dismantling and demobilisation of Hamas and the Gaza Strip.”
Trump said last month that Iran-backed Hamas, which ruled Gaza for nearly two decades before carrying out the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel that triggered the Gaza war, had agreed to lay down its weapons.
Hamas avoids the use of the term “disarmament” and said the group agreed to hand over weapons to be stored under a US-backed Palestinian technocrat administration that would run the affairs in Gaza under the supervision of Trump’s Board of Peace.
Hamas said it agreed to the plan in order to spare the people in Gaza a possible resumption of war, but it added that the implementation of the deal would depend on Israel first meeting its own commitments, including withdrawal.
Since the US-mediated agreement reached in October to end the war, Israel vowed to hunt down everyone who had taken part in the October 2023 attack before stopping the targeted attacks on Monday.
More than 1,250 people have been killed in the Israeli attacks since the ceasefire, most of them civilians, according to Gaza health officials. Hamas has not disclosed the number of its fighters killed.
Israeli troops have occupied and depopulated two-thirds of the enclave, leaving nearly all its more than two million residents confined to a tiny strip of land under Hamas control along the coast, most in makeshift tents or damaged buildings.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu Rejects Gaza Plan: Israel Won’t Withdraw Until Hamas Is ‘Genuinely Disarmed’
sources.text:
Netanyahu Rejects Gaza Plan: Israel Won’t Withdraw Until Hamas Is ‘Genuinely Disarmed’
Authored by Tom Gantert via The Epoch Times,
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu restated on Aug. 9 that Israel has rejected U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace’s plan for Gaza and will not withdraw until Hamas is fully disarmed.
Trump posted on Truth Social in July that an agreement had been reached for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.
Trump said the agreement is part of his plan that will be implemented in phases. As disarmament takes place, Israeli forces would withdraw, while an International Stabilization Force and a new Palestinian police force would assume responsibility for security.
Gaza would ultimately be governed by a new Palestinian government working with the Board of Peace.
The Board of Peace is an international organization chaired by Trump that seeks to promote stability, establish lawful governance, and secure lasting peace in areas affected by conflict. Its founding members include the United States, Israel, Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and more than 20 other countries committed to international peace-building efforts, according to its website.
Speaking at the start of a government meeting on Aug. 9, Netanyahu said disarmament must include all of Hamas’s weapons and must be genuine rather than “fictitious.”
He said Israel is discussing the issue with the United States and that some U.S. proposals are acceptable to Israel, while others are not.
Netanyahu also said Israeli forces would continue acting against threats to Israeli troops and civilians.
He rejected the establishment of a Palestinian state.
“As for the Gaza Strip: First and foremost, I wish to clarify the main point: As long as I am Prime Minister, a Palestinian state will not be established, neither in Gaza nor in Judea and Samaria,” Netanyahu said in a statement.
He also addressed Iran and Lebanon, pledging to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and saying Israel is conducting an important military operation in Lebanon aimed at eliminating threats.
Israel has been conducting operations in Lebanon.
Two Israeli reservists were killed and four others were seriously wounded during operations recently in southern Lebanon, according to the Israeli military. Lebanese authorities said an Israeli strike also killed one person and wounded 12 others in the town of Tibnin, Lebanon.
Israel gave an evacuation warning to residents before the strike.
The incidents come as the United States conducts talks aimed at reducing hostilities along the Israel-Lebanon border and advancing a broader peace agreement. U.S. officials said the discussions include the disarmament of Hezbollah and other Iran-backed threats, the redeployment of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon, and the implementation of a pilot zone process transferring security responsibilities to the Lebanese army.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump's Board of Peace plan for Gaza
sources.text:
Donald Trump's 15-point peace plan for Gaza has been rejected by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has vowed not to pull back his offensive on Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.
A long-term peace solution appeared to be an increasing possibility last month, when Trump's Board of Peace announced it had secured an agreement for a "completed disarmament" among Gazan armed groups, including Hamas.
But Hamas insists any moves to demobilise will depend on Israel pulling out of Gaza entirely and stopping "all forms of aggression", leading once again to a stalemate, BBC News reports.
Despite agreeing to a ceasefire last October, Israel has continued to rain down drone strikes on Gaza.
In a cabinet meeting on Sunday, Netanyahu categorically state that "Israel rejects the 15-point document", adding that the military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens".
Netanyahu is said to have hesitated for some time before rejecting the deal, keen not to alienate the US - which stands as Israel’s most important international ally.
The Israeli Prime Minister said he was holding meetings with US officials to discuss a path forward, adding: "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters."
Israel is due to hold elections within the next few months and Netanyahu is reportedly under pressure from members of his right-wing coalition to take a hard line on Gaza.
Elsewhere, a Hamas spokesman told the BBC that the group is ready to reaffirm its commitment to the ceasefire deal and is ready to "engage seriously and responsibly" in the 15-point plan.
Hamas has also called for mediators to enter negotiations in order to be sure "that all parties comply with what has been agreed".
Read More
Trump’s Board of Peace has been promoting the 15-point plan since September last year and Netanyahu’s rejection of the deal is deemed a significant blow.
The strategy included the creation of a Board of Peace to maintain peace in the region, disarmament of Hamas and the removal of Israeli soldiers as well as a large-scale rebuilding scheme for Gaza.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu rejects Trump’s Gaza plan in rare public break with US president
sources.text:
JERUSALEM, Aug 10 — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu yesterday rejected a US-led Gaza plan endorsed by Hamas, putting distance between himself and President Donald Trump as he tries to shore up his base ahead of close elections.
After more than a week of gradually escalating criticism of the plan, and despite receiving assurances that Israel would not need to start withdrawing in Gaza immediately, Netanyahu explicitly opposed the deal following pushback from his right-wing allies.
“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said, referring to the plan Hamas agreed to in late July.
The Israeli military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed, and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens”, he told a cabinet meeting.
Netanyahu described Trump, who had hailed the Gaza deal as a milestone for peace, as “our greatest friend in the White House” — but quickly made clear he was willing to challenge him, saying Israel was raising its objections with the United States.
“They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters,” he said.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader, is running even or trailing in some polls ahead of October 27 elections, the country’s first since the devastating October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas that sparked the Gaza war.
Polls show that the Gaza plan is unpopular with Netanyahu’s right-wing base, and far-right members of his cabinet have urged him to kill it.
‘Only way forward’
The head of Trump’s body implementing the plan, dubbed the Board of Peace, defended the plan as a way to prevent a repeat of October 7.
“The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again,” Nickolay Mladenov, the board’s high representative for Gaza, told Israel’s Channel 12 television.
He said he hoped for a “positive outcome” from follow-up discussions with Israel, and characterised the latest stage of the deal as a commitment involving the United States, Hamas and the Board of Peace — notably leaving out Israel.
Mladenov again promised that Israel would not face any obligations until Hamas gave up all its weapons, down to Kalashnikov rifles — but said Israel would eventually need to pull out.
Hamas, which publicly backed the plan days after selecting a new leader, Khalil al-Hayya, called on Washington to push Netanyahu.
“We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap, and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons,” Bassem Naim, a member of Hamas’s political bureau, told AFP.
Hamas in a statement said it was still committed to the plan.
Friction with Trump
Netanyahu until recently campaigned on the strength of his relationship with Trump, who has taken unprecedented steps to back Israel, including moving the US embassy to Jerusalem.
Trump joined Netanyahu in late February in launching a war against Iran, but the two diverged when Trump sought a ceasefire and subsequent settlement to the conflict as it sapped his popularity and sent oil prices soaring.
Netanyahu told his cabinet that “with an agreement or without an agreement, as long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons”, a goal he has long alleged Tehran is pursuing.
Netanyahu last week also ordered fresh strikes on Lebanon in response to what Israel called a ceasefire violation by Iran-backed Hezbollah, just as Israel and Lebanon were holding US-mediated talks.
The Gaza plan was the latest stage in a US-brokered ceasefire announced in October that has reduced, but not ended, Israeli operations there.
Despite Netanyahu’s stance, Israel appears to have decreased operations in Gaza since the deal was announced, without halting them completely.
Israeli gunfire yesterday injured several people including a child who was taken to hospital in Khan Yunis, civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal told AFP.
Israeli operations in Gaza have killed 1,258 Palestinians since the ceasefire, according to the territory’s health ministry, which operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
The Israeli army has reported five deaths in its ranks during the same period. — AFP

sources.news_title: Israeli PM Netanyahu Rejects "Gaza Roadmap"
Israel rejects Trump’s Gaza plan, more details emerge on the Strait of Hormuz and other Mideast news - Regional Media News
sources.text:
(AP) – Israel has rejected a proposed Gaza deal announced by President Donald Trump, drawing a clear line in the sand: Israel will not pull back until Hamas is genuinely disarmed. At a Cabinet meeting, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dismissed what he called the “15-point document,” emphasizing that Israel’s military will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed in reality-not in promises.
Netanyahu also said Israel is still discussing plans for Gaza with Washington, suggesting negotiations continue even as the current proposal has been rejected outright. A fragile ceasefire is still holding, but Israeli control remains heavy across the Palestinian enclave-about half of the territory-after a war that has devastated large parts of Gaza. Hamas, for its part, insists the “road map” remains the path forward and expects mediators-and the United States-to pressure Netanyahu.
But tensions between Israel and Hamas remain unresolved, and now it’s the Trump administration’s challenge to manage. The administration backed the peace framework and helped build momentum around it, but its closest regional ally says the plan has not yet met Prime Minister Netanyahu’s core demand: that Hamas fully disarm before Israeli forces withdraw from Gaza.
Meanwhile, the Middle East security picture is growing more dangerous on multiple fronts. Iran has again reshuffled leadership at the top of its Supreme National Security Council, naming Mohsen Rezaei to replace Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr. This is part of a broader pattern of changes among Iran’s senior ranks as the country adjusts to losses during the war.
Iran’s posture toward the Strait of Hormuz also remains firm. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says negotiations with Oman over “new maritime routes” are in late stages, but he stressed that the strait does not automatically “reopen.” He pointed to conditions that, according to Iran, have been communicated through intermediaries.
Those conditions are sweeping: Iran is demanding that the United States correct its behavior, end hostilities, lift naval restrictions on Iranian ports, remove sanctions, withdraw U.S. forces from the region, and compensate Iran for war damage-while also unfreezing assets and ending threats.
In parallel, reports suggest Iran and Oman are working to finalize a temporary arrangement tied to managing the strait. The reported framework would allow ships to enter near Iran and exit near Oman without paying fees during the interim period. But key restrictions are emerging as well: a preliminary plan outlined by Iran’s security and parliamentary structures indicates that vessels connected to “hostile countries” would be barred unless Iran receives compensation for past harm.
And in Yemen, Iranian-backed Houthi forces struck a government-held port on the Red Sea coast. That escalation deepens fears about interference with strategic shipping lanes-exactly the kind of instability that threatens global commerce and reinforces the need for strong deterrence.
Bottom line: while diplomats talk, regional actors keep preparing for confrontation. Israel is refusing to move without real disarmament. Iran is demanding major concessions. And dangerous attacks around the Red Sea continue. In times like these, American leadership-and credible strength-are not optional.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu, at odds with Trump, rejects Gaza peace plan
sources.text:
Netanyahu, at odds with Trump, rejects Gaza peace plan
August 10, 2026
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday rejected US President Donald Trump's plan for Gaza, saying Israeli troops would not withdraw from the territory until Hamas was fully disarmed.
"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu told a Cabinet meeting, referring to the US-backed roadmap agreed to by Hamas in late July.
The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed," Netanyahu said, adding that this included "heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry."
Netanyahu said Israel remained in talks with Washington despite its objections. He described Trump as "our greatest friend in the White House," but added: "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters."
The White House did not immediately comment.
What does Trump's Gaza plan say about Hamas disarmament?
Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough on a 15-point roadmap aimed at ending the war in the Gaza Strip.
The plan drawn up by his Board of Peace calls for Israeli troops to withdraw as Hamas gives up its weapons. An International Stabilization Force would then work alongside a new Palestinian police force to secure Gaza.
Hamas is designated as a terrorist organization by Israel, the United States, the European Union and several other countries.
The group has avoided using the term "disarmament." It says it agreed to hand over its weapons for storage under a US-backed Palestinian technocratic administration that would govern Gaza under the supervision of the Board of Peace.
Hamas has said implementation also depends on Israel meeting its obligations, including withdrawing troops and halting attacks.
"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap, and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," Hamas political bureau member Bassem Naim said.
Hamas said Sunday it remained committed to the roadmap.
Gaza plan rejected by Netanyahu 'only way forward':
Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza, said Israel would face no obligations until Hamas had surrendered all its weapons, including assault rifles.
However, Mladenov told Israel's Channel 12 that Israeli troops would eventually have to withdraw "sector by sector" once Hamas' weapons had been collected and rendered unusable.
"The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again," he said, referring to the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, which triggered the war against Hamas in the Gaza Strip.
Mladenov said discussions with Israel were continuing and that he hoped for a "positive outcome."
How are Israel's elections affecting Netanyahu's Gaza policy?
The disagreement comes at a politically sensitive moment for Netanyahu ahead of elections scheduled for October 27, Israel's first national vote since the Hamas led attacks that sparked an ongoing Israeli military campaign in Gaza.
The prime minister is running level with or behind rivals in some polls and faces pressure from far-right members of his government who oppose concessions to Hamas.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich welcomed Netanyahu's position.
"We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas," he said. "The [military] cannot withdraw even a millimetre from the Gaza Strip."
The dispute is the latest sign of differences between Netanyahu and Trump. The two leaders are considered as close allies, but have recently disagreed over how to deal with the conflicts in Iran, Lebanon and Gaza.
The Gaza roadmap builds on a US-mediated ceasefire reached in October 2025.
Gaza health officials say more than 1,250 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since then. The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed during the same period.
Despite the ongoing negotiations over the roadmap, Israeli forces continue to control large parts of Gaza, while most of the enclave's more than 2 million residents have been displaced and are living in a much smaller coastal area, many in tents or damaged buildings.
Edited by: Louis Oelofse

sources.text:
Netanyahu Rejects Gaza Plan: Israel Won't Withdraw Until Hamas Is 'Genuinely Disarmed'
Authored by Tom Gantert via The Epoch Times,
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu restated on Aug. 9 that Israel has rejected U.S. President Donald Trump's Board of Peace's plan for Gaza and will not withdraw until Hamas is fully disarmed.
Trump posted on Truth Social in July that an agreement had been reached for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.
Trump said the agreement is part of his plan that will be implemented in phases. As disarmament takes place, Israeli forces would withdraw, while an International Stabilization Force and a new Palestinian police force would assume responsibility for security.
Gaza would ultimately be governed by a new Palestinian government working with the Board of Peace.
The Board of Peace is an international organization chaired by Trump that seeks to promote stability, establish lawful governance, and secure lasting peace in areas affected by conflict. Its founding members include the United States, Israel, Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and more than 20 other countries committed to international peace-building efforts, according to its website.
Speaking at the start of a government meeting on Aug. 9, Netanyahu said disarmament must include all of Hamas's weapons and must be genuine rather than "fictitious."
He said Israel is discussing the issue with the United States and that some U.S. proposals are acceptable to Israel, while others are not.
Netanyahu also said Israeli forces would continue acting against threats to Israeli troops and civilians.
He rejected the establishment of a Palestinian state.
"As for the Gaza Strip: First and foremost, I wish to clarify the main point: As long as I am Prime Minister, a Palestinian state will not be established, neither in Gaza nor in Judea and Samaria," Netanyahu said in a statement.
He also addressed Iran and Lebanon, pledging to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and saying Israel is conducting an important military operation in Lebanon aimed at eliminating threats.
Israel has been conducting operations in Lebanon.
Two Israeli reservists were killed and four others were seriously wounded during operations recently in southern Lebanon, according to the Israeli military. Lebanese authorities said an Israeli strike also killed one person and wounded 12 others in the town of Tibnin, Lebanon.
Israel gave an evacuation warning to residents before the strike.
The incidents come as the United States conducts talks aimed at reducing hostilities along the Israel-Lebanon border and advancing a broader peace agreement. U.S. officials said the discussions include the disarmament of Hezbollah and other Iran-backed threats, the redeployment of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon, and the implementation of a pilot zone process transferring security responsibilities to the Lebanese army.

sources.news_title: ACM: Netanyahu says no … what next for Trump “the peace maker”?!
sources.text:
Trump’s Gaza 15 point “peace plan” has fallen apart (quelle surprise) because Netanyahu has said that Israel (which now is occupying 64% of the Gaza Strip, and that Yellow Line keeps moving) will not leave Gaza until Hamas is “genuinely disarmed”. 
You may ask, what does genuinely disarmed actually even mean? Netanyahu is demanding that the Palestinians groups disarm and then, only then, will Israel withdraw from Gaza. But, Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza have agreed to Trump’s so-called peace deal and in July they re-negotiated and agreed that they will gradually disarm as Israel leaves. “This agreement is a critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the Board of Peace to help the Palestinian people,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Thursday.

The National Committee will then oversee the “inventory and storage” process, with the international verification committee observing, and the Palestinian factions participating.”

Since the ceasefire in October 2025, according to Al Jazeera, the Israeli government and military has killed 1,250 people and wounded 4,120; bodies are beginning to be pulled out of the rubble (800 bodies so far). In the July 2026 article, Mohammed Azzam (the mayor of Sebastia), all of these will come under control of Israeli civil authorities:
“Israeli authorities have presented their archaeological work as an innocent search for Jewish history, and as necessary for research and preservation of the site. What we are witnessing is not archaeology for the sake of scientific research,” he said. “It is an attempt to reshape history and impose a new reality through facts on the ground. When historical evidence cannot be altered, the occupation tries to impose its narrative through the barrel of a gun.”

Genocide and Accountability

Look how much credibility as democracies these governments have lost to protect the Israeli government and military.  To throw out all the talking points about how democracies are accountable and allow opposition is an incredible cost.
The genocide in Gaza is literally a textbook case of genocide. Looking at the UN Convention on genocide (1948), of the five types of actions in Article II of the Convention that describe the crime of genocide, the only one which is missing is the fifth (the forcible removal of children and I would argue that is due to racism in political Zionism and the dehumanisation of Palestinians). I am putting this here so that you do know the definition and can judge for yourself. Palestinians have been killed because they are Palestinians, that’s it. 
 
Article II of the Convention on Genocide
In the present Convention, genocide means any of the following acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group, as such:
(a) Killing members of the group;
(b) Causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group;
(c) Deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part;
(d) Imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group;
(e) Forcibly transferring children of the group to another group.” This denial of genocide (and, as such, international law and human rights law) and the refusal to allow the arrest and prosecution of Israeli war criminals has clearly demonstrated that international law, international humanitarian law and human rights law have little meaning in practice.

Is it because countries that still send weapons and money to Israel concerned about how it looks, does it have something to do with maintaining economic and military imperialism in the Middle East?! If US allies have no problems with the genocide in Gaza, why would they care that this is a blow to Trump’s “Board of Peace”? This is obvious, this is self-defence. It is not only military and armed action, there are many ways to sustain a people, but you must have the right to protect yourself and fight for yourself.
If you are having trouble thinking about it, that’s fair; let’s think of some historical struggles, think about the French-Algeria war, think of the long struggle to overthrow Apartheid and white rule in South Africa, think of the overthrow of military dictatorships in Latin America, think of Viet Nam against the French and then the Americans. What we are seeing in the current genocide denial and the nonsense that states have the right to exist (how can we explain the non-existence of Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, the USSR), this is clearly an attempt to blame the victim of 78 years of occupation.
