sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump’s Gaza plan, more details emerge on the Strait of Hormuz
sources.text:
Israel rejects Trump’s Gaza plan, more details emerge on the Strait of Hormuz
(AP) - Israel on Sunday rejected a deal announced by U.S. President Donald Trump for Gaza. Details emerged on the potential deal between Iran and Oman on managing the Strait of Hormuz as Tehran suggested that vessels linked to “hostile countries” would be barred. Iran also shuffled its top security post.
Meanwhile, Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels struck a government-held port on the country’s Red Sea coast, deepening fears over threats to strategic shipping routes and a potential return to civil war.
Here’s a look at developments across the Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
Netanyahu insists no Gaza withdrawal until Hamas disarms
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dismissed the deal on Gaza announced by Trump last month, saying Israel’s military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.”
Netanyahu told a Cabinet meeting that “Israel rejects the 15-point document” but is still discussing plans for Gaza with Washington, after making similar comments last week. Trump had said Israeli forces would withdraw as the Hamas militant group’s disarmament is completed. Israeli forces control over half the Palestinian enclave of about 2 million people that’s been largely destroyed.
There was no immediate White House comment on Netanyahu’s statement.
“We remain committed to the road map,” said a member of the Hamas political bureau, Bassem Naim, adding that the group expects mediators and the U.S. to pressure Netanyahu — who also faces domestic tensions as he struggles to hold onto power ahead of the next elections scheduled for Oct. 27.
The Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, sparked the war in Gaza. A fragile ceasefire continues.
Houthis target Aramco refinery and Red Sea port
Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen attacked the government-held port city of Mocha late Sunday night. It was the second attack on the Red Sea coast city in less than 24 hours.
A Houthi military source told the Houthi-controlled Al-Masirah TV that the attack targeted weapons depots and Saudi troop concentrations.
A statement from the Yemeni Armed Forces posted on X said residential neighborhoods were targeted by ballistic missiles and drones in the attack, and that air defense systems managed to intercept some of the drones.
Drones and missiles were also used during the earlier attack on Sunday. The Yemeni government-allied National Resistance Forces said at least seven people — four troops and three civilians — were killed and 15 civilians were injured in that strike.
Fayed al-Noman, the information ministry’s assistant undersecretary, said the attack severely damaged port buildings and piers as well as commercial goods and food supplies. The military later said missiles landed in several areas, including near a television station.
Mocha is a main port under Yemen’s internationally recognized government and has been renovated to handle shipping that avoids the Houthi-held port of Hodeida.
The Houthis said they targeted military forces and warehouses.
Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesperson, said they also targeted an Aramco refinery in the Saudi city of Jazan with a drone in response to Saudi drones breaching Yemen’s airspace over Hajjah and Saada provinces.
The Saudi Energy Ministry reported a fire at a facility belonging to the Aramco refinery, with no casualties. The ministry did not say the cause. The attacks threaten to reignite Yemen’s civil war after a 2022 truce.
— Samy Magdy in Cairo
Iran’s top security post changes again
Iran named a new head of its powerful Supreme National Security Council, state media reported. Mohsen Rezaei had been a military adviser to Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei and a former Revolutionary Guard commander.
It was the latest shuffle at the top for the politburo-like body, which has a range of political opinions and rivalries and is adapting to the loss of several senior officials in the war.
Rezaei replaces Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who took up the role after Ali Larijani was killed by an Israeli strike in March. Zolghadr will become a political adviser to Khamenei.
Rezaei earlier this month said Iran will never allow an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz, which was considered an international waterway before the war and Tehran’s assertion of control.
Iran says negotiations ‘cannot resume’ until conditions met
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters that negotiations with Oman about “new maritime routes” on the Strait of Hormuz were in the final stages but “this, however, does not mean that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen.” That step requires conditions that “have been conveyed through intermediaries.”
The Supreme National Security Council on Saturday said the strait will not reopen until the U.S. “corrects its behavior.” It demanded that the U.S. never threaten Iran again, a permanent end to the war with Iran and its armed allies, a lifting of the naval blockade of Iranian ports and a withdrawal of the U.S. military from the area. The U.S. also must “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets.
The United States did not comment on the demands. Trump on Sunday asserted to Axios that “we are only semi-negotiating” with Iran and letting economic pressures take their toll.
Araghchi said an “exchange of messages through intermediaries” continues with the U.S. but that doesn’t constitute negotiations, which he said can’t resume until violations of the interim deal end and the U.S. “has remedied” provisions it violated.
Details emerge about a potential Iran-Oman deal
Iran and Oman, located on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz, are working to finalize a temporary deal that would reopen it, with ships entering near Iran and exiting near Oman, according to two people familiar with the talks who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Ships would transit without paying fees or tolls during the interim period.
The agreement is designed to restore the separate interim deal between the U.S. and Iran. The two people said the agreement is endorsed by Gulf Cooperation Council members and is expected to be jointly announced by Iran, Oman, the U.S. and the U.N.’s International Maritime Organization. But they stressed the terms still could change.
The Iranian parliament’s National Security Committee approved “general outlines” of a plan to manage the strait, the state broadcaster reported, but a lawmaker said transits by vessels belonging to “hostile countries” would be prohibited. The member of parliament’s presiding board said countries that have “caused damage” to Iran cannot transit until they compensate for it. There were no further details.
— Michelle Price in Washington and Aamer Madhani in New York

sources.news_title: Netanyahu bluntly rejects Trump’s Gaza plan to disarm Hamas
sources.text:
Netanyahu bluntly rejects Trump’s Gaza plan to disarm Hamas
Jerusalem: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected a proposal by US-backed mediators for disarming Hamas, hardening his position after voicing misgivings at the suggestion that Israel reciprocate with phased withdrawal from Gaza.
“Israel does not accept the 15-point document,” Netanyahu told his weekly cabinet meeting on Sunday (Israel time), according to an official translation. In his original remarks, he used a Hebrew verb that could be understood as “Israel rejects” or “rules out”.
“The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed, and it will continue to thwart threats against our forces and citizens,” Netanyahu added, referring to the Israel Defence Forces.
He was responding to a “roadmap” published last month by the Board of Peace, an international consortium set up to implement US President Donald Trump’s postwar vision for the ravaged Palestinian territory. The president has lauded the roadmap as an “historic agreement” and “a major milestone”.
There was no immediate White House comment on Netanyahu’s statement.
Hamas has given only a hedged consent to the roadmap, saying it would hand over heavy weapons to a proposed new Gaza administration and conditioning this on Israeli withdrawals and the creation of a Palestinian state. The roadmap speaks of the new administration empowering individual Palestinians to keep their small arms.
Trump’s original plan envisaged Israeli troops and tanks leaving the Gaza Strip entirely, and discussions of eventual statehood – while casting these as end results of a complete demilitarisation and post-Hamas stabilisation of the territory.
The Board of Peace sounded circumspect about Netanyahu’s remarks, describing the road map as its deal with Hamas, rather than with Israel – and the timeline as protracted.
“Nobody is required to do anything, last of all lsrael, before we actually have verified steps on the ground” by the Palestinian cadres, the board’s top envoy, Nickolay Mladenov, told Israel’s Channel 12 television.
While predicting that decommissioning Hamas tunnels – another requirement of Trump’s plan – may take years, Mladenov said that with each eventual success in clearing a sector of territory “Israel is required to move back, progressively, step by step, in stages, ultimately to the fence of Gaza”.
The initial, ceasefire phase of the Trump plan was clinched in October. There’s been little diplomatic progress since, and the Israeli army has advanced beyond armistice lines against a shrinking Hamas fiefdom where some 2 million Palestinians are crammed.
Israel launched the war in response to an October 2023 invasion by Hamas that blindsided Netanyahu’s religious-rightist government. Three years on, Netanyahu is hoping for re-election in October. With Hamas still undefeated, he has pointed to Israel’s continued grip on Gaza as a lesser victory.
Far-right ministers in Netanyahu’s coalition have been upset by the roadmap. One of them, Orit Strock, called it a “bloodshed map” in a radio interview before Sunday’s cabinet meeting. Following Netanyahu’s remarks, her party’s leader, Bezalel Smotrich, praised the prime minister for issuing the “clarification”.
Hamas, which is blacklisted as a terrorist group in the West, said it was committed to the roadmap and accused Netanyahu of “obstructing the process for domestic, political and electoral reasons”.
“We expect the mediators and the US guarantor to exert pressure on Netanyahu and his government to compel him to abide by the roadmap,” Hamas negotiator Bassem Naim said in a statement.
A surge of Israeli air strikes in July that targeted Hamas commanders – which also killed dozens of civilians – has ceased since August 3, a tacit sign that Netanyahu heeded Mladenov’s calls not to endanger the diplomacy.
A source familiar with Israel’s position said it had agreed that the military would only act against what it perceives as immediate threats in Gaza and no longer carry out targeted assassinations as it had been doing on a near-daily basis, Reuters reported.
In another signal of potential progress, the Board of Peace on Saturday said it brought together experts to plan temporary housing for displaced Palestinians, an interim measure before the permanent reconstruction that Mladenov has said would require Hamas to disarm first.
Separately, Netanyahu’s office said work was underway on a new tent city, funded by the United Arab Emirates, in an area that the IDF had cleared of Hamas and weaponry.
Bloomberg, AP
Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world. Sign up for our weekly What in the World newsletter.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu Rejects U.S.-Backed Gaza Plan, Says Israeli Troops Will Stay Until Hamas Is Disarmed
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected a 15-point U.S.-backed proposal for the gradual disarmament of Gaza and withdrawal of Israeli forces, saying Israel will not pull back until Hamas has been fully disarmed.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday that Israel will not accept a U.S.-backed 15-point plan governing the disarmament of Gaza and the withdrawal of Israeli troops, putting his government at odds with elements of a proposal developed last month by President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace.
Netanyahu announced the decision during a Cabinet meeting, according to a readout from his office.
“I want to be clear here — Israel is ruling out the 15-point plan,” Netanyahu said.
The proposal calls for Gaza to be gradually disarmed while Israeli forces withdraw from the territory. Netanyahu said he has already communicated Israel’s objections to the Trump administration and made clear that Israeli military withdrawals would depend on Hamas first surrendering its weapons.
The Israeli military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens,” Netanyahu said.
Despite rejecting the existing proposal, Netanyahu indicated that discussions with Washington are continuing.
“We are now discussing this with the Americans,” he said. “They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand up to those things.”
Netanyahu also used the meeting to restate his opposition to the creation of a Palestinian state, extending that position to both Gaza and the West Bank.
“As long as I am prime minister, no Palestinian state will be established — not in Gaza and not in the West Bank,” Netanyahu said.
The dispute over the proposed Gaza framework comes as Netanyahu and his governing coalition prepare for a difficult re-election vote scheduled for late October.
Netanyahu said Israel would continue to make security decisions based on what his government considers necessary, even when those decisions conflict with the positions of close allies.
“Contrary to all those who preach to us, we do what must be done for Israel’s security and we can and will stand our ground even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu added.
Hamas has also attached conditions to the disarmament process. The group has said it would surrender its heavy weapons only if Israel ends “all forms of aggression” and withdraws from Gaza.
Bassem Naim, a member of Hamas’ politburo, called Sunday for outside mediators and the United States to press Netanyahu’s government to follow the proposed roadmap.
“We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons,” Naim said on X Sunday.
Israel has continued conducting strikes in Gaza since the cease-fire reached last October.
Israeli forces currently occupy more than half of the territory, while Netanyahu’s far-right coalition allies have suggested they favor expanding Israeli control.
Those allies welcomed Netanyahu’s rejection of further withdrawal under the proposed plan.
“The [Israeli military] cannot retreat one millimeter in the Gaza Strip,” Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said.

Netanyahu Rejects 15-Point Plan Until Hamas ‘Genuinely’ Disarmed
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday that Israel will not accept the Peace Council’s 15-point plan for the Gaza Strip, insisting that the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) will remain in place until Hamas undergoes genuine disarmament.
Netanyahu told the Cabinet that Israel and the United States were discussing proposals concerning Gaza but said Jerusalem would not agree to measures that contradict its demands regarding Hamas’ weapons.
“The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed,” Netanyahu said.
He said Israel was seeking the actual removal of Hamas’ weapons rather than a process that amounts to what he described as fictitious disarmament.

President Trump’s Board of Peace said last month that an agreement had been reached under which Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza would relinquish their weapons completely. Hamas subsequently made the surrender of its heavy weapons conditional on Israel ending what the group called “all forms of aggression” and withdrawing its forces from the Gaza Strip.
Israeli political leaders have repeatedly said in recent weeks that the IDF will not pull back from the Yellow Line in Gaza.
N12 reported Saturday, however, that Israel’s security establishment has recently considered limited withdrawals by IDF troops from some locations in the Strip. The discussions include proposals for a multinational force to deploy in areas from which Israeli forces withdraw.
A security official questioned whether the proposed multinational force would have sufficient personnel to assume that role.
“The number of soldiers [from the multinational force who will arrive in Israel] is simply not enough. We are talking about a handful of soldiers, and they are trying to build castles on the basis of this force. This is very worrying,” the official said.
“The Americans are not leaving too many options—but they are putting us in a difficult situation in Gaza.”

sources.text: Benjamin Netanyahu has formally rejected Donald Trump’s 15-point Board of Peace roadmap, vowing Israeli troops will not leave Gaza until Hamas gives up every weapon—heavy, light and everything in between. The plan envisioned a phased, internationally verified process: Palestinian technocrats in the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza would take over civil rule while Hamas disarmed and Israel withdrew. But the core dispute is timing. Hamas says strikes must end and troops must pull back as disarmament begins; Netanyahu demands total disarmament first and again rejects Palestinian statehood.

sources.news_title: Israel Rejects Trump’s 15-Point Plan to End the Gaza War
sources.text:
Israel Rejects Trump’s 15-Point Plan To End The Gaza War
Israel · GEOPOLITICS
Key Facts
—Israel’s rejection: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on 9 August 2026 that Israel had rejected Donald Trump’s 15-point Board of Peace plan and would not withdraw until Hamas is fully disarmed.
—The sequencing clash: Washington’s framework ties phased Israeli withdrawal to disarmament and an international transition, while Israel demands “genuine disarmament” first.
—Governance architecture: The plan proposes a technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) and an International Stabilization Force (ISF) to oversee security.
—Reconstruction funding: Trump’s Board of Peace had secured US$7 billion in pledges from member states, with a US$10 billion commitment from the United States, according to NPR.
—Coalition pressure: Police Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called the draft unacceptable and argued that Israel’s policy of assassinating Hamas leaders must continue.
—Hamas position: Hamas had agreed in principle to a phased disarmament roadmap but had not accepted full surrender of weapons on Israel’s terms.
Israel has formally rejected Donald Trump’s 15-point Gaza plan, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insisting that Israeli forces will not withdraw until Hamas is genuinely disarmed, deepening a standoff over the sequencing of any ceasefire.
Netanyahu draws a red line on the 15-point Gaza plan
On 9 August 2026, Reuters reported that Netanyahu told a cabinet meeting Israel had rejected the “Board of Peace” 15-point document. Al Jazeera quoted the prime minister saying the army would not withdraw until Hamas is “genuinely disarmed.”
The New York Times had earlier reported that Netanyahu’s office said the framework did “not reflect Israel’s positions.” The fuller rejection confirmed what weeks of Israeli hesitation had signalled: the plan’s core bargain was unacceptable to the government in Jerusalem.
Israeli officials told Reuters there would be no withdrawal from the Yellow Line until Hamas is disarmed and Gaza is demilitarised. That position effectively freezes the diplomatic track Washington had championed as a breakthrough.
Sequencing versus preconditions: the unbridgeable gap
The fundamental dispute is over sequencing. Trump’s plan envisages a phased withdrawal of Israeli forces linked to Hamas disarmament, supervised by an International Stabilization Force and a technocratic Palestinian administration.
Hamas and mediators want steps to move in parallel, Reuters reported. Israel insists Hamas must first undergo “genuine disarmament” before any pullback begins. That gap has so far proven unbridgeable.
Hamas had agreed in principle to a phased disarmament roadmap, according to Reuters and The Guardian. But it had not accepted full surrender of weapons on Israel’s terms, leaving the two sides far apart on the most sensitive question.
A governance blueprint that reshapes power in Gaza
The plan is not merely a ceasefire document. It is a governance architecture that would replace direct Israeli military control with a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), a technocratic Palestinian interim authority under international supervision.
Trump would chair a Board of Peace overseeing the transition. The BBC published the White House’s 20-point version of the framework, which includes immediate aid entry and reconstruction overseen by international mechanisms.
For Netanyahu’s coalition, this structure is politically explosive. Hardline figures oppose any arrangement that could lead to a durable Palestinian governing structure in Gaza, seeing it as a step toward statehood rather than a temporary administrative fix.
The money behind the 15-point Gaza plan
NPR reported that Trump’s Board of Peace had already secured US$7 billion in reconstruction pledges from member states. The United States committed US$10 billion of its own, giving Washington enormous leverage over Gaza’s post-war political order.
Reconstruction contracts, aid flows, and security coordination are all tied to compliance with the United States-led framework. That funding structure was designed to pull Arab and Muslim states into the arrangement through financial and diplomatic endorsement.
The International Stabilization Force was described by NPR as potentially involving 20,000 soldiers and 12,000 police officers under Major General Jasper Jeffers. Those planning figures underscore the scale of the security operation Washington envisages.
Domestic politics and the coalition calculus
Netanyahu’s rejection cannot be separated from his coalition’s composition. Police Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called the draft unacceptable and argued that Israel’s policy of assassinating Hamas leaders must continue, Reuters reported.
The Guardian and Chatham House both frame the plan as a direct challenge to Israeli extremists. It points toward Palestinian administration and eventual statehood conditional on compliance, not indefinite occupation, which hardline ministers have vowed to prevent.
Any concession that appears to reward Hamas or create a pathway to Palestinian governance risks fracturing the coalition. That domestic reality shapes Israel’s negotiating position as much as any security assessment on the ground.
Great-power stakes and what comes next
The United States is using the Gaza file to anchor a broader regional order combining security guarantees, reconstruction finance, and political conditionality. Israel’s rejection shows that even a Washington-backed framework can be blocked when it conflicts with Israeli domestic politics and battlefield priorities.
Reuters noted the plan had initially been celebrated by Trump, mediators, and Arab states as a breakthrough. Israel’s position was later relayed through officials and allies who insisted it had not signed on, leaving Washington managing both sides simultaneously.
The White House must now pressure Hamas toward demilitarisation while preventing an Israeli collapse of the framework through unilateral military action. For readers tracking how great powers and regional players contest territory and resources, this dynamic fits squarely within the patterns explored in Africa: The New Scramble.
Frequently Asked Questions
Why did Israel reject Trump’s 15-point Gaza plan?
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel would not withdraw until Hamas is genuinely disarmed, rejecting the plan’s phased approach that linked withdrawal to disarmament steps.
What is the Board of Peace in Trump’s Gaza framework?
The Board of Peace is a supervisory body chaired by Donald Trump that would oversee Gaza’s transition, backed by US$7 billion in pledged reconstruction funds and a US$10 billion United States commitment.
What does the International Stabilization Force propose to do in Gaza?
The proposed International Stabilization Force would work alongside a new Palestinian police force to provide security during the transition, with planning figures suggesting up to 20,000 soldiers and 12,000 police officers.

sources.news_title: Israeli government rejects Trump's Gaza peace plan
sources.text:
Israeli government rejects Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan
In short:
Israeli Prime Minster Benjamin Netanyahu says Hamas's proposed plan for disarming is "unacceptable", rejecting the Trump administration's plans to end fighting in the Palestinian territory.
Announcing the deal last week, US President Donald Trump claimed Israel was "very happy" about it.
But the deal has been sharply criticised by members of the Israeli establishment.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has expressly rejected the latest Trump administration-backed push for peace in Gaza, criticising Hamas's proposed process for disarming as "unacceptable".
Speaking ahead of his weekly Sunday cabinet meeting, Mr Netanyahu said his government was in discussions with the United States on the matter and acknowledged the two countries had differing views.
"They have ideas, some of them are acceptable to us and some are unacceptable to us," he said.
"Israel rejects the 15-point plan.
"The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until the dismantling of Hamas and its weapons. And when I say dismantling Hamas and its weapons, that means heavy weaponry, less heavy weaponry and smaller arms, all weaponry.
"We're talking about a true dismantling, not a fictitious dismantling."
Just over a week ago, US President Donald Trump was heralding a major breakthrough in the peace process after his Board of Peace brokered a deal for Hamas to hand over its weapons.
Hours after making his announcement on social media, he claimed Israel was "very happy about it", comments now at odds with Mr Netanyahu's remarks.
The Israeli prime minister's rhetoric is not entirely surprising, given much of the Israeli establishment has railed against the proposal for the past week.
But it does show how difficult negotiations on reaching the next phase of the ceasefire in Gaza will be, particularly ahead of an Israeli election, and proves that there are some limits to the White House's sway over the Netanyahu government.
Since October 2025, when the truce was announced, Palestinian health authorities reported more than 1,200 people had been killed in Israeli strikes, among them many women and children.
Israel intensifies strikes on Gaza
In announcing it would disarm on Friday, July 31, Hamas revealed there were certain conditions that needed to be met by Israel.
Specifically, Israel would need to stop almost daily deadly attacks across the strip and its forces would need to withdraw from large swathes of territory.
Since the ceasefire in Gaza was declared, Israel has pushed deeper into the strip — increasing its control from just over 50 per cent of the land to more than 60 per cent.
The Yellow Line, the name given to the boundary of Israeli control, has moved during that period, displacing more Palestinians in the process.
Hamas also said it would hand over its weapons for storage by the new US-backed Palestinian technocratic organisation, known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.
It still has not been allowed to enter the strip by Israel, and has been forced to conduct its affairs from the Egyptian capital, Cairo.
Hours after Hamas's declaration, Israel unleashed some of its deadliest attacks on the strip, prompting a thinly veiled rebuke from the Trump administration's Board of Peace and its high representative for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov.
Mr Mladenov met with Mr Netanyahu in Israel days later. The Reuters news agency is reporting Israel agreed to show restraint in some of its strikes.
"We expect the mediators and the US guarantor to press Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the road map and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons, while continuing to jeopardise the region's security and stability," Hamas official Basem Naim told Reuters.
The Israeli prime minister also, once again, rejected any notion of potential Palestinian statehood, which is a politically sensitive issue in Israel at any moment, let alone before an election.
"As long as I am prime minister, a Palestinian state will not be established," he said.
"Not in Gaza and not in Judea and Samaria, not a 'Fatah-stan' and not a 'Hamas-stan'."
Judea and Samaria is the Biblical name for the area commonly referred to as the West Bank.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu Rejects Trump-Backed Gaza Plan, Says Israel Will Not Withdraw Until Hamas Fully Disarms
sources.text:
Netanyahu Rejects Trump-Backed Gaza Plan, Says Israel Will Not Withdraw Until Hamas Fully Disarms
Key Facts
- Netanyahu formally rejected the U.S.-backed 15-point Gaza roadmap, saying Israel will not withdraw until Hamas is completely disarmed.
- Israel is demanding the surrender of all Hamas weapons, rejecting arrangements that could allow the terrorist organization to retain its arsenal under another authority.
- Netanyahu praised President Trump but said Israel will resist even its closest ally when necessary to protect Israeli security interests.
by Emmitt Barry, Worthy News Washington D.C. Bureau Chief
JERUSALEM (Worthy News) – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday formally rejected a U.S.-backed 15-point plan for Gaza, declaring that Israeli forces will not withdraw from territory in the Strip until Hamas undergoes what he called complete and genuine disarmament.
“I want to clarify here,” Netanyahu told ministers at the weekly Cabinet meeting. “Israel rejects the 15-point document.” He insisted that Hamas must surrender not merely its heavy weapons but its entire arsenal before Israel considers pulling back.
“When I say Hamas must be disarmed, I mean the heavy weapons, the less-heavy weapons, all weapons,” Netanyahu said, stressing that Israel would accept only “genuine disarmament, not a fictitious one.”
The dispute centers on a roadmap advanced by the U.S.-backed Board of Peace, which seeks to move Gaza toward postwar reconstruction and a new governing structure. Hamas has said it accepts the framework but has stopped short of agreeing to conventional disarmament, instead offering to place its weapons into storage under a Palestinian technocratic administration backed by Washington. Israeli officials have warned that such an arrangement could allow Hamas to preserve its military infrastructure while buying time against renewed Israeli operations.
Netanyahu: Israel Can Say No to Washington
Netanyahu made clear that his rejection of the proposal was not intended as a break with President Donald Trump, whom he described as a strong friend of Israel. But he said Israel’s security requirements would take precedence even when Jerusalem and Washington disagree.
“I have great appreciation for President Trump,” Netanyahu said, pointing to cooperation between the two nations against Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Nevertheless, he said Israel knows “how to stand our ground even against our very best friends when necessary.”
Israel continues discussing the Gaza proposal with Washington, Netanyahu said, adding that some American ideas are acceptable while others are not.
The prime minister also reiterated that he would oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state in either Gaza or Judea and Samaria while he remains in office.
Hamas Calls for U.S. Pressure on Israel
Senior Hamas official Basem Naim told Reuters that Hamas remains committed to the roadmap negotiated in Cairo and called on the United States and other mediators to pressure Netanyahu’s government to accept it.
The Israeli government remains deeply skeptical, however, that Hamas intends to permanently relinquish its weapons or political power.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich welcomed Netanyahu’s rejection, arguing that Israel entered the war with the central objective of destroying Hamas as both a military organization and governing authority. He said reconstruction should not move forward until Hamas has been completely dismantled and Gaza can no longer threaten southern Israel.
For Jerusalem, the dispute increasingly comes down to a fundamental question: Does Hamas actually disappear as an armed force, or does an international agreement merely rearrange how and where its weapons are held?
Netanyahu made Israel’s position unmistakable Sunday. Israeli forces, he said, will not withdraw on the strength of promises alone.

sources.text:
The landscape of the Gaza conflict shifted significantly this week as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu officially rejected the latest peace initiative proposed by the United States and the Board of Peace. This development marks a major point of friction between the Israeli government and President Donald Trump, who has been pushing for a resolution to the ongoing violence.
According to CNN, the 15-point plan was announced by Trump on July 31. It was reportedly intended to serve as a roadmap for lasting peace in the territory. However, the Israeli government has signaled that it is far from ready to adopt the terms as they currently stand. Reuters reported that Netanyahu made his statements during televised remarks to his cabinet members, stating, “I want to be precise here: Israel rejects the 15-point document.”
He further clarified that the Israeli military would “not withdraw at all until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and citizens.” Reuters reported that the Prime Minister emphasized the nature of this requirement, noting that it means “heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry” must be addressed. He specifically characterized the necessary outcome as “genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament.”
The diplomatic back and forth
Per the outlets, Netanyahu acknowledged that his government is in active discussions with American officials regarding the proposal. He noted, “They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand up to those things.” Per Reuters, he made similar remarks on social media earlier this week, where he indicated that while some U.S. concepts are workable, others are entirely unacceptable to his administration.
Reuters noted that the political pressure on Netanyahu is immense. With an election scheduled for October 27, the Prime Minister is navigating a difficult path between his key military backer, the United States, and the demands of his right-wing coalition. Far-right ministers have been vocal in their support for his hardline stance.
According to CNN, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich was particularly explicit in a statement, saying, “The (Israel Defense Forces) cannot retreat one millimeter in the Gaza Strip.” Smotrich added that no reconstruction process can begin until the complete dismantling and demobilization of Hamas occurs.
Hamas, meanwhile, is attempting to maintain its position within the framework of the previously negotiated ceasefire. CNN reported that Bassem Naim, a senior member of the Hamas politburo, took to X to address the situation.
He stated, “We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons.” Naim also told Reuters that the group remains committed to the roadmap established with mediators in Cairo about ten days ago. It was a hard-won roadmap, considering that the negotiations had stalled because of the Iran war.
The central disagreement reportedly revolves around the timing of troop withdrawals and disarmament. Hamas has insisted that Israel must halt its strikes and pull back its forces before the group begins the process of turning over its weapons. Conversely, Israel maintains that no withdrawal will occur until the group has been fully disarmed.
Interestingly, Hamas has avoided the term disarmament. However, per the outlet, it has indicated it would be willing to store weapons under a U.S.-backed Palestinian technocrat administration supervised by the Board of Peace.
The humanitarian situation in the region remains dire. Since the conflict began following the October 7, 2023, attacks, much of Gaza has been reduced to ruins. Reuters reports that Israeli troops now control roughly two-thirds of Gaza, pushing more than 2 million residents into a shrinking strip of territory along the coast.
There was a brief surge in Israeli strikes following Trump’s initial announcement on July 31. However, the frequency of these attacks has reportedly declined since Monday, when Nikolay Mladenov, the Gaza envoy for the Board of Peace, met with Netanyahu. A source familiar with the situation indicated that Israel has agreed to act only against immediate threats and to cease the targeted assassinations that were occurring on a near-daily basis.
Despite the current friction, the relationship between Netanyahu and Trump has historically been very close. Last year, Netanyahu described the U.S. President as “the greatest friend that the state of Israel has ever had in the White House.” Trump has even suggested that Netanyahu should receive a pardon regarding his ongoing corruption charges.
Nevertheless, the Prime Minister continues to assert his independence. Referring to military actions in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran, Netanyahu remarked, “Contrary to all those who preach to us, we do what must be done for Israel’s security and we can and will stand our ground even against our best friends when necessary.”

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday that Israel is rejecting a peace proposal put forward by President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace.
“I want to clarify this: Israel rejects the 15-point document. I have heard people saying, ‘You didn’t say that.’ So here I am saying it again,” Netanyahu told members of his Cabinet.
“The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed,” the Israeli prime minister added.
Trump last month hailed what he described as a major step forward in efforts to secure a Gaza peace deal, but the plan appeared to run into a serious obstacle Sunday after Netanyahu rejected a central element of the proposal. The Israeli leader insisted that Hamas must hand over all weapons before Israeli forces leave the territory.
The president had previously celebrated a breakthrough in the talks, saying Hamas had agreed to disarm. But the Board of Peace roadmap envisions Israel gradually pulling troops out of Gaza while Hamas disarms — a timeline Netanyahu made clear he will not support.
“When I say Hamas must be disarmed, I mean heavy weapons, lighter weapons, all weapons. We are talking about genuine disarmament, not a fictitious one,” Netanyahu said Sunday, stressing that Israeli troops would remain in Gaza until the terror group is fully stripped of its arsenal.
Hamas has argued for the reverse sequence. The group said last month that it would disarm only after Israel completely withdraws from Gaza and halts military operations, with the surrender of heavy weapons to follow later and only if a Palestinian state is established.
Netanyahu also reaffirmed his longstanding opposition to Palestinian statehood, saying: “As long as I am Prime Minister, there will be no Palestinian State.” The remarks come as he heads into a bitter political battle ahead of October elections, with the wars in Gaza and Iran expected to be central issues in the campaign.

Rabat – Iran has ruled out direct negotiations with the United States for now, but says communication has not stopped. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi confirmed that messages continue to pass through intermediaries, while efforts aim to prepare the ground for eventual talks.
The cautious tone reflects a region on edge. In southern Saudi Arabia, Yemen’s Houthi movement said it struck a Saudi Aramco facility in Jizan, sparking a fire and raising new concerns over the vulnerability of energy infrastructure. The claim, if confirmed, points to a war that continues to spill across borders.
Tehran has also raised the stakes at sea. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) set out conditions for reopening a strategic waterway, calling for an end to what it describes as a US naval blockade, along with compensation for war damage. The demands tie maritime security to broader political grievances, and risk further strain on global shipping routes.
In Gaza, diplomacy faces another setback. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a US-backed “Board of Peace” plan designed to end the war, despite its endorsement by Hamas last month.
“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said during a cabinet meeting on Sunday. He made clear that any Israeli withdrawal depends on the complete disarmament of Hamas.
“The army will not withdraw until Hamas is genuinely disarmed,” he added.
Netanyahu noted that discussions with Washington remain active, but drew clear lines. Some proposals, he said, align with Israeli priorities, while others do not. “We know how to stand firm,” he added.
The White House and Hamas have yet to respond publicly.
US President Donald Trump had presented the plan on July 30 as a “historic” pathway to lasting security. The proposal centers on dismantling Hamas’s military capacity in stages, starting with heavy weapons, production sites, storage facilities, and the group’s tunnel network.
Israel, however, insists on a broader definition of disarmament. Netanyahu stressed that all weapons must disappear, including small arms, not only major systems.
The plan also outlines a future for Gaza under a technocratic Palestinian administration, supervised by the Board of Peace. Yet the body’s limited authority raises doubts about its ability to move forward without Israeli backing.
On the ground, skepticism runs deep. Observers warn that Netanyahu’s position disrupts months of mediation efforts and clouds any clear path out of the war.
“This puts the entire sequence of steps into question,” said Al Jazeera correspondent Hani Mahmoud from Gaza City.
From Bethlehem, Nour Odeh described Israel’s conditions as a serious obstacle for mediators. “This effectively resets the process,” she said.
Despite a ceasefire announced last October, bloody massacres have not stopped. Israeli strikes continue across Gaza, and the human toll keeps rising. Gaza’s health ministry reports at least 1,250 deaths and more than 4,100 injuries since the truce began, with hundreds still missing under rubble.
The broader war has left more than 73,000 people dead and over 174,000 wounded since October 2023.
With indirect diplomacy, contested ceasefires, and expanding flashpoints from Gaza to the Red Sea, the region now stands at a fragile crossroads. Each side signals openness to negotiation, yet conditions harden, and the gap between positions remains wide.

Netanyahu Defies Trump Over Gaza Peace Plan: Israeli PM Rejects 15-Point Deal and Demands Hamas Disarm First
Israeli PM Netanyahu dismisses Trump's Gaza peace proposal, insisting on complete Hamas disarmament before any troop withdrawal
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has publicly rejected Donald Trump's 15-point Gaza peace plan, declaring that Israeli forces will not withdraw from the enclave until Hamas is 'genuinely' disarmed, in the clearest policy clash so far between the two allies over how and when the war should end.
Speaking at his weekly cabinet meeting in Jerusalem on Sunday, Netanyahu said he opposed the framework in full. 'Israel rejects the 15-point document,' he said, adding that the Israel Defense Forces 'will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens.'
In televised remarks, he clarified: 'I mean the heavy weapons, the less heavy weapons, all the weapons. And we are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament.' He also restated that, as long as he is prime minister, there would be no Palestinian state in Gaza or the West Bank, and Iran would not be allowed nuclear weapons.
Trump Plan Stalls as Sides Disagree on Who Moves First
Trump's so-called Board of Peace announced last month that it had reached agreement with Hamas for the 'complete disarmament' of the group and other armed factions in Gaza. The framework, unveiled nearly a year after Trump first set out his Gaza plan, envisaged Hamas handing over its weapons to a new Palestinian administration, Israeli troops gradually pulling back, and international donors moving in to rebuild Gaza.
Hamas, however, said any surrender of heavy weapons would only begin once Israel ended 'all forms of aggression' and withdrew its forces. The result is a critical impasse: Hamas insists on withdrawal before disarmament; Israel insists on disarmament before withdrawal – neither is willing to move first.
Hamas remains publicly committed to the deal. A senior official said the group 'reaffirms its commitment' to the 15-point agreement and is ready 'to engage seriously and responsibly in implementing' it, while another senior figure, Basem Naim, said Hamas expects US mediators to 'press Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap.'
Israeli analysts cited by local media have expressed scepticism that Hamas would ever fully surrender its arsenal.
Election Pressures Harden Netanyahu's Position
Netanyahu's stance is shaped as much by domestic politics as by the battlefield, with Israeli elections only months away and pressure mounting from his right-wing and far-right coalition partners to show no flexibility on Gaza. National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir has already dismissed the draft plan as 'not acceptable' and urged a cabinet vote to formally bury it.
Netanyahu told ministers he was 'talking to the Americans about this issue,' saying: 'They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters.' The White House has yet to publicly respond to the Israeli rejection.
The Human Toll and a Plan Running Out of Time
The human cost of the conflict remains severe. According to UN figures, about 1.9 million people, roughly 90 per cent of Gaza's population, have been displaced since the war began following Hamas's 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, which killed about 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage.
Israel's military campaign in response has killed more than 73,000 people in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry, whose data is regarded as broadly reliable by the UN. Palestinian officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, have said more than 1,250 people have been killed in Israeli strikes since the initial ceasefire last October alone.
Israel has scaled back some attacks following a meeting between Netanyahu and the Board's Gaza envoy, Nikolay Mladenov, who criticised recent strikes that killed civilians and destroyed medical supplies. But Israeli forces continue operations in the strip, and the 15-point plan's original 14-day timetable for a full agreement is already looming, with Israel and Hamas still arguing over who disarms or withdraws first.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Gaza peace plan as Netanyahu, facing elections, digs in for continued war
sources.text:
Israel rejects Gaza peace plan as Netanyahu, facing elections, digs in for continued war
Gazans now feel more uncertain as nobody talks about Justice for Palestinians
As Netanyahu demands ‘genuine’ Hamas disarmament before considering pull-out from Gaza, a look at what happens next.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected United States President Donald Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza, saying that Israeli forces will not withdraw until Hamas is “genuinely disarmed”.
“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” he said at a cabinet meeting, stressing that Hamas must give up all of its weapons before any pull-back.
Trump late last month announced a breakthrough in the US-led ceasefire framework, saying that Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza had accepted a phased plan under which they would surrender their weapons to a new Palestinian governing body, and Israel would begin pulling out troops in tandem with disarmament.
Netanyahu, under pressure from his right-wing base ahead of elections, has seemingly hardened his stance after days of mounting criticism of the plan.
So, what is Trump’s 15-point plan, and why has Israel rejected it?
What is Trump’s 15-point plan?
On July 30, the US-led Board of Peace proposed a 15-point roadmap for Gaza, detailing a phased, conditional framework for disarmament and reconstruction in the war-torn coastal enclave.
The plan mandates that Hamas disarm in exchange for a full Israeli military withdrawal and the transition of governance to an independent Palestinian National Committee, supported by an international security force.
The Board of Peace, created by Trump in October with him serving as its lifetime chair, is led by the US government. United Nations Security Council (UNSC) Resolution 2803 designates it the body responsible for overseeing the Gaza peace plan.
Trump said the agreement would be implemented in stages, with Israeli forces withdrawing as the disarmament process advances.
Despite the framework, significant challenges remain, as Hamas hinges its compliance on an end to Israel’s genocidal actions.
A member of Hamas’s negotiating delegation last month told Al Jazeera that the group’s implementation of the agreement will be dependent on Israel fulfilling its commitments.
However, the Board of Peace earlier this week said an Israeli withdrawal from Gaza will only take place after the disarmament of Hamas is complete.
Israel has killed more than 73,300 Palestinians in Gaza since its genocidal war began in October 2023. And since agreeing to a US-mediated “ceasefire” with Hamas in October 2025, it has continued to carry out strikes on Gaza, killing more than 1,200 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
What did Netanyahu say while rejecting the deal?
The Israeli army “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens”, the Israeli prime minister said.
Netanyahu added that Israel was engaging with Washington over its concerns about the plan.
“They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us, and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters,” he said.
The Israeli leader, who is expected to face a tough national election in October this year, with successive surveys showing he is on course to lose, said that Hamas must give up all of its weapons.
“We are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament,” Netanyahu said.
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from the occupied West Bank, said discussions around the 15-point plan, including Hamas’s disarmament and Israel’s potential withdrawal, “are extremely controversial for the [Netanyahu-led] right-wing government”.
“It seems that Netanyahu, so close to elections, has hit the reset button, saying that none of that will happen under his watch,” she said.
“This is extremely problematic for the Board of Peace and the mediators who have been working for months now to try to find a way to carry out the disarmament of Hamas and have Israel commit to a phased withdrawal from Gaza.”
How have Palestinians reacted?
Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, reporting from Gaza City, said most people in the war-battered coastal enclave “expected” Israel to reject the proposal.
“The only concern that people have right now is that this is translating into greater uncertainty,” he reported, adding that the plan “was meant to provide more structure and a framework”.
“There are important elements that were part of the plan in terms of security: Israeli withdrawal from the area that it has been occupying over the past years across Gaza known as the ‘Yellow Line’, the disarmament of Hamas, as well as the entry of international stabilization forces. Now, the full rejection here puts the sequencing and the steps to complete that into serious question. It translates into no clear end to hostilities and wars.”
Political analyst and former adviser to the Palestinian negotiations team Xavier Abu Eid says the Board of Peace and UNSC Resolution 2803 were accepted late last year because it was argued at that time that they were the only way to end the Israeli genocide in Gaza.
“But it was very clear from the very beginning that the 20-point plan of President Trump and the 15-point disarmament and implementation plan that followed were more about meeting Israeli interests than the Palestinian right to self-determination,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Justice for Palestinians is something that nobody talks about. So, certainly, this remains a position,” he said, adding that Trump is unlikely to be happy with Netanyahu’s rejection.
“But at the same time, Trump has never even pretended to push any sort of accountability measures for Netanyahu violating even their own agreements,” the analyst said.
What do the experts say?
Israeli analyst Dan Perry said Netanyahu’s move against the proposed Gaza plan is “misaligned with what the people in Israel would generally want, if they understood correctly what’s going on”.
“I have no naivety about Hamas. But even if there is an idea that there is a declarative agreement to disarm, it is something that should be welcomed so clearly,” Perry, the former chief of The Associated Press news agency in Europe, Africa and the Middle East, told Al Jazeera.
“I keep hearing about a trade-off between Israeli security demands and the obvious needs of the Palestinian people, the need to alleviate and fix the humanitarian disaster in Gaza, but these are not at loggerheads.”
Much of Israeli society has backed the genocidal war on Gaza following the October 7 attack on southern Israel, as well as the war on Lebanon and Iran.
Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli diplomat, says Netanyahu needs “a forever war”.
“This Israeli rejection of the Gaza plan … should be viewed entirely in the context of the upcoming Israeli election on October 27,” he told Al Jazeera.
Pinkas said Netanyahu made a “calculation that this is risk-free”, “that he can supposedly defy Trump because Trump doesn’t care enough, because of the sequence, because Hamas hasn’t disarmed yet, because he can get away with it”.
“And this is all about the forever war and the election,” he concluded.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu rejects Trump’s plan to disarm Hamas
sources.text:
TEL AVIV, Israel — The Israeli government has rejected a 15-point plan backed by the Trump administration aimed at disarming the Palestinian militant group Hamas in the Gaza Strip, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday.
It appeared to be an unusually public break with President Donald Trump, whose relationship with Netanyahu has had a dizzying and often unpredictable arc. The two leaders launched the war against Iran together in late February. But they have since clashed over how to end it, as well as over the future of Israel’s military campaigns in Gaza and Lebanon.
Trump announced the agreement between his Board of Peace and Hamas late last month, lauding it as a major breakthrough. Netanyahu’s office had initially expressed reservations, saying that the framework did “not reflect Israel’s positions,” but stopped short of outright rejecting it.
The U.S.-backed proposal envisions a phased process in which Hamas would hand over its weapons in stages to a new Palestinian administration in Gaza. In exchange, Israel would gradually withdraw from the more than half of Gaza that it has controlled since the ceasefire in October.
On Sunday, Netanyahu openly dismissed the plan, saying that Israeli forces “would not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed.” He said that meant “heavy weapons, lighter weapons, all weapons,” adding, “We are talking about real disarmament.”
At a Cabinet meeting of government ministers, Netanyahu said, “I want to be clear here: Israel is ruling out the 15-point document.”
A spokesperson for the Board of Peace did not immediately comment on Netanyahu’s remarks.
The Israeli prime minister — who faces a tough reelection campaign this fall — promised “absolute victory” over Hamas after the group led the Oct. 7, 2023, attack that ignited the war in Gaza. But nearly three years later, Hamas still controls parts of the territory that it has dominated for nearly two decades.
Hamas has publicly accepted the U.S.-backed agreement. But Israeli analysts are skeptical that the Palestinian militants actually intend to follow through on handing over weapons to a new Palestinian administration in Gaza, as armed struggle against Israel is one of the group’s core precepts.
The deal followed months of delicate talks between Hamas’ leaders in exile and officials from Trump’s Board of Peace, a new body established to oversee the Gaza ceasefire. The board includes heads of state, including Netanyahu, and is chaired by Trump.
In practice, however, a small number of Trump appointees led the negotiations, including Nickolay Mladenov, a former U.N. Mideast envoy. The U.S.-backed negotiators sought to find a formula that would relieve Hamas of its weapons but that the militant group would still accept.
According to the text of the accord, Israel would first have to fulfill several outstanding conditions from the initial ceasefire with Hamas in October which ended the two-year war in Gaza, including a “cessation of military operations.”
Despite the ceasefire, Israel has continued attacking on a near-daily basis in Gaza, killing more than 1,000 people since October, according to Palestinian health officials. Those killed have included senior Hamas officials, but also civilians, including children.
Israeli bombardment intensified the weekend after the deal was concluded, with more than 18 people killed, Gaza health officials said.
But those attacks largely ceased after Mladenov met with Netanyahu last Monday. Mladenov had criticized the strikes, which he said had “killed civilians and destroyed medical supplies that people depend on.”
Under the Trump plan, an international committee was supposed to verify Israel’s compliance with the ceasefire reached in October. Hamas would then “decommission and store” heavy weapons as part of a process overseen by a group of U.S.-backed Palestinian technocrats.
Israel would gradually withdraw from Gaza, and Palestinian militias armed by Israel to fight Hamas would similarly give up their weapons.
The timeline, along with other details, has yet to be negotiated. The 15-point agreement specifies that they are meant to be concluded within 14 days, which would be later this week. It is unclear whether that can be realized given the doubts hanging over the deal.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump's Board of Peace roadmap to disarm Hamas: Netanyahu
Netanyahu Rejects Trump’s 15-Point Peace Plan for Gaza
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday that his country rejects U.S. President Donald Trump’s latest peace plan for Gaza.
The 15-point plan, issued by Trump’s Board of Peace, envisioned a phased peace process. Through it, Hamas would gradually cede its weapons and power to a new Palestinian administration, while Israel would withdraw its troops to the “yellow line” established in the ceasefire deal both sides signed in October 2025.
When it was released by the Board of Peace on July 31, Netanyahu remained silent for multiple days and then acknowledged that the Trump Administration had “sent us a draft.”
“We did not agree,” he continued. “It is not our draft. We sent our comments. This is our position.”
However, Sunday was the first time that he formally declared a refusal to endorse it.
“I want to be precise here: Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting. “The [Israel Defense Forces] will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed.”
“As long as I am Prime Minister, no Palestinian state will be established—not in Gaza and not in the West Bank,” he continued.
While discussing the peace roadmap, Trump said that Hamas and “all other armed groups” in Gaza had agreed to disarm, paving the way for a resolution to the conflict that began when the militant group launched a terrorist attack on Oct. 7, 2023, that killed 1,200 people in Israel.
Soon after Netanyahu’s comments, Hamas encouraged mediators to continue putting pressure on Israel.
Basem Naim, a senior Hamas official, wrote on X that the group is still “committed to the roadmap reached.”
“We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to press Netanyahu and his government to compel him to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the path for internal political and electoral reasons,” he said.
More than 1,250 people have been killed in the Israeli attacks since the original ceasefire in October 2025, most of them civilians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. Over 73,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the war began, the ministry said. Hamas has not disclosed how many of its fighters have been killed.
What Is Netanyahu’s Response to Trump?
Netanyahu has long enjoyed a cordial relationship with the U.S. President, whom he has called “the greatest friend that the state of Israel has ever had in the White House.” However, the relationship has appeared more strained since the countries worked together in strikes against Iran on Feb. 28.
Trump told the New York Post in June that he called Netanyahu “crazy” after being “a little bit perturbed at his constantly fighting with Lebanon.” Continued Israeli military operations in Lebanon have complicated U.S. efforts to negotiate an end to hostilities with Iran.
Netanyahu has since joined Trump at the White House, during a trip to the U.S. to attend Sen. Lindsey Graham’s funeral on July 28. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said afterward that the two leaders had a “positive and productive” meeting, and Trump said on Truth Social that “many important subjects were discussed,” though he offered no further details.
“I greatly appreciate Trump,” Netanyahu said at his cabinet meeting Friday. “I greatly appreciate the historical partnership with the U.S. against Iran’s attempts to acquire nuclear weapons.”
And he went on to comment on Jerusalem’s continued cooperation with Washington on Sunday, saying: “Right now, we are talking with the Americans about this issue. They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us, some of which are unacceptable.”
However, he continued, Israel refuses to accept its 15-point peace plan. “I have heard people say: ‘You didn’t say it.’ So here I am saying it again,” he emphasized.
His firm stance directly contradicts statements from Trump shortly after it was announced.
“We do have an understanding with Israel,” Trump told reporters at his Cabinet meeting at Camp David on July 31. “Israel is very happy about it. Israel helped us. They’ve been very good.”
However, the hard-right Prime Minister faces an uphill battle this year in his reelection campaign after an inconclusive war with Iran, and amid ongoing military operations in Lebanon, as well as unfulfilled vows of “total victory” over Hamas. That vow has remained a central point of tension as negotiations continue, adding to strains in relations with the U.S.
The public disagreement represents rare friction between the two allies and underscores the limits of their alignment on key regional issues.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu rejects Trump’s 15-point Gaza plan
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a 15-point plan for Gaza, put forward by U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, saying that Israeli forces will not withdraw from the territory until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.
Speaking at the start of a Cabinet meeting Sunday, Netanyahu said Israel would not accept what he characterized as a merely symbolic disarmament process.
His objections center on the sequence of the proposal, which links Hamas’ disarmament to a phased Israeli withdrawal and the transfer of Gaza’s administration to a U.S.-backed Palestinian committee. Netanyahu also reaffirmed his opposition to the creation of a Palestinian state and insisted that Israel must retain the ability to act against threats from Gaza.
What Did Netanyahu Say?
Netanyahu used his opening remarks at Sunday’s Cabinet meeting to dismiss suggestions that Israel had accepted the proposal.
"I wish to be precise here: Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said.
The prime minister said Israel would not begin the phased troop withdrawal envisioned by the plan before Hamas surrendered its entire arsenal.
"The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed," he said.
Netanyahu defined that demand broadly, saying it covered "the heavy weapons, the less-heavy weapons, all weapons." He added: "We are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament."
This position conflicts with a central mechanism of the proposal, which links phased Israeli withdrawals to the phased decommissioning of Hamas' weapons.
Netanyahu indicated that negotiations with Washington were continuing but made clear that Israel would not automatically accept proposals advanced by its closest ally.
"They have ideas. Some of them are acceptable to us and some are not acceptable to us," Netanyahu said, adding that Israel knew how to "stand our ground on these matters."
Hamas, meanwhile, said it remains committed to the proposal despite Netanyahu's objections. "We remain committed to the road map," Bassem Naim, a member of the group's political bureau, said Sunday, adding that the group expected mediators and the United States to press Israel to meet its obligations under the plan.
Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's envoy for Gaza, also expressed hope that discussions would continue despite Israel's objections. "We have asked Israel to give the process a chance," he said in an interview with Israeli media. "I hope that these discussions will lead to a positive outcome for everyone."
Despite those calls to keep negotiations alive, Netanyahu said the Israeli military would "continue to thwart threats against our forces and against our citizens," signaling that operations in Gaza could continue while the dispute remains unresolved.
He also reiterated his opposition to Palestinian statehood, saying: "As long as I am prime minister, there will be no Palestinian state, not in Gaza and not in Judea and Samaria." He added: "Neither ‘Fatahstan’ nor ‘Hamastan,’" using the biblical term for the occupied West Bank and disparaging labels derived from the names of the rival Palestinian factions Fatah and Hamas.
What Was in the 15-Point Gaza Roadmap?
The 15-point proposal was not a separate peace agreement but a road map for implementing the second phase of Trump’s broader 20-point Gaza plan. Published by Trump’s U.S.-led Board of Peace on July 30, it sought to connect Hamas’ disarmament with an Israeli withdrawal, a transfer of governing authority and the reconstruction of Gaza.
Under the proposal, Israel and Hamas would cease military operations and complete their remaining commitments under the October 2025 ceasefire agreement. Within 14 days of all sides approving the road map, officials would establish a timetable and mechanisms for carrying it out.
Hamas and other Palestinian factions would surrender all civilian and security authority to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, or NCAG, an interim body of Palestinian technocrats backed by the Board of Peace. Hamas would be barred from interfering in the committee’s work, while the NCAG would assume responsibility for public services, government finances and internal security.
The security provisions were based on the principle of "One Authority, One Law, One Weapon." Police officers would be vetted and their weapons placed under NCAG authority. Hamas and other armed groups would gradually surrender heavy weapons, production facilities, weapons depots and tunnels, while militia members would be prohibited from joining Gaza’s new police service.
An International Verification Committee would determine whether each side had fulfilled its obligations before the process moved forward. A temporary International Stabilization Force would monitor the ceasefire, help train Palestinian police, protect aid deliveries and separate Israeli troops from areas controlled by the NCAG.
Crucially, the plan tied verified steps toward disarmament to a phased Israeli withdrawal rather than requiring one side to complete all its obligations first. Israeli forces would pull back as weapons were decommissioned, with each stage dependent on confirmation that the previous commitments had been met.
The final point called for Gaza’s reconstruction to proceed under a plan prepared and supervised by the Board of Peace and the Palestinian committee. The road map also said its implementation should create conditions for "a credible pathway" toward Palestinian self-determination and statehood—language that directly conflicts with Netanyahu’s opposition to a Palestinian state.
The proposal had received conditional backing from Hamas, which said implementation depended on Israel halting its attacks and meeting its own obligations. However, the disagreement over which steps must come first—Hamas’ disarmament or an Israeli withdrawal—remained the central obstacle.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu Formally Rejects Trump's 15-Point Gaza Plan
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday that his government rejects the 15-point Gaza plan put forward by President Donald Trump's Board of Peace, marking his first explicit public rejection of the framework and vowing that Israeli forces will not withdraw from the territory until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed. "I want to be precise here: Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu told a Cabinet meeting Sunday, adding that the Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and citizens." The statement marks a sharp reversal from the posture Netanyahu struck alongside Trump last year, when the two leaders jointly announced what Trump called a "historic agreement for the complete disarmament of Hamas and all other groups in Gaza."
Netanyahu said Israel's definition of disarmament leaves no room for compromise. "When I say Hamas must be disarmed, I mean the heavy weapons, the less heavy weapons, all weapons," he said, adding that Israel is seeking "real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament." He said his government remains in active talks with Washington over the issue, describing a mix of proposals from American officials. "They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us, and we know how to stand firm on these matters," he said. Netanyahu also used the moment to reaffirm his long-standing opposition to Palestinian statehood in any form. "As long as I am prime minister, there will be no Palestinian state, not in Gaza and not in Judea and Samaria," he said, adding that Israel would accept "neither Fatahstan nor Hamastan."
The rejection drew an immediate response from Hamas, whose politburo member Bassem Naim said on social media that the group remains committed to the roadmap and called on mediators and the American government to press Netanyahu to comply. "We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," Naim wrote. Within Netanyahu's own coalition, the response was celebratory: Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, a leading voice among the government's far-right bloc, said "the IDF cannot retreat one millimeter in the Gaza Strip." Israeli forces currently occupy more than half of Gaza's territory, concentrated in the east and south, and senior ministers have signaled a desire to expand that control further rather than draw it down.
Sunday's statement lands against the backdrop of a peace process that, on paper, has already reached an advanced stage. The Gaza peace plan — formally the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict — was announced by Trump at the White House alongside Netanyahu on Sept. 29, 2025, signed on Oct. 9, and took effect the following day. The United Nations Security Council endorsed the framework on Nov. 17. But the plan's second phase, which requires Hamas's disarmament and a corresponding Israeli withdrawal, has remained the most contentious unresolved piece of the agreement, with negotiations over its core sequencing yet to formally conclude. The Board of Peace released a draft roadmap for that next phase on July 31, with the body's high representative for Gaza, Nickolay Mladenov, stating at the time that "withdrawal must move in lockstep with decommissioning" — the specific sequencing formula Netanyahu's government is now rejecting outright.
The disagreement is not new, even if Sunday's language was unusually blunt. Tension between Netanyahu's government and the Trump administration's Gaza team has simmered for months over who ultimately controls implementation of the plan's later phases. Netanyahu has separately objected to the makeup of an "executive board" overseeing Gaza's transition, which reports to the Board of Peace and includes representatives from Turkey and Qatar — countries Netanyahu has insisted should have no governing role in the territory. A senior U.S. official close to the process has previously dismissed those objections bluntly, telling reporters that responsibility for Gaza's next phase rests with Washington rather than Jerusalem. That friction has coexisted uneasily with the closeness Netanyahu has otherwise expressed toward Trump, whom he described last year as "the greatest friend that the state of Israel has ever had in the White House."
Netanyahu's rejection also arrives as he faces a difficult domestic political landscape, with elections scheduled for October and both the Gaza and Iran conflicts likely to weigh heavily on the outcome. His far-right coalition partners have repeatedly pressed him to harden Israel's negotiating posture and resist further troop withdrawals, and Sunday's remarks give that flank a clear, public commitment to point to. At the same time, hardline resistance to any further pullback risks colliding directly with the Board of Peace's stated timeline and with Hamas's insistence that it has already met its obligations under the plan by agreeing to the 15-point document, even as Israeli officials maintain that Hamas has not matched its stated agreement with any verified reduction in its weapons stockpile.
That gap between Hamas's claimed compliance and Israel's insistence on disarmament before any further withdrawal illustrates how far apart the two sides remain on the practical mechanics of ending the war, even ten months after the ceasefire nominally took hold and despite UN Security Council backing for the broader framework. Netanyahu's explicit, on-the-record rejection — after weeks of more ambiguous criticism — removes any doubt about where his government currently stands, but it does not resolve the underlying sequencing dispute that has stalled the plan's second phase since the draft roadmap's release in late July.
Attention going forward is likely to center on how the Trump administration responds to Netanyahu's rejection, given the White House's past insistence that Gaza's next phase remains under its own direction rather than Israel's veto. Continued monitoring of any formal U.S. counterproposal, Hamas's public and private response beyond Naim's statement, and whether Netanyahu's domestic political calculus ahead of October's elections further hardens his position is expected to remain a relevant thread as the dispute unfolds.
