Israel has discussed the issue of Hamas' disarmament with U.S. officials, Netanyahu said. "They [the Americans] have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable, and we know how to stand firm against these things."
In a statement, Hamas said it urged the board, mediators and Arab states to ensure all parties adhere to the agreement and refrain from violations "that could disrupt its implementation."
Hamas has avoided the use of the term "disarmament" and said the group agreed to hand over weapons to be stored under the Palestinian technocratic committee that would run the affairs in Gaza under the supervision of the board.
Hamas said it agreed to the plan to spare the people in Gaza a possible resumption of war, but it added that the implementation of the deal would depend on Israel first meeting its own commitments, including withdrawal.
Speaking to Reuters, Basem Naim, a senior Hamas official, said the group remained committed to the roadmap agreed with mediators in Cairo 10 days ago.
"We expect the mediators and the U.S. guarantor to press Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons, while continuing to jeopardise the region's security and stability," he said.
On Monday, the board retracted its plan to require Israel to gradually withdraw from Gaza simultaneously alongside Hamas' disarmament. The board's decision followed a statement from a senior Israeli official saying Israel would not fully withdraw and would retain the freedom to strike in Gaza.
Netanyahu also met Monday with the Board of Peace's top envoy, Nickolay Mladenov, to discuss the emerging deal in Gaza. Shortly after the meeting, the board issued a statement implying withdrawal would take place alongside the disarmament process.
Minutes later, however, the board revised the statement. The updated wording suggests that any Israeli withdrawal would take place only after Hamas' disarmament has been completed.
Israel has scaled back attacks in Gaza since the meeting. A source familiar with Israel's position told Reuters it had agreed that the military would only act against what it perceives as immediate threats in Gaza and no longer carry out targeted assassinations as it had been doing on a near-daily basis.
The Gaza Health Ministry reported that one person was killed in an Israeli strike over the past day.
Earlier this month, Mladenov criticized Israeli strikes in Gaza in a rare rebuke after at least 18 people were killed in one day. The strikes came two days after the Board of Peace and Hamas announced that they had agreed on a framework for the group's disarmament.
More than 1,250 people have been killed in the Israeli attacks since the October cease-fire, most of them civilians, according to Gaza health officials. Hamas has not disclosed the number of its fighters killed.
Israeli troops have occupied and depopulated two-thirds of the enclave, leaving nearly all its more than 2 million residents confined to a tiny strip of land under Hamas control along the coast, most in makeshift tents or damaged buildings.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump's Gaza plan, more details emerge on the Strait of Hormuz
sources.text:
Israel on Sunday rejected a deal announced by U.S. President Donald Trump for Gaza. Details emerged on the potential deal between Iran and Oman on managing the Strait of Hormuz as Tehran suggested that vessels linked to “hostile countries” would be barred from the key waterway.
Meanwhile, Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels struck a government-held port on the country’s Red Sea coast, deepening fears over threats to strategic shipping routes and a potential return to civil war. They also said they attacked an oil facility in neighboring Saudi Arabia.
Here’s a look at developments across the Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
Netanyahu insists no Gaza withdrawal until Hamas disarms
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dismissed the deal on Gaza announced by Trump last month, saying Israel’s military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.”
Netanyahu told a Cabinet meeting that “Israel rejects the 15-point document” but is still discussing plans for Gaza with Washington, after making similar comments last week. Trump had said Israeli forces would withdraw as the Hamas militant group’s disarmament is completed. Israeli forces control over half the Palestinian enclave of about 2 million people that's been largely destroyed.
There was no immediate White House comment on Netanyahu's latest.
“We remain committed to the road map,” said a member of the Hamas political bureau, Bassem Naim, adding that the group expects mediators and the U.S. to pressure Netanyahu — who also faces domestic tensions as he struggles to hold onto power ahead of the next elections scheduled for Oct. 27.
The Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, sparked the war in Gaza. A fragile ceasefire continues.
Iran says negotiations ‘cannot resume’ until conditions met
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters that negotiations with Oman about “new maritime routes” on the Strait of Hormuz were in final stages but “this, however, does not mean that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen.” That step requires conditions that “have been conveyed through intermediaries.”
Iran’s powerful Supreme National Security Council on Saturday said the strait will not reopen until the U.S. “corrects its behavior.” It demanded that the U.S. never threaten Iran again, a permanent end to the war with Iran and its armed allies, a lifting of the naval blockade of Iranian ports and a withdrawal of U.S. military from the area. The U.S. also must “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets.
The United States did not comment on the demands. Trump on Sunday asserted to Axios that “we are only semi-negotiating” with Iran and letting economic pressures take their toll.
Araghchi said an “exchange of messages through intermediaries” continues with the U.S. but that doesn’t constitute negotiations, which he said can’t resume until violations of the interim deal end and the U.S. “has remedied” provisions it violated.
Details emerge about a potential Iran-Oman deal
Iran and Oman, located on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz, are working to finalize a temporary deal that would reopen it, with ships entering near Iran and exiting near Oman, according to two people familiar with the talks who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Ships would transit without paying fees or tolls during the interim period.
The agreement is designed to restore the separate interim deal between the U.S. and Iran. The strait, crucial to global supplies of oil and natural gas, was considered an international waterway before the war.
The two people said the deal is endorsed by Gulf Cooperation Council members and is expected to be jointly announced by Iran, Oman, the U.S. and the U.N.’s International Maritime Organization. But they stressed the terms could change before the deal is final.
Iran on Sunday signaled progress on a plan to manage the strait, but a lawmaker said transits by vessels belonging to “hostile countries” would be prohibited.
Parliament’s National Security Committee approved “general outlines,” the state broadcaster reported. It cited a member of parliament’s presiding board as saying countries that have “caused damage” to Iran cannot transit until they compensate for it. There were no further details.
— Michelle Price in Washington and Aamer Madhani in New York
Houthis target Aramco refinery and Red Sea port
The Yemeni government-allied National Resistance Forces said at least seven people — four troops and three civilians — were killed and 15 civilians were injured in the Houthi attack on the port of Mokha.
Fayed al-Noman, the information ministry's assistant undersecretary, said the rebels fired missiles and drones, severely damaging port buildings and piers as well as commercial goods and food supplies. The military later said missiles landed in several areas, including near a television channel.
Mokha is a main port under Yemen’s internationally recognized government and has been renovated to handle shipping that avoids the Houthi-held port of Hodeida.
The Houthis said they targeted military forces and warehouses.
Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesperson, said they also targeted an Aramco refinery in the Saudi city of Jazan with a drone in response to Saudi drones’ breaching Yemen’s airspace over Hajjah and Saada provinces.
The Saudi Energy Ministry reported a fire at a facility belonging to the Aramco refinery, with no casualties. The ministry did not say the cause. The attacks threaten to reignite Yemen's civil war after a 2022 truce.
— Samy Magdy in Cairo
Pentagon seeks boost in weapons production
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell on Saturday said the department was focused on boosting munitions acquisitions to provide “the weapons our warfighters need at the pace the threat demands.”
The war with Iran has used up more of the U.S. military’s already diminished stockpiles of advanced missile interceptors, says a new analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies. The shortage has caused concern among allies like Ukraine and Taiwan who seek more U.S. military support.
Parnell's statement said the push was part of a broader modernization effort that predated the war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28.

sources.news_title: In new break from Trump, Netanyahu rejects Gaza plan
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday rejected a US-led Gaza plan endorsed by Hamas, taking fresh distance from US President Donald Trump as he faces razor-tight elections.
After more than a week of gradually escalating criticism of the plan, Netanyahu explicitly opposed it in the face of pushback from his right-wing base.
"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said, referring to a plan signed off on by Hamas in late July.
The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting.
Netanyahu described Trump, with whom he has also had a growing break on Iran, as "our greatest friend in the White House" – but quickly made clear he was willing to challenge him.
He said Israel was raising its objections to the Gaza plan with the United States.
"They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader, is running even or trailing in some polls ahead of October 27 elections, the country's first since the devastating October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas.
Polls show that the Gaza plan is widely unpopular with Netanyahu's right-wing base and far-right members of his cabinet, having urged him to call a new vote to kill the Gaza plan.
Hamas, days after selecting a new leader, Khalil al-Hayya, announced it supported the Gaza plan. It called on the United States to pressure Netanyahu.
"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," Bassem Naim, a member of Hamas's political bureau, told AFP.
Netanyahu until recently campaigned on the strength of his relationship with Trump, who since his first term has taken unprecedented steps to back Israel, including moving the US embassy to Jerusalem.
Trump joined Netanyahu in late February in attacking Iran. But the two diverged when Trump sought a ceasefire with Iran in April as the war sapped his popularity at home and sent oil prices soaring.
Netanyahu told his cabinet that "with an agreement or without an agreement, as long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons", a goal he has long alleged Tehran is pursuing.
Netanyahu last week also ordered fresh strikes on Lebanon in response to what Israel called a ceasefire violation by Iran-backed Hezbollah, just as Israel and Lebanon were holding US-mediated talks.
The Gaza plan was the latest stage in a US-brokered ceasefire announced in October that has reduced but not ended Israeli operations in Gaza.
Trump had described as a "major milestone" the agreement by Hamas to surrender weapons to a nascent Palestinian governing body.
The plan said Israel would begin pulling out forces in tandem with the disarmament, a timeline adamantly rejected by Israel.
After meeting Netanyahu last week, Trump's body implementing the deal, dubbed the Board of Peace, backtracked and said Israel would only need to withdraw after "complete" disarmament, but it was apparently not enough for the Israeli leader.
Netanyahu said that Hamas must give up all of its weapons.
"We are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament," Netanyahu said. (AFP)
Edited by Edmond Fong

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump’s peace plan for Gaza
sources.text:
Israel rejected a U.S.-backed peace plan for Gaza Sunday, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu saying that Israel will not withdraw from the enclave until Hamas has been “genuinely disarmed.”
In dismissing the 15-point plan drawn up by U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, Netanyahu also said that as long as he is prime minister, “a Palestinian state will not be established” in Gaza or the West Bank.
The peace plan announced by the White House at the end of July would require Hamas to disarm and relinquish its governance in Gaza, while Israel would be required to withdraw its military forces from the territory.
Advertisement
Hamas has said that it would begin disarming, but in recent days an Israeli official said the country still had “serious security concerns.”
The rejection is a blow to peace negotiations the Trump administratoin has been brokering since September. The U.S. president had described the plan, now rejected by Israel, as a “critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government” and giving Israel “the security it deserves.”
Israel appears unlikely to pull back significant forces or make other concessions ahead of legislative elections scheduled for October. Netanyahu faces a tough reelection battle, with his far-right coalition partners urging him to keep up the pressure on Hamas and leave forces in Gaza. Opponents also accuse him of failing to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack when Hamas-led militants attacked Israeli communities, killing about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and taking 251 others hostage. Israel responded with a punishing military offensive that has killed more than 73,000 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
Netanyahu said on Sunday that he is now in discussions with U.S. officials about how to move forward. “They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us, and we know how to stand up to these things,” he said.

sources.news_title: Blow For Donald Trump As Benjamin Netanyahu Rejects His 15-Point Gaza Peace Plan
sources.text:
Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected Donald Trump’s 15-point plan for peace in Gaza.
The Israeli prime minister said his country’s troops will not withdraw from the region until Hamas has “genuinely” disarmed.
His comments are a major blow for Trump’s hopes of ending the conflict.
The US president’s Board of Peace announced last month it had reached an agreement for the “complete disarmament” of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.
But Hamas said that was contingent on Israel ending “all forms of aggression” and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.
Speaking on Sunday, Netanyahu said: “Israel rejects the 15-point document.”
“The Israel Defense Forces will not carry out any withdrawal until the dismantling of Hamas and its weapons,” he said.
“And when I say dismantling Hamas and its weapons, that means heavy weaponry, less heavy weaponry and smaller arms. All weaponry.
“We’re talking about a true dismantling and not a fictitious dismantling.”
Trump first announced his peace plan for Gaza last September.
Listen to Commons People, the podcast that makes politics easy. Every week, Kevin Schofield and Kate Nicholson unpack the week’s biggest stories to keep you informed. Join us for straightforward analysis of what’s going on at Westminster.

sources.news_title: Trump Humiliated as Ally Flat-Out Rejects His Demands
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the latest peace plan for Gaza that the Trump administration offered.
The blow comes less than a week after Trump announced, through his so-called “Board of Peace,” a 15-point plan aimed at securing stable peace in the territory. The administration had portrayed the plan as a historic agreement and massive breakthrough, as it would secure the disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.
But Netanyahu on Sunday made his country’s side clear: “I want to be precise here: Israel rejects the 15-point document.”
“We are now discussing this with the Americans,” he continued. “They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand up to those things.”
“As long as I am prime minister, no Palestinian state will be established — not in Gaza and not in the West Bank,” he added.
The news comes as Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition is facing a tough election at the end of October. Polling suggests that his coalition will fall short of the 61-seat required majority to form a government.
Netanyahu had promised “absolute victory” over Hamas after the terrorist group led the Oct. 7 attack that sparked Israel’s war in Gaza. But as the war continues three years later, Hamas still controls most of the territory as it has for nearly two decades.
Israel and Hamas had agreed to an initial U.S.-backed cease-fire in Gaza in October, but questions still remain about the future of Hamas’ control of the territory.
Trump’s new peace plan had required that Hamas give up its weapons, also one of the core demands from Israel. Hamas had said it would only agree to the deal if Israel ceased its strikes in Gaza and pulled its troops back to the “yellow line,” as defined by the October ceasefire agreement.
Israeli forces occupy the majority of Gaza, and senior officials have signaled that they want to expand that control further.
Netanyahu’s rejection of the Trump-backed peace plan comes as the two world leaders have had a rocky relationship in recent weeks.
Trump, who has dubbed himself the “president of peace,” has grown increasingly frustrated with Netanyahu’s repeated strikes in Gaza and Lebanon, especially as he attempts to negotiate an end to his disastrous war in Iran.
In June, he launched a profanity-ridden attack on Netanyahu after Israel struck Lebanon during talks with Iran.
Trump said he told Netanyahu at the time, “Why did Bibi have to do a f---ing attack? I was so p---ed off. I let him know. He has no f---ing judgement. I let him know that.”

Trump’s Gaza Plan Is a Blueprint for Permanent Subjugation
Netanyahu rejects Trump’s peace plan for Gaza as he refuses to withdraw until Hamas is disarmed
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared Sunday that his government is rejecting a 15-point peace proposal advanced by President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, according to a report from the Daily Mail.
The announcement marks a sharp setback for efforts to end the prolonged conflict in Gaza, with Netanyahu insisting Israeli forces will remain in the territory until Hamas is completely stripped of its weapons.
“I want to clarify this: Israel rejects the 15-point document. I have heard people saying, ‘You didn’t say that.’ So here I am saying it again,” Netanyahu told a meeting of his Cabinet. He added firmly, “The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed.”
Last month, Trump had hailed what he called a breakthrough in negotiations after suggesting Hamas had agreed to lay down its arms. The Board of Peace roadmap envisioned a phased Israeli pullback from Gaza tied to progressive disarmament by the militant group. Netanyahu made clear that sequence is unacceptable. Israeli troops, he insisted, will stay put until genuine and total disarmament occurs.
“When I say Hamas must be disarmed, I mean heavy weapons, lighter weapons, all weapons. We are talking about genuine disarmament, not a fictitious one,” the Israeli leader declared.
Hamas has staked out the opposite position. The group previously stated it would consider disarming only after a full Israeli withdrawal from Gaza and an end to military operations, with the surrender of heavier weapons postponed further and conditioned on the establishment of a Palestinian state.
Netanyahu also reiterated his longstanding rejection of Palestinian statehood, stating, “As long as I am Prime Minister, there will be no Palestinian State.” The comments come as he prepares for a hard-fought election campaign in October, in which the wars in Gaza and Iran are expected to play central roles.
Senior Hamas official Basim Naeem sharply criticized Netanyahu’s stance, calling on U.S. officials and international mediators to pressure the Israeli leader to adhere to the agreed roadmap and “prevent him from obstructing the process for domestic political and electoral considerations.” Naeem said Hamas remains committed to the Board of Peace proposal, framing it as an act of “national responsibility” that serves the interests of the Palestinian people.
Despite the public rejection, Netanyahu acknowledged that discussions with Washington continue. “We are currently discussing this issue with the Americans,” he said. “They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand firm on these matters.”

sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu restated his rejection of Donald Trump’s latest Gaza plan in televised remarks to his right-wing government on Sunday, even as Israel’s military has effectively halted attacks in the territory under pressure from the United States President.
Netanyahu is in campaign mode as he seeks re-election at a vote due on October 27 but is caught between far-right ministers angered by concessions in Gaza and his key military backer, Trump, who wants progress toward ending the conflict there with a new 15-point peace plan.
Israel has scaled back attacks in Gaza since Monday, when Nikolay Mladenov, the Gaza envoy for Trump’s Board of Peace that oversees the Gaza ceasefire, met with Netanyahu.
A source familiar with Israel’s position said it had agreed that the military would only act against what it perceives as immediate threats in Gaza and no longer carry out targeted assassinations as it had been doing on a near-daily basis.
ISRAEL AND HAMAS DISAGREE OVER TIMINGS IN TRUMP’S PLAN
Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough in his plan to end the war, to which both Israel and Hamas agreed, with Israeli forces withdrawing as Hamas disarms and an International Stabilisation Force working with a new Palestinian police force to secure the enclave.
But complications have swiftly emerged. Israel has said that Israeli troops in Gaza would not move before Hamas disarms. Hamas has insisted that Israel halt attacks before it begins implementing the part of the agreement dealing with its arms.
“Israel does not accept the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at the start of a meeting with cabinet ministers. The military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed … it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry.
“And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament,” he said, noting that Israel is in talks with the United States on the plan. Netanyahu made similar remarks in a social media post on Tuesday.
“They [the United States] have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us,” Netanyahu said without elaborating.
Basem Naim, a senior Hamas official, told Reuters on Sunday that the group remained committed to the roadmap agreed with mediators in Cairo 10 days ago.
“We expect the mediators and the United States guarantor to press Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons, while continuing to jeopardise the region’s security and stability.”
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich praised Netanyahu.
“We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas,” he said in a statement. “The (military) cannot withdraw even a milimetre from the Gaza Strip. The Gaza Strip cannot begin any process of reconstruction before the complete dismantling and demobilisation of Hamas and the Gaza Strip.”
Trump said last month that Iran-backed Hamas, which ruled Gaza for nearly two decades before carrying out the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel that triggered the Gaza war, had agreed to lay down its weapons.
Hamas avoids the use of the term “disarmament” and said the group agreed to hand over weapons to be stored under a United States-backed Palestinian technocrat administration that would run the affairs in Gaza under the supervision of Trump’s Board of Peace.
Hamas said it agreed to the plan in order to spare the people in Gaza a possible resumption of war, but it added that the implementation of the deal would depend on Israel first meeting its own commitments, including withdrawal.
Since the United States-mediated agreement reached in October to end the war, Israel had vowed to hunt down every militant who had taken part in the October 2023 attack before stopping the targeted attacks on Monday.

sources.news_title: Israel "rejects" US Gaza plan accepted by Hamas
sources.text:
At a cabinet meeting, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the army would make 'no withdrawal until Hamas is truly disarmed,' effectively rejecting the plan.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the latest US roadmap accepted by Hamas to launch the second phase of the Gaza peace plan, taking fresh distance from President Donald Trump as he faces razor-tight elections.
After more than a week of gradually escalating criticism of the plan, Netanyahu explicitly opposed it in the face of pushback from his right-wing base.
The Israeli government says any withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Gaza Strip is conditional on the Islamist group being "genuinely" disarmed.
"Israel rejects the 15-point document" presented at the end of July by Donald Trump’s Peace Council, Benjamin Netanyahu said during a cabinet meeting.
The Israeli army would carry out "no withdrawal as long as Hamas is not genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens," Netanyahu said.
US efforts ditched
Israeli PM described Trump, with whom he has also had a growing break on Iran, as "our greatest friend in the White House" — but quickly made clear he was willing to challenge him.
He said Israel was raising its objections to the Gaza plan with the United States.
"They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us, and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.
Hamas, days after selecting a new leader, Khalil al-Hayya, announced it supported the Gaza plan. It called on the United States to pressure Netanyahu.
"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," Bassem Naim, a member of Hamas's political bureau, told AFP.
Growing friction with Trump
Netanyahu until recently campaigned on the strength of his relationship with Trump, who since his first term has taken unprecedented steps to back Israel, including moving the US embassy to Jerusalem.
Trump joined Netanyahu in late February in attacking Iran. But the two diverged when Trump sought a ceasefire with Iran in April, as the war sapped his popularity at home and sent oil prices soaring.
Netanyahu told his cabinet that "with an agreement or without an agreement, as long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons", a goal he has long alleged Tehran is pursuing.
Netanyahu last week also ordered fresh strikes on Lebanon in response to what Israel called a ceasefire violation by Iran-backed Hezbollah, just as Israel and Lebanon were holding US-mediated talks.
The Gaza plan was the latest stage in a US-brokered ceasefire announced in October that has reduced but not ended Israeli operations in Gaza.
Trump had described, as a "major milestone," the agreement by Hamas to surrender weapons to a nascent Palestinian governing body.
Netanyahu's base scorn plan
The plan said Israel would begin pulling out forces in tandem with the disarmament, a timeline adamantly rejected by Israel.
After meeting Netanyahu last week, Trump's body implementing the deal, dubbed the Board of Peace, backtracked and said Israel would only need to withdraw after "complete" disarmament, but it was apparently not enough for the Israeli leader.
Netanyahu said that Hamas must give up all of its weapons.
"We are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament," Netanyahu said.
Polls show that the Gaza plan is widely unpopular with Netanyahu's right-wing base and far-right members of his cabinet, who have urged him to call a new vote to kill the Gaza plan.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader, is running even or trailing in some polls ahead of the 27 October elections, the country's first since the devastating 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point Gaza plan
sources.text:
Israel has rejected US President Donald Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu saying Israeli forces will remain occupying the territory until Hamas gives up its weapons.
Netanyahu announced the decision during an Israeli cabinet meeting on Sunday, 9 August, placing Israel at odds with a roadmap promoted by the US-led Board of Peace.
“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu told ministers.
“The Israeli military will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens,” he said.
Netanyahu said Israel wanted the removal of all Hamas weapons, including lighter weapons. The initial stages described in the 15-point roadmap focus on heavy weapons, arms production facilities, weapons depots and Hamas’s tunnel network.
The Israeli prime minister said discussions with Washington were continuing despite his rejection of the document.
“They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some are not acceptable to us, and we know how to stand firm on these things,” Netanyahu said.
The White House and Hamas had not issued an immediate response to Netanyahu’s rejection.
Trump announced on 30 July that an agreement had been reached for the “complete disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza”. He described the agreement as “a monumental step toward lasting peace and security”.
Hamas confirmed that it had accepted a draft agreement but said implementation depended on Israel meeting its commitments under the ceasefire. The group said Israel must complete the first phase of the agreement, including withdrawing its forces from Gaza and ending military operations, before the second phase begins.
The Board of Peace later said an Israeli withdrawal would occur only after Hamas completed its disarmament. That position followed talks between Netanyahu and the board’s director, Nickolay Mladenov.
Netanyahu's announcement also comes before elections in Israel and amid pressure from members of his governing coalition.
The BBC reported that Netanyahu has faced demands from far-right coalition partners for another cabinet vote on the Gaza framework. National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir has rejected the draft, describing it as “not acceptable”.
The “ceasefire” that began last October reduced the scale of the genocidal war but did not end Israeli military action, near-daily strikes and settler attacks inside Gaza.
Gaza’s health ministry says more than 1,250 people have been killed since the truce took effect in mid-October 2025. The ministry says at least 4,120 people have been wounded during the same period, while more than 800 bodies have been recovered from rubble.
The ministry puts the number of people killed in Gaza since October 2023 at more than 73,300 and the number wounded at more than 174,000.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point Gaza peace plan
sources.text:
World News
Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point Gaza peace plan
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump’s 15-point plan for ending the war in Gaza.
Netanyahu said Israel would not withdraw its troops from Gaza until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.
Trump’s Board of Peace said last month that an agreement had been reached for the “complete disarmament” of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.
However, Hamas said it would only hand over its heavy weapons if Israel ended all forms of aggression and withdrew its forces from the territory.
Israel has continued to carry out strikes in Gaza despite an initial ceasefire agreement reached last October.
“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at a Cabinet meeting on Sunday.
He added that the Israeli military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens”.
Trump described the plan as “a monumental step toward lasting peace and security” after Hamas said it had accepted a plan for the disarmament of armed groups in Gaza.
However, Netanyahu said Hamas must be fully disarmed before any Israeli withdrawal, stressing that the process could not involve “fictitious disarmament”.
He said he was currently holding discussions with US officials on how to move forward with the plan.

sources.news_title: Israel ‘rejects’ Trump’s 15-point peace plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
sources.text:
Israel ‘rejects’ Trump’s 15-point peace plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on Google
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has fully rejected the 15-point plan to disarm Hamas after President Trump announced a breakthrough last week, in which his Board of Peace announced a deal with the terror group.
Trump claimed last month that his panel cut a deal with Hamas for the terror group to disarm in exchange for Israel withdrawing from the Gaza Strip, but Netanyahu voiced skepticism about its sincerity.
“I want to be precise here: Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at a weekend cabinet meeting.
Netanyahu declared that Israel will “not withdraw at all until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and citizens.”
“We are now discussing this with the Americans,” the Israeli leader said. “They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand up to those things.”
“As long as I am prime minister, no Palestinian state will be established — not in Gaza and not in the West Bank,” he added.
Despite their once famously chummy relationship, Netanyahu and Trump have been at odds over key details of the president’s push for peace in the region.
Last October, Trump’s administration cut a 20-point Gaza peace plan, featuring three phases: cease-fire and humanitarian support, demilitarization and reconstruction, and recognition of a Palestinian state.
Trump’s team has been working to get into phase 2 of that overarching plan, and the president is the chair of the Board of Peace overseeing the effort.
The 15-point proposal Trump announced last month had been seen as a potential breakthrough. Hamas and other Palestinian groups conditioned agreeing to the proposal on Israel committing to moving its forces back to the “yellow line” in the 20-point peace plan.
At the moment, Israel has forces on the ground in over half of the Gaza Strip, including in its east and south. Some members of Netanyahu’s cabinet have expressed interest in expanding the footprint in the Palestinian enclave.
Hamas also insisted that Israel cease all strikes in the Gaza Strip.
“Contrary to all those who preach to us, we do what must be done for Israel’s security and we can and will stand our ground even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu further said Sunday.
After Netanyahu revealed his opposition to the 15-point plan, a top leader in Hamas demanded the US pressure the Israeli leader to get on board.
“We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons,” Bassem Naim, a member of Hamas’ politburo, posted on X.
Netanyahu, who has long been a hardliner, is facing an election in October, and his coalition is underwater in a lot of polling.
He had a meeting with Trump and Vice President JD Vance during his trip to Washington, DC, last month to attend the funeral of late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC).

sources.news_title: Netanyahu Rejects Gaza Plan: Hamas Must Disarm Before IDF Withdraws
sources.text:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has drawn a clear line regarding the future of Gaza: Israel will not withdraw from territory currently held by the IDF until Hamas has been genuinely disarmed.
Netanyahu announced that Israel rejects the Board of Peace’s 15-point Gaza plan, making clear that any diplomatic framework must conform to Israel’s fundamental security requirements rather than force Israel to surrender its military leverage before those requirements are met.
“The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed,” Netanyahu said.
That sentence goes to the heart of the dispute.
For Israel, the issue is not simply whether Hamas formally agrees to disarmament. The question is whether Hamas actually loses the military capabilities that allowed it to carry out the October 7 massacre and wage war against Israel.
Israel has learned the consequences of confusing diplomatic promises with realities on the ground.
The 2005 Gaza disengagement removed every Israeli soldier and Jewish community from Gaza. Instead of producing peace, the territory eventually became a massive terrorist stronghold filled with rockets, tunnels and armed Hamas forces.
Israel cannot afford to repeat that mistake.
Any Israeli withdrawal conducted before Hamas is verifiably disarmed risks creating another security vacuum. Hamas could use that space to regroup, rebuild its military infrastructure, recruit new terrorists and prepare for another round of war.
That is why the territory currently controlled by the IDF represents more than a negotiating position. It is strategic leverage.
Netanyahu’s message therefore appears straightforward: disarmament must come first. Withdrawal can only be discussed afterward.
The broader question is whether international negotiators will accept Israel’s post-October 7 security doctrine or continue promoting frameworks based on Israeli withdrawals followed by promises of future demilitarization.
For Netanyahu, that sequence is no longer acceptable.
Israel is insisting that the reality on the ground change first.
Only then can the map change.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu Rejects Gaza Plan: Israel Won’t Withdrawal Until Hamas Is ‘Genuinely Disarmed’
sources.text:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu restated on Aug. 9 that Israel has rejected U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace’s plan for Gaza and will not withdraw until Hamas is fully disarmed.
Trump posted on Truth Social in July that an agreement had been reached for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.
Trump said the agreement is part of his plan that will be implemented in phases. As disarmament takes place, Israeli forces would withdraw, while an International Stabilization Force and a new Palestinian police force would assume responsibility for security.
Gaza would ultimately be governed by a new Palestinian government working with the Board of Peace.
The Board of Peace is an international organization chaired by Trump that seeks to promote stability, establish lawful governance, and secure lasting peace in areas affected by conflict. Its founding members include the United States, Israel, Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and more than 20 other countries committed to international peace-building efforts, according to its website.
Speaking at the start of a government meeting on Aug. 9, Netanyahu said disarmament must include all of Hamas’s weapons and must be genuine rather than “fictitious.”
He said Israel is discussing the issue with the United States and that some U.S. proposals are acceptable to Israel, while others are not.
Netanyahu also said Israeli forces would continue acting against threats to Israeli troops and civilians.
He rejected the establishment of a Palestinian state.
“As for the Gaza Strip: First and foremost, I wish to clarify the main point: As long as I am Prime Minister, a Palestinian state will not be established, neither in Gaza nor in Judea and Samaria,” Netanyahu said in a statement.
He also addressed Iran and Lebanon, pledging to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and saying Israel is conducting an important military operation in Lebanon aimed at eliminating threats.
Israel has been conducting operations in Lebanon.
Two Israeli reservists were killed and four others were seriously wounded during operations recently in southern Lebanon, according to the Israeli military. Lebanese authorities said an Israeli strike also killed one person and wounded 12 others in the town of Tibnin, Lebanon.
Israel gave an evacuation warning to residents before the strike.
The incidents come as the United States conducts talks aimed at reducing hostilities along the Israel–Lebanon border and advancing a broader peace agreement. U.S. officials said the discussions include the disarmament of Hezbollah and other Iran-backed threats, the redeployment of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon, and the implementation of a pilot zone process transferring security responsibilities to the Lebanese army.

"It needs to be genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament," Netanyahu said.
"When I say Hamas is disarmed, that means the heavy weapons, the less heavy weapons, all the weapons," he added.
Hamas remains committed to a Gaza roadmap agreed with mediators and representatives of the Board of Peace in Cairo 10 days ago, senior Hamas official Basem Naim told Reuters.
Hamas expects mediators and the United States to "press Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap," he added.
Trump had teased a disarmament of the Hamas terrorist group in Gaza as a landmark step toward peace, but there remained skeptics, including Israel's Netanyahu, whose Sunday comments put him at odds with the latest Board of Peace proposal as the Trump administration seeks to move forward with a broader plan for Gaza following the ceasefire reached last year.

The Israeli leader’s rejection of the 15-point proposal underscores the hurdles facing efforts to turn the ceasefire into a lasting settlement, particularly over the sequence of Hamas’ disarmament and an Israeli military withdrawal.

Netanyahu indicated Israel would continue working with Washington but said the government would hold firm on its security demands, particularly its insistence that Hamas be fully stripped of its weapons before Israeli troops leave their positions in Gaza.
Netanyahu also used his remarks Sunday to address Israeli operations elsewhere in the region, saying the military had recently acted "forcefully" in Lebanon and carried out what he described as "very important activity."
On Iran, Netanyahu said Tehran has refrained from striking Israel because "it knows what a powerful blow we will deal it if it does," while praising Trump and the U.S.-Israel alliance over efforts to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.

"And I wish to emphasize once again: With or without an agreement, as long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have a nuclear weapon. Because the existence of our precious country, the country of all of us, the existence of Israel, is not up for negotiation."

sources.text:
Netanyahu rejects Gaza withdrawal before Hamas disarms
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the US-backed Board of Peace roadmap for disarming Hamas in the Gaza Strip in return for withdrawal by the Israeli military.
"Israel does not accept the 15-point document," Netanyahu said during a cabinet meeting in Jerusalem on Sunday.
"The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed," he added, referring to the Israel Defense Forces
Netanyahu said this applied to all weapons, not just heavy weapons. The prime minister also reaffirmed his opposition to an independent Palestinian state.
The Board of Peace stated nearly a week ago that it expected Israel to make a complete withdrawal from the coastal enclave only after Hamas had been disarmed.
Under the roadmap, Israel and Hamas are supposed to halt the fighting.
A Palestinian transitional administration, supported by an international stabilisation force, is to take control of administration and security as the Israeli military withdraws.
The weapons handed over by Hamas under international supervision would remain under Palestinian control. Israel rejects this, however, and insists that the weapons be removed from Palestinian territory.
Hamas made the surrender of heavy weapons conditional on several requirements, including the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the Gaza Strip and the establishment of a Palestinian state.
As part of a peace plan brokered by US President Donald Trump, an internationally staffed Board of Peace was established at the beginning of the year.
It is tasked with overseeing the reconstruction of the Gaza Strip and the postwar political order in the devastated coastal territory.

sources.news_title: 'No 'Fatahstan' nor 'Hamastan'': Netanyahu rejects Trump's Board of Peace 15-point plan
sources.text:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday rejected reports of Israeli weakness or withdrawals on multiple fronts, declaring that Israel remains determined to protect its security interests and will not accept a Palestinian state in either Gaza or Judea and Samaria.
Speaking at the start of the Government meeting, Netanyahu said Iran has refrained from attacking Israel because it knows the consequences of doing so.
“You have surely noticed an interesting point: Iran attacks all the countries in the region, and even outside the region, but there is one country it does not attack - the State of Israel," Netanyahu said.
“It has not attacked thus far; it might attack, but why have long weeks passed and it has not attacked us? Because it knows the massive blow we will inflict upon it if it does so."
Netanyahu said the comments came amid what he described as “a wave of rumors about Israeli weakness and Israeli withdrawals on all fronts."
Turning to Iran, Netanyahu praised US President Donald Trump and the partnership between Israel and the US in confronting Iran's nuclear ambitions.
“I greatly appreciate President Trump. He is the greatest of our friends in the White House," Netanyahu said.
“I greatly appreciate the historical partnership with the US against Iran's attempts to acquire nuclear weapons."
“With or without an agreement, as long as I am Prime Minister, Iran will not have a nuclear weapon," he added. “Because the existence of our precious country, the country of all of us, the existence of Israel, is not up for negotiation."
Regarding Lebanon, Netanyahu said Israel has recently conducted operations against terrorists and threats in the country.
“In recent days, Israel has acted with force in Lebanon, eliminating terrorists, including on the Ali Taher ridge," he said. “We are in the midst of a very important operation."
He said Israel was acting “prudently and wisely-with both determination and wisdom," while working alongside the IDF to eliminate threats.
On Gaza, Netanyahu reiterated his opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state.
“As long as I am Prime Minister, a Palestinian state will not be established, neither in Gaza nor in Judea and Samaria," he said. “Neither 'Fatahstan' nor 'Hamastan'."
Netanyahu also addressed the 15-point proposal published by President Donald Trump's Board of Peace for Gaza.
“Israel does not accept the 15-point document," he stated.
“I have heard people saying: 'You didn't say it.' So here I am saying it again: Israel does not accept the 15-point document."
He stressed that the IDF would not withdraw until Hamas had been fully disarmed.
“The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed," Netanyahu said. “And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry."
“We are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament," he added.
Netanyahu said Israel is currently discussing the issue with the Americans, noting that some US proposals are acceptable to Israel while others are not.
“They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable, and we know how to stand firm against these things," he said.
“The IDF will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens," Netanyahu added.
Concluding his remarks, Netanyahu said Israel's security interests would remain non-negotiable.
“The existence of Israel and the security of all Israeli citizens are not up for negotiation," he said. “We stand firm on these interests."
“We do not do this in advertising agencies; we actually do it on the ground," Netanyahu continued, citing Israel's operations in Rafah and the Philadelphi Corridor, Lebanon, and Iran.
“Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel's security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary."

sources.news_title: No Palestinian state as long as I am PM: Netanyahu rejects Gaza peace plan - The Tribune
sources.text:
Tel Aviv [Israel], August 9 (ANI): Israel has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point Gaza peace plan and will not withdraw its forces from the enclave until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced on Sunday.
"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said, referring to a proposal endorsed in late July by Hamas, according to Israeli media.
Speaking at a cabinet meeting, Netanyahu emphasised that the Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed, and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens."
Facing pressure from far-right coalition partners urging a fresh cabinet vote to abandon the peace plan, Netanyahu, who is locked in a competitive electoral race according to opinion polls, noted that Israel remains in discussions with Washington on the issue.
"They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us, and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he stated.
Trump's 15-point framework outlines a phased strategy aimed at terminating the Gaza conflict, disarming armed factions, withdrawing Israeli troops, and transitioning governance of the strip to a Palestinian technocratic body, the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.
Under the roadmap, heavy weaponry, arms depots, military sites, and tunnels would be placed under the committee's control, while an international stabilisation force would be deployed to separate Israeli troops from Palestinian-administered areas.
Israeli forces would then withdraw in stages, paving the way for reconstruction and a longer-term political process towards Palestinian self-determination.
However, a core impasse remains: while Trump previously stated that both sides accepted the framework and that Hamas agreed to lay down its arms, Israel insists full demilitarisation of Hamas must precede any troop pullout, even as it continues military strikes despite the ceasefire established last October.
The widening rift over the peace plan has drawn a rare, unified reaction from eight Muslim-majority countries.
The United Arab Emirates joined Qatar, Jordan, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, and Egypt in issuing a joint declaration condemning ongoing Israeli military operations in Gaza.
The foreign ministers warned that continued military action risks undermining international peace efforts, cautioning that it could "derail the political process", provoke further regional escalation, and deepen the humanitarian crisis in Gaza. (ANI)

"This agreement is a critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the Board of Peace to help the Palestinian people," the president wrote. Israel rejects Trump’s Gaza peace plan and won’t withdraw until Hamas disarms
Trump claimed there had been a breakthrough in his plan to end the war which both Israel and Hamas had agreed
Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected Donald Trump’s Gaza peace plan, insisting Israel will not withdraw until Hamas fully disarms.
The US president claimed last month that there had been a breakthrough in his plan to end the war, which both Israel and Hamas agreed to last year and which started with the ceasefire.
Trump said that Hamas, which ruled Gaza for nearly two decades before carrying out the 7 October 2023 attack on Israel that triggered the Gaza war, had agreed to lay down its weapons.
“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday.
The Israeli military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens”, he added.
The Israeli prime minister said he is now in discussions with US officials about how to go forward, deeming some ideas “acceptable” while some “are not”.
Last month, Egypt, which is mediating negotiations between Israel and Hamas, said that both sides had agreed to a new 15-point roadmap and that a future meeting would be held in Cairo “to discuss implementation mechanisms”.
Trump had thanked Egypt, Qatar and Turkey for brokering the agreement and called the deal “historic”.
A senior Hamas negotiator said at the time that the group’s disarmament was conditional on Israel fulfilling its commitments under the agreement, including withdrawing from Gaza and allowing the establishment of a national committee and reconstruction efforts.
Senior Hamas official Ghazi Hamad said: “The agreement contains a clear provision stating that Israel must commit to and implement its obligations. If Israel does not implement the agreement, neither will we.”
Israel’s rejection of the plan is a further blow for Trump, who announced his Gaza peace plan in September last year.
Just months away from Israeli elections, Netanyahu is considered unlikely to pull back from his hardline stance.
Last month, the Israeli prime minister told his cabinet that he would not agree to requests from the US to withdraw troops from locations in Syria, Lebanon, and Gaza, according to Channel 13.
Sources told the broadcaster that Netanyahu said he would “stand on my own two feet and resist” amid growing pressure from the Israeli far-right for the military campaign to continue.
What was in Trump’s 15-point plan for peace in Gaza?
The deal included the total disarmament of Hamas and other groups in Gaza as well as the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the territory.
It also stipulated that Hamas and “other factions” agree that “all civilian governance and security functions in Gaza shall be handed over” to a new technocratic body set up to run the enclave.
With that, the technocratic body would take over responsibility for handling “internal security incidents”.
The 15-point plan also said that the process would be “linked” to an Israeli withdrawal “in phases”, towards a complete withdrawal from the Palestinian enclave. There was no mention of a reconstruction process.
Under the initial deal to end the war, Israel was supposed to pull back to a demarcation point termed the Yellow Line, separating 47 per cent of the land controlled by the Palestinians from the 53 per cent controlled by Israel. Israel was supposed to steadily withdraw from its position, but has instead increased its area of control to around two-thirds.
The Board of Peace on Monday had hailed a “constructive and detailed” meeting between Netanyahu, Israeli officials and Gaza envoy Nikolay Mladenov.
The Board noted that the full withdrawal of the Israeli military beyond the Yellow Line “will take place only once decommissioning is complete, as Hamas committed to the mediators”.
Hamas rejected the word “disarmament” but has said it would hand over its weapons for storage under the control of a US-backed Palestinian administration after Israel halted operations and withdrew its forces in line with last year’s ceasefire.

Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.

But Hamas said handing over its heavy weapons was contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.
On Sunday, a senior Board of Peace official insisted the US-backed peace plan for the territory remained the only way forward.
Israel has continued to carry out strikes on Gaza since agreeing to an initial ceasefire in the territory last October.
"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday.
The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he added.
A Hamas official told the BBC on Sunday the group "reaffirms it commitment" to the agreement and it was ready "to engage seriously and responsibly in implementing" the 15-point plan.
They called on mediators to ensure "that all parties comply with what has been agreed".
Israel's rejection signals another blow for Trump's Gaza peace plan which was announced in September last year.
The plan included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza.
Netanyahu's statement does not come as a surprise.
But he has taken some time to make it, perhaps reflecting the difficult position the Israeli leader is in.
He clearly is unhappy with Trump's plan but at the same time he will not want to upset his closest ally.
It's just over a week since Trump announced what he called a "monumental step toward lasting peace and security" - that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm, on condition that Israel withdraws its forces from Gaza.
On Sunday, Netanyahu was clear that was not going to happen under his watch. He said Hamas had to disarm first, adding that it couldn't be some "fictitious disarmament" - it had to be real.
The reality is any disarmament and withdrawal of Israeli forces would likely need to be phased.
Netanyahu said he was now in discussion with US officials about how to go forward.
"They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.
But just months before Israeli elections and under pressure from members of his right-wing coalition to take a tough stance on Gaza, he is unlikely to want to make concessions.
He has faced calls from far-right parts of the coalition to hold a new cabinet vote and end the Gaza plan, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir who dismissed the draft as "not acceptable".
Nickolay Mladenov - a senior diplomat tasked with implementing Donald Trump's peace plan - defended the plan on Sunday and said discussions were ongoing in the hope of a "positive outcome".
The board's high representative for Gaza told Israel's Channel 12 that Israel had been asked "to give the process a chance" and said the plan was "the only way forward" to ensure there was no repeat of the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas.
Mladenov said the plan was built on a process that was "verifiable, that is reversible, that at each stage can be stopped, and that we have built up with a very clear-eyed understanding of what are the challenges ahead".
He also said that Israel would not be required to withdraw until it could be verified that Hamas was taking steps to disarm.
According to the United Nations, about 1.9 million people - 90% of Gaza's population - have been displaced in the territory since the war in Gaza started.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

Mr Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader, who according to polls is in a tight race to stay in power, has faced calls from his far-right allies to hold a new cabinet vote and end the Gaza plan.
He said that Israel was speaking with the United States about its objections.
"They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.
Mr Netanyahu said that Hamas must give up all of its weapons, a goal that Board of Peace members say is not realistically achievable.
"We are talking about real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament," he added.
Hamas, head of board remain committed to plan
The head of Mr Trump's body implementing the plan, dubbed the Board of Peace, defended the plan as a way to prevent a repeat of 7 October.
"The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again," Nickolay Mladenov, the board's high representative for Gaza, told Israel's Channel 12 television.
He said he hoped for a "positive outcome" from follow-up discussions with Israel, and characterised the latest stage of the deal as a commitment involving the United States, Hamas and the Board of Peace - notably leaving out Israel.
Mr Mladenov again promised that Israel would not face any obligations until Hamas gave up all its weapons, down to Kalashnikov rifles - but said Israel would eventually need to pull out.
Hamas, which publicly backed the plan days after selecting a new leader, Khalil al-Hayya, called on the US to push Mr Netanyahu.
"We expect the mediators and the American guarantor to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap, and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons," Bassem Naim, a member of Hamas's political bureau, said.
Hamas in a statement said it was still committed to the plan.

JERUSALEM - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced Sunday that Israel rejects a 15-point Gaza peace roadmap plan presented by the US-led "Board of Peace," maintaining that Israeli forces will not withdraw until Hamas is fully disarmed.

The plan was drafted in May by Nickolay Mladenov, "high representative for Gaza" of the "Board of Peace," and officially announced by US President Donald Trump in late July, who said back then the board had reached an agreement on the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.
A day after Trump's announcement, Hamas said it had agreed to the "latest version of the roadmap" for the second phase of the Gaza ceasefire agreement after "fierce" negotiations, but conditioned weaponry arrangements on a complete halt to "aggression," Israeli withdrawal from the enclave, and progress on reconstruction.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu rejects Trump's Gaza Peace Plan, demands Hamas disarm first
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected President Trump’s 15-point peace plan for Gaza, saying Israeli forces will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is “genuinely disarmed.”
“We are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament,” he said at a meeting with government ministers Sunday.
Netanyahu’s comments come just over a week after President Trump announced that his Board of Peace had reached a deal with the Palestinian militant group to completely give up its weapons.
“Today, the Board of Peace reached a HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza. This is a monumental step toward lasting PEACE and SECURITY,” Trump wrote on social media in late July.
Under Trump’s proposed peace deal, Board of Peace officials said Hamas and other militant groups would hand their arms over to a vetted international policing force.
But a senior Hamas official previously told NPR that the group would only hand over their weapons if Israel withdrew from parts of Gaza first.
The latest dispute follows an initial ceasefire reached between Israel and Hamas in October 2025, alongside Trump’s broader 20-point Gaza plan.
That first phase of the peace plan halted major fighting, provided for the release of remaining hostages in exchange for some 2,000 Palestinian prisoners, increased humanitarian aid, and called for a partial Israeli withdrawal. More contentious issues – including Hamas’s disarmament and further Israeli withdrawals – were left to later negotiations.
Trump’s new 15-point roadmap, published on July 31, sought to move those unresolved issues forward. It envisioned Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza and Hamas’s disarmament as part of a phased process, rather than requiring Hamas to fully disarm before Israeli forces began pulling back.
The Board of Peace had already backed Netanyahu on that key point, saying on Aug. 3 that Israeli forces would not withdraw beyond the Yellow Line until Hamas’s weapons were fully decommissioned. Netanyahu’s decision to emphasize his demand again comes less than three months before Israel’s Oct. 27 election, with polls showing his coalition is at risk of losing its majority.
The apparent stalemate comes as Israel still controls roughly 70% of Gaza, according to Palestinian officials and aid agencies.
Hamas released a press statement Sunday saying it was still committed “to the roadmap agreed upon” in the agreement.
NPR’s Anas Baba contributed to this report from Gaza.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump’s Gaza peace plan: No withdrawal until Hamas disarms
sources.text:
Israel rejects Trump’s Gaza deal while Iran shuffles top security official
(AP) — Israel on Sunday rejected a deal announced by U.S. President Donald Trump for Gaza. Details emerged on the potential deal between Iran and Oman on managing the Strait of Hormuz as Tehran suggested that vessels linked to “hostile countries” would be barred. Iran also shuffled its top security post.
Meanwhile, Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels struck a government-held port on the country’s Red Sea coast, deepening fears over threats to strategic shipping routes and a potential return to civil war.
Here’s a look at developments across the Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
Netanyahu insists no Gaza withdrawal until Hamas disarms
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dismissed the deal on Gaza announced by Trump last month, saying Israel’s military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.”
Netanyahu told a Cabinet meeting that “Israel rejects the 15-point document” but is still discussing plans for Gaza with Washington, after making similar comments last week. Trump had said Israeli forces would withdraw as the Hamas militant group’s disarmament is completed. Israeli forces control over half the Palestinian enclave of about 2 million people that’s been largely destroyed.
There was no immediate White House comment on Netanyahu’s statement.
“We remain committed to the road map,” said a member of the Hamas political bureau, Bassem Naim, adding that the group expects mediators and the U.S. to pressure Netanyahu — who also faces domestic tensions as he struggles to hold onto power ahead of the next elections scheduled for Oct. 27.
The Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, sparked the war in Gaza. A fragile ceasefire continues.
Iran’s top security post changes again
Iran named a new head of its powerful Supreme National Security Council, state media reported. Mohsen Rezaei had been a military adviser to Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei and a former Revolutionary Guard commander.
It was the latest shuffle at the top for the politburo-like body, which has a range of political opinions and rivalries and is adapting to the loss of several senior officials in the war.
Rezaei replaces Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who took up the role after Ali Larijani was killed by an Israeli strike in March. Zolghadr will become a political adviser to Khamenei.
Rezaei earlier this month said Iran will never allow an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz, which was considered an international waterway before the war and Tehran’s assertion of control.
Iran says negotiations ‘cannot resume’ until conditions met
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters that negotiations with Oman about “new maritime routes” on the Strait of Hormuz were in the final stages but “this, however, does not mean that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen.” That step requires conditions that “have been conveyed through intermediaries.”
The Supreme National Security Council on Saturday said the strait will not reopen until the U.S. “corrects its behavior.” It demanded that the U.S. never threaten Iran again, a permanent end to the war with Iran and its armed allies, a lifting of the naval blockade of Iranian ports and a withdrawal of the U.S. military from the area. The U.S. also must “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets.
The United States did not comment on the demands. Trump on Sunday asserted to Axios that “we are only semi-negotiating” with Iran and letting economic pressures take their toll.
Araghchi said an “exchange of messages through intermediaries” continues with the U.S. but that doesn’t constitute negotiations, which he said can’t resume until violations of the interim deal end and the U.S. “has remedied” provisions it violated.
Details emerge about a potential Iran-Oman deal
Iran and Oman, located on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz, are working to finalize a temporary deal that would reopen it, with ships entering near Iran and exiting near Oman, according to two people familiar with the talks who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Ships would transit without paying fees or tolls during the interim period.
The agreement is designed to restore the separate interim deal between the U.S. and Iran. The two people said the agreement is endorsed by Gulf Cooperation Council members and is expected to be jointly announced by Iran, Oman, the U.S. and the U.N.’s International Maritime Organization. But they stressed the terms still could change.
The Iranian parliament’s National Security Committee approved “general outlines” of a plan to manage the strait, the state broadcaster reported, but a lawmaker said transits by vessels belonging to “hostile countries” would be prohibited. The member of parliament’s presiding board said countries that have “caused damage” to Iran cannot transit until they compensate for it. There were no further details.
— Michelle Price in Washington and Aamer Madhani in New York
Houthis target Aramco refinery and Red Sea port
The Yemeni government-allied National Resistance Forces said at least seven people — four troops and three civilians — were killed and 15 civilians were injured in the Houthi attack on the port of Mokha.
Fayed al-Noman, the information ministry’s assistant undersecretary, said the rebels fired missiles and drones, severely damaging port buildings and piers as well as commercial goods and food supplies. The military later said missiles landed in several areas, including near a television station.
Mokha is a main port under Yemen’s internationally recognized government and has been renovated to handle shipping that avoids the Houthi-held port of Hodeida.
The Houthis said they targeted military forces and warehouses.
Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesperson, said they also targeted an Aramco refinery in the Saudi city of Jazan with a drone in response to Saudi drones’ breaching Yemen’s airspace over Hajjah and Saada provinces.
The Saudi Energy Ministry reported a fire at a facility belonging to the Aramco refinery, with no casualties. The ministry did not say the cause. The attacks threaten to reignite Yemen’s civil war after a 2022 truce.
— Samy Magdy in Cairo

sources.news_title: Netanyahu: Israel rejects Board of Peace roadmap on Hamas disarmament
sources.text:
The Israel Defense Forces will not carry out any withdrawal from the Gaza Strip until the Hamas terrorist organization is fully disarmed, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday.

Disarming the Iranian-backed terrorist group means that Hamas gives up its “heavy weapons, the less heavy weapons, all the weapons,” he reiterated, saying there had to be “real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament.”
Jerusalem is discussing the matter with the Trump administration, the premier said, adding that the Americans “have ideas, some of them acceptable to us and some not acceptable to us.”
The IDF will continue to thwart threats against Israeli forces and civilians, he vowed.
Israeli Energy and Infrastructure Minister Eli Cohen said on Saturday that Jerusalem opposes the 15-point Roadmap for Gaza “in its current form,” adding that “Hamas is planning a deception.”
Hamas “will say that it intends to abide by the agreement, hand over some of its weapons, and obtain what we used to call, in the language of the past, a hudna. [But] the era of hudna is over,” Cohen told Israel’s Channel 14 broadcaster.
“Hudna” means truce or armistice in Arabic. Hamas has used ceasefires in the past only to regroup ahead of renewed assaults on the Jewish state.
Cohen continued, “Ultimately, Hamas is a murderous terrorist organization. We do not believe a single piece of paper that Hamas [signs].”
Hamas violated the Gaza ceasefire 17 times in a single day, Doron Spielman, Netanyahu’s international spokesman, said on Saturday.

He added that the terrorist organization is in blatant violation of the 20-point plan brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump, which requires Hamas to lay down its arms.
Spielman drew a sharp distinction between the Trump framework, to which Israel agreed, and the 15-point BoP proposal reached with Hamas terrorists through Qatar, Turkey and Egypt. Jerusalem is not a party to the newer plan, he said.
Netanyahu publicly rejected the 15-point framework last week, stating that no Israeli withdrawal will occur before full disarmament.

“I am standing firm on our security interests: We will not withdraw from our current lines until Hamas is completely disarmed,” Netanyahu said in a Hebrew-language video posted to his Facebook page.
He added that IDF soldiers had been instructed “to do everything necessary to defend themselves, to defend our territory, to defend our citizens.”
U.S. President Donald Trump and his team believe they can persuade Hamas to demilitarize the Gaza Strip, he said, adding, “We are examining that.”
