sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, PM Netanyahu says
No Palestinian state as long as I'm PM: Netanyahu rejects Trump's Gaza peace plan
sources.text:
No Palestinian state as long as I'm PM: Netanyahu rejects Trump's Gaza peace plan
Benjamin Netanyahu's remarks came more than a week after Trump hailed the plan as a "major milestone" and said it would pave the way for the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday ruled out a Palestinian state in Gaza or the West Bank and rejected the 15-point Gaza peace plan, dealing a major blow to US President Donald Trump’s claim of a breakthrough towards ending the war.
Hamas, meanwhile, said it remained committed to the roadmap but insisted that Israel must first fulfil its obligations.
“As long as I am Prime Minister, there will be no Palestinian state in Gaza or the West Bank,” Netanyahu said.
Rejecting the 15-point plan announced by the US President, Netanyahu also said Israel would not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas was fully disarmed.
The remarks came more than a week after Trump hailed the roadmap as a “major milestone” and a “great breakthrough."
With Israel rejecting key parts of the plan and Hamas attaching conditions to its implementation, the two sides remain far apart on how the US-backed roadmap should move forward.
ISRAEL RULES OUT WITHDRAWAL BEFORE HAMAS DISARMS
An Israeli official said last week that there would be “no withdrawal whatsoever” of the Israeli military from its current positions unless Hamas underwent what Israel considered genuine disarmament.
Netanyahu has now reinforced that position, saying Israeli forces would not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas was completely disarmed.
The Israeli Prime Minister's outright rejection also sits uneasily with what Trump said after hosting Netanyahu in Washington last week, days before Sunday's remarks.
"Israel helped us, and they've been very good," Trump had said then, calling Israel 'very happy' with the agreement.
Trump, however, acknowledged that implementing the plan could prove difficult. “Will it go through its ups and downs? It’s a very complex situation over there,” he said.
An Israeli political source said Gaza was not discussed during Netanyahu's meeting with Trump in Washington, raising questions over how closely the two leaders are actually aligned on implementing the plan.
HAMAS: COMMITTED TO ROADMAP, BUT SETS CONDITIONS
Hamas, meanwhile, said it remained committed to the roadmap agreed with mediators and representatives of Trump’s Peace Council in Cairo, while insisting that Israel must first fulfil its obligations.
Senior Hamas official Basem Naim told Reuters that the group expected mediators and the United States to pressure Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap.
“We remain committed to the roadmap agreed with mediators and representatives of the Peace Council in Cairo,” Naim said.
Hamas has maintained that Israel must first halt its attacks and fulfil commitments under the earlier ceasefire agreement before the group moves towards giving up its weapons.
“The first step towards an agreement” would have to be an Israeli commitment to stop the killing and end its attacks, the group said.
Ghazi Hamad, another senior Hamas official involved in the negotiations, said the group was prepared to accept what he described as a “difficult and painful” agreement, but stopped short of accepting immediate disarmament.
Hamad said Israel would first have to implement the initial phase of the Sharm el-Sheikh agreement, including ending attacks, withdrawing its forces to earlier positions and allowing greater flows of goods and humanitarian aid into Gaza.
Only after those steps, Hamas said, would it agree to place its weapons under the control of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the Palestinian technocratic body proposed to govern the enclave during the transition.
WHAT TRUMP’S 15-POINT PLAN SAYS
Trump’s 15-point roadmap lays out a phased plan to end the Gaza war, disarm armed groups, withdraw Israeli forces and shift governance of the enclave to a Palestinian technocratic body.
Under the plan, Israel and Hamas would first have to complete their existing ceasefire commitments before moving to the next phase.
Hamas and other Palestinian factions would then hand over Gaza’s civil administration and internal security to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.
The plan also calls for heavy weapons, arms depots, military sites and tunnels to be identified and placed under the committee’s control.
An international stabilisation force would be deployed to separate Israeli troops from Palestinian-administered areas and monitor implementation of the agreement.
Israeli forces would withdraw from Gaza in stages under an agreed timeline, while reconstruction and the restoration of public services would begin under international supervision.
The roadmap also speaks of a longer-term political process aimed at Palestinian self-determination and the establishment of a Palestinian state.
The central hurdle, however, remains unchanged: Israel says Hamas must disarm before troops withdraw, while Hamas insists Israel must first halt its attacks and begin withdrawing its forces.
8 NATIONS WARN ISRAEL AGAINST DERAILING PEACE PLAN
The widening gap between Israel and Trump’s roadmap has also drawn a rare, coordinated response from several Muslim-majority countries.
The United Arab Emirates joined Qatar, Jordan, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Egypt on Thursday in condemning Israel’s continuing military operations in Gaza and warning that they could derail efforts to implement the next phase of the US-backed peace plan.
In a joint statement, the eight countries said Israel’s actions were undermining international efforts to move the agreement forward after Palestinian factions accepted the framework announced by Trump.
The statement marked a notable show of unity among countries that have often differed sharply in their approach towards Israel, ranging from the UAE, a close US partner with diplomatic ties to Israel, to Turkiye, one of its strongest regional critics.
The foreign ministers warned that continued Israeli military action could “derail the political process”, trigger renewed escalation and deepen the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza, stoking tensions with US
sources.text:
Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza, stoking tensions with US
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says Israel will not withdraw forces from Gaza until Hamas fully disarms.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insists he has rejected President Donald Trump’s plan for Gaza and will not withdraw forces until the Palestinian group Hamas fully disarms, risking more obstacles in the increasingly complex efforts to reduce escalation on multiple fronts in the region.
“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday, referring to the plan endorsed last month by Hamas.
The Israeli army “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed … and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens”, Netanyahu said, adding that Israel is “talking to the Americans about this issue”.
“They have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some are not acceptable to us, and we know how to stand firm on these things,” Netanyahu said.
There was no immediate response from the White House.
In a statement published on Telegram later on Sunday, Hamas said it remained committed to fully implementing the plan.
The Palestinian armed group called on mediators and guarantor countries to “assume their responsibilities” and prevent any “violations or breaches” that could derail the process.
Israel has continued to carry out near-daily deadly attacks across the Gaza Strip regardless of a so-called “ceasefire” with Hamas last October.
Trump announced a “historic” agreement on on July 30 that entailed “the complete disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza”, which he called “a monumental step toward lasting peace and security”. The deal was credited to the US-led Board of Peace, inaugurated in February 2026 and including roughly 40 countries – including Israel and several Arab states, though no Palestinian representatives – with Trump installed as its chair for life.
Speaking to his cabinet Sunday, Netanyahu vowed that “as long as I am prime minister, no Palestinian state will arise” and emphasised that Israel would not abide by the US-backed plan.
Israel’s desire for “real disarmament, not fictitious disarmament” would mean the removal of all weaponry, including lighter weapons, he said.
The 15-point plan calls for initially focusing on Hamas’s heavy weaponry, military production sites, weapons depots and the group’s extensive tunnel network.
Reporting from Washington DC, Al Jazeera’s Patty Culhane said that Netanyahu is playing a “very dangerous game” with Trump.
Israel is becoming increasingly unpopular in the US, with the Democratic Party “very much sliding towards the Palestinian cause”, said Culhane.
Furthermore, Trump could decide to “say it is time to split with Israel”, which would likely see many in the Republican Party, “the last staunchest ally of Israel in the US”, follow suit, Culhane said.
Reporting from Gaza City, Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud said Netanyahu’s statement raises “serious questions” for Palestinians about the path out of hostilities.
“The full rejection here puts the sequencing and the steps into question,” Mahmoud said.
Reporting from Bethlehem in the occupied West Bank, Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said Netanyahu’s stated conditions could prove “extremely problematic for the Board of Peace and the mediators who have been working for months now to try to carry out the disarmament of Hamas”.
The roadmap would eventually involve transferring Gaza’s day-to-day administration to a technocratic Palestinian committee operating under the oversight of the Board of Peace.
But the board has “very limited power” to move forward without Israeli support, Odeh said.
“Netanyahu has hit the reset button,” she said.
Since Hamas and Israel agreed to a nominal ceasefire last October, experts have expressed scepticism that Israel would honour the agreement as its forces have continued to pummel Gaza, killing hundreds of people.
At least one child was injured in Israeli army gunfire in the Al-Najjar neighbourhood of Khan Younis on Sunday, the Palestinian Wafa news agency reported.
Since the “ceasefire” started in mid-October last year, at least 1,258 people have been killed and 4,139 wounded with more than 800 bodies recovered from rubble, according to Gaza’s health ministry.
The overall death toll in Gaza since October 2023 is at least 73,386 and 174,250 wounded.
Attacks by Israeli forces, settlers across the occupied West Bank
Israeli forces and settlers continue to launch near daily attacks across the occupied West Bank, as Netanyahu’s party courts the settler vote less than three months before Israel’s general elections.
The Israeli military ransacked multiple homes after storming several villages in the Nablus governorate and multiple towns east of Bethlehem, reported Wafa.
Israeli settlers and soldiers carried out attacks in the areas of Tubas, al-Mughayyir, Masafer Yatta and Wadi al-Rakhim while also levelling farmland, according to Al Jazeera journalists on the ground.
In conjunction with Israeli police, Israeli worshippers stormed the Al-Aqsa mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem.
The compound, which is Islam’s third holiest site, is where Prophet Muhammad is believed to have ascended into heaven.
It is also the holiest site in Judaism, known as the Temple Mount, where the ancient Temple of Jerusalem previously stood.
A group of Israeli settlers protected by military forces also stormed the town of Beit Ur al-Tahta, west of Ramallah, while another group of settlers simultaneously stormed the al-Batin area on the outskirts of the village of Jaljulia, north of Ramallah, Wafa reported.
Israeli settlers conducted raids in multiple locations across the Ramallah and el-Bireh governorates.
Israeli settlers also attacked Palestinian properties near Bethlehem and cut down olive trees and damaged water tanks in Deir Sharaf, west of Nablus.
Israeli settlers under military protection attacked Palestinian farmers in Al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah.
Israeli ministers and parliament members attended an event to establish Emek Dotan, a new illegal Israeli settlement in Arrabeh, southwestern Jenin.

Israeli forces currently occupy more than half of Gaza, in the east and south of the territory and senior ministers have signaled they want to expand control.
Far-right members of Netanyahu’s cabinet welcomed Netanyahu’s stand on Sunday.
“The (Israel Defense Forces) cannot retreat one millimeter in the Gaza Strip,” said Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
Netanyahu’s rejection of Trump’s initiative will further strain a close relationship. Last year, he described the US president as “the greatest friend that the state of Israel has ever had in the White House.”
Trump has suggested that Netanyahu should receive a pardon rather than face corruption charges, saying in March that Israel’s President Isaac Herzog “must give Bibi a pardon today. I don’t want there to be anything troubling Bibi other than the war with Iran.”
But there has also been growing friction over Israeli strikes in Lebanon this year, and the Netanyahu government only reluctantly accepted the ceasefire in April with Iran.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point Gaza peace plan, Netanyahu says
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu restated his rejection of Donald Trump’s latest Gaza plan in televised remarks to his right-wing government on Sunday, even as Israel’s military has effectively halted attacks in the territory under pressure from the U.S. President.
Netanyahu is struggling in the polls as he seeks re-election at a vote due on Oct. 27 but is caught between far-right ministers angered by concessions in Gaza and his key military backer, Trump, who wants progress toward ending the conflict there with a new 15-point peace plan.
Israel has scaled back attacks in Gaza since Monday, when Nikolay Mladenov, the Gaza envoy for Trump’s Board of Peace that oversees the ceasefire, met with Netanyahu.
A source familiar with Israel’s position said it had agreed that the military would only act against what it perceives as immediate threats in Gaza and no longer carry out targeted assassinations as it had been doing on a near-daily basis.
Mladenov said on Sunday that discussions on the new road map were ongoing.
Israel and Hamas disagree over timings in Trump’s plan
Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough in his plan to end the war, to which both Israel and Hamas agreed, with Israeli forces withdrawing as Hamas disarms and an International Stabilization Force working with a new Palestinian police force to secure the enclave.
But complications have swiftly emerged with questions over the plan’s timeline. “Israel does not accept the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at the start of a meeting with cabinet ministers. The military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed . . . it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry.
Netanyahu made similar remarks in a social media post on Tuesday and Israeli officials have said reservations have been shared with Washington.
He added that Israel was in talks with the United States on the plan. “They (the U.S.) have ideas, some of which are acceptable to us and some of which are unacceptable to us and we know how to stand firm against these things,” Netanyahu said.
In an interview with Israeli N12 News, Mladenov said Israel would be required to withdraw “sector by sector” once weapons have been taken from Hamas and rendered unusable.
Basem Naim, a senior Hamas official, told Reuters on Sunday that the group remained committed to the road map agreed in Cairo 10 days ago.
“We expect the mediators and the U.S. guarantor to press Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the road map and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons,” he said.
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich praised Netanyahu. “We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas,” he said in a statement. “The (military) cannot withdraw even a millimetre from the Gaza Strip.”
Trump said last month that Iran-backed Hamas, which ruled Gaza for nearly two decades before carrying out the Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel that triggered the Gaza war, had agreed to lay down its weapons.
Hamas avoids the use of the term “disarmament” and said the group agreed to hand over weapons to be stored under a U.S.-backed Palestinian technocrat administration that would run the affairs in Gaza under the supervision of Trump’s Board of Peace.
Hamas said it agreed to the plan to avoids resumption of war, but it added that the implementation of the deal would depend on Israel first meeting its own commitments, including withdrawal and halting attacks.
Israel had vowed to hunt down militants who had taken part in the October 2023 attack before halting the targeted attacks on Monday.
Since the U.S.-mediated ceasefire reached in October, 2025, more than 1,250 people have been killed in the Israeli attacks, most of them civilians, according to Gaza health officials. Hamas has not disclosed the number of its fighters killed. Four Israeli soldiers have been killed in this time in Gaza.
Israeli troops have occupied and depopulated two-thirds of the enclave, leaving nearly all its more than 2 million residents confined to a tiny strip of land under Hamas control along the coast, most in makeshift tents or damaged buildings.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza, PM Benjamin Netanyahu says
sources.text:
Israel will not accept the 15-point plan for Gaza set out by President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday.
“I want to clarify this: Israel rejects the 15-point document. I have heard people saying, ‘You didn’t say that.’ So here I am saying it again,” he told a Cabinet meeting, referring to the peace plan set out by Trump last year. “The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed,” he added.
Trump last month touted a breakthrough in his Gaza peace plan, saying that Hamas has agreed to lay down arms.
The peace plan called for a phased withdrawal of Israel’s troops from Gaza alongside the disarmament of Hamas, but Netanyahu said Israeli forces are not going anywhere until Hamas completely disarms first.
“When I say Hamas must be disarmed, I mean heavy weapons, lighter weapons, all weapons. We are talking about genuine disarmament, not a fictitious one,” Netanyahu said Sunday.
Hamas had last month said that it would disarm, but only after Israel withdraws completely and stops all hostilities. The group also said that laying down its heavy weapons would come later in the process, conditional on the establishment of a Palestinian state.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, reaffirmed that “as long as I am prime minister, there will be no Palestinian state.” The leader is currently facing a domestic political battle for survival ahead of elections set for October, with the status of the Gaza and Iran wars likely to prove pivotal.
The explicit rejection of the peace plan, frequently touted by Trump as a key foreign policy achievement, also comes after months of growing tensions between the White House and Israel’s leadership over Iran. The White House did not immediately comment on the remarks.
Netanyahu said of Washington: “We are currently discussing this issue with the Americans. They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand firm on these matters.”
The Israeli leader may consider it worthwhile to “enter a new confrontation with President Trump,” said Ronni Shaked, a research fellow at the Harry S. Truman Institute at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, as his own popularity wanes ahead of October’s election.
“After three years, he is without any victory, and he just wants to show now to the people of Israel, before the election, that look at me, I have victory, and the victory is that we are going to disarm Hamas,” Shaked said in a phone interview, referring to the tactic as an “illusion.”
Responding to Netanyahu’s statement Sunday, senior Hamas official Basim Naeem said that the group expects the mediators and the U.S. to “exert pressure” on Netanyahu and his government to abide by the road map and “prevent him from obstructing the process for domestic political and electoral considerations.”
A further Hamas statement reaffirmed its commitment to the agreed-upon road map, reiterating the group’s “seriousness in engaging responsibly in implementing the fifteen points agreed upon and establishing a clear timetable for their implementation.”
Mohammad Dahlan, a member of the Palestinian Legislative Council, said Netanyahu’s announcement “represents a challenge, contempt, and deception of the American administration and President Trump’s team,” adding that Washington “now realizes that Netanyahu is an obstacle to achieving security and stability.”
Netanyahu’s far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, welcomed his announcement after seeking to pressure the leader into a more hard-line stance. “I congratulate the Prime Minister for responding to our demand and clarifying unequivocally,” he said on X.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, meanwhile, “emphasized the necessity for all parties to fulfill their commitments and refrain from taking any actions that could hinder the implementation process or undermine the progress achieved,” his office said in a statement.
Despite agreeing to halt attacks in October, Israel has continued its deadly strikes on the Palestinian enclave. On Saturday, recovery operations concluded at the Karam Building in Gaza after 19 bodies were found under the rubble, according to the Gaza civil defense. Israel and Hamas both regularly accuse the other of breaching the ceasefire.
More than 73,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Oct. 7, 2023, according to the enclave’s health officials, including more than 1,200 people since the ceasefire began in October. Israel launched its war in Gaza in response to the Hamas-led attack in which around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage.

sources.news_title: Israel Rejects Trump's Gaza Peace Plan, Says No Pullout Until Hamas Disarms
Israel rejects Trump's Gaza roadmap, Netanyahu says
sources.text:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly rejected the Board of Peace’s 15-point Gaza document on Sunday, saying Israel would not carry out any IDF withdrawal from the Strip before Hamas is fully disarmed.
Speaking at the opening of the weekly Cabinet meeting, Netanyahu addressed criticism that he had not personally stated Israel’s opposition to the plan.
“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” he said. “I heard people saying, ‘You didn’t say it.’ So here I am saying it again: Israel rejects the 15-point document. The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed.”
The Board of Peace and the broader Gaza framework are backed by U.S. President Donald Trump. Meanwhile, Israel has refrained since last Monday from carrying out strikes and targeted killings in the Gaza Strip.
Netanyahu also spelled out what Israel considers Hamas disarmament.
“When I say disarming Hamas, that means the heavy weapons, the less heavy weapons, all the weapons,” he said. “And we are talking about real disarmament, not fake disarmament.”
“We are talking with the Americans about this,” Netanyahu added. “They have ideas, some of them are acceptable to us and some are not acceptable to us, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters. We proved that in the past and we are proving it today as well.”
He added that the IDF would continue acting against threats to Israeli troops and civilians.
“The IDF will continue to thwart threats against our forces and against our citizens,” he said.
The dispute over phased withdrawal
The agreement with Hamas calls for a gradual process in which Hamas and other terror organizations in Gaza would be disarmed alongside a full Israeli withdrawal from the Strip.
The process is meant to take place in stages. At the outset, the IDF would withdraw back to the “yellow line” established under the first hostage deal, after Israeli forces subsequently seized additional territory and expanded their control to roughly 70% of Gaza.
Nikolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative, presented the 15-point implementation plan for the “Comprehensive Peace Plan” in May.
At the center of his presentation was a new roadmap which he said had been developed together with Egypt, Turkey, Qatar and the United States, incorporating feedback from Palestinian factions.
According to Mladenov, the plan is based on reciprocity: each move by one side triggers a corresponding step by the other, with an independent verification committee approving each stage before the process advances.
That mechanism is at the heart of Israel’s objection.
Cabinet ministers said last week that the roadmap calls for a gradual Israeli withdrawal in parallel with partial stages of Hamas disarmament, rather than requiring Hamas to fully disarm before any withdrawal begins.
“The Israeli position was that withdrawals begin only when Hamas disarms, and now they are saying that every time Hamas gives up part of its weapons, we have to withdraw a little,” ministers said.
They also sharply criticized the proposed disarmament mechanism.
“All the demilitarization is fake,” they said. “There is no disarmament, but rather the transfer of weapons into Palestinian hands, and they will operate according to Palestinian law that applies in Ramallah.”
The ministers argued that such an arrangement would fail to meet Israel’s demand for the complete dismantling of Hamas’ military capabilities.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects 15-point plan to disarm Hamas, withdraw Israeli troops
Netanyahu Draws a Hard Line on Gaza: No Israeli Withdrawal Until Hamas Is 'Genuinely' Disarmed
sources.text:
Benjamin Netanyahu just told the body created to implement President Donald Trump’s Gaza peace plan that Israel isn’t signing off on it, at least not as written.
Netanyahu rejected the Board of Peace’s 15-point Gaza roadmap during Sunday’s Cabinet meeting, drawing a line that puts him at odds with the very framework Washington has spent months building. His message was blunt: the Israel Defense Forces are not leaving Gaza until Hamas hands over every weapon in its arsenal, no exceptions and no partial credit.
“Israel rejects the 15-point Gaza document proposed by the Board of Peace,” Netanyahu said. “The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed.”
What the Board of Peace Proposed
The Board of Peace, the international body Trump stood up to oversee implementation of his Gaza peace framework, published its 15-point roadmap in late July. The plan is built in phases. Israel would complete its remaining obligations under the Sharm el-Sheikh Protocol and halt military operations, while Hamas would hand civilian governance and security functions over to a transitional body called the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.
A separate International Verification Committee would certify compliance at each stage before the next phase begins, including full Hamas disarmament and an eventual Israeli withdrawal. But it’s the sequence of events that remains a sticking point for Israel. Netanyahu doesn’t trust the verification process to actually deliver disarmament before Israeli troops are asked to leave.
“It needs to be genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament,” Netanyahu said with the kind of skepticism that has defined Israeli deal-making with Hamas for two decades. “When I say Hamas is disarmed, that means the heavy weapons, the less heavy weapons, all the weapons.”
Hamas Says It’s Still on Board, Sort Of
Hamas insists it’s still committed to the roadmap negotiated in Cairo ten days before Netanyahu’s remarks. Senior Hamas official Basem Naim told Reuters the group expects mediators and the United States to pressure Netanyahu’s government into following through on the agreement as written.
However, this is the same Hamas that controlled Gaza for nearly two decades before the Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attack that triggered the current war. It’s also the same Hamas whose recent announcement that it was dissolving its Gaza governing body Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar dismissed as a Hezbollah-style trick, one designed to hand off garbage collection and municipal services to a technocratic committee while Hamas quietly stays the dominant armed force on the ground.
Given their track record, Netanyahu’s insistence on verified disarmament before withdrawal isn’t exactly coming out of nowhere.
Netanyahu, however, was careful to frame this as not breaking with the Trump administration. He praised Trump directly, calling him “the greatest of our friends in the White House” and crediting the U.S.-Israel alliance for keeping Iran from a nuclear weapon. The daylight between his Sunday statement and the Board of Peace’s own roadmap is still real, though, and it comes at a moment when the administration has been publicly selling momentum on Gaza, including a claimed breakthrough last month in which Trump said Hamas had agreed to lay down its weapons.
Netanyahu used the same Cabinet remarks to reiterate that Israel will not accept a Palestinian state in Gaza or the West Bank under his government, dismissing what he called “Fatahstan” and “Hamastan” alike. He also said Israeli forces had recently acted “forcefully” in Lebanon, calling it “very important activity,” and said Iran has held off attacking Israel directly only because Tehran knows the cost of retaliation.
The lingering tension between Israel and Hamas is now the Trump administration’s to manage. It built and endorsed the Board of Peace framework, and its closest ally in the region has now publicly stated that the framework doesn’t yet meet Netanyahu’s one non-negotiable condition: Hamas fully disarmed before Israeli forces leave Gaza.

sources.news_title: Netanyahu Challenges Trump’s Gaza Roadmap, Rejects Palestinian State
sources.text:
Highlights
- Netanyahu said there will be no Palestinian state in Gaza or the West Bank while he remains prime minister.
- Israel will not withdraw its forces from Gaza until Hamas is completely disarmed, according to Netanyahu.
- Trump has described his 15-point Gaza roadmap as a “major milestone” and a “great breakthrough” toward ending the war.
- Hamas has rejected immediate disarmament and wants Israel to stop its attacks and withdraw before surrendering control of its weapons.
- Eight Muslim-majority countries have warned that Israel’s continuing military operations could undermine the US-backed roadmap.
US President Donald Trump presented his Gaza peace roadmap as a major step toward ending the war and securing the release of the remaining hostages held by Hamas. But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has made clear that Israel does not accept two of the plan’s most important provisions: the proposed timetable for an Israeli military withdrawal and its longer-term political objective involving a Palestinian state.
“As long as I am Prime Minister, there will be no Palestinian state in Gaza or the West Bank,” Netanyahu said Sunday.
Netanyahu also ruled out an Israeli military withdrawal from Gaza until Hamas has been completely disarmed. His position creates a significant divide between the optimism expressed by Trump in Washington and the conditions being publicly outlined by Israel’s prime minister.
Trump has characterized the 15-point proposal as a “major milestone” and a “great breakthrough” toward bringing the Gaza war to an end. However, Netanyahu’s latest comments indicate that major disagreements remain over how the plan would be implemented.
Netanyahu sets conditions for Gaza withdrawal
For Netanyahu, the issue of Hamas disarmament comes before an Israeli military withdrawal.
An Israeli official said last week there would be “no withdrawal whatsoever” from the military’s current positions unless Hamas underwent what Israel considered genuine disarmament.
Netanyahu has now reiterated that position, saying Israeli forces will remain in Gaza until Hamas is completely disarmed. The stance conflicts with the structure of Trump’s proposed roadmap, which calls for Israeli forces to withdraw in stages as other elements of the agreement are carried out.
Trump appeared confident following his meeting with Netanyahu in Washington.
“Israel helped us, and they’ve been very good,” Trump said, describing Israel as “very happy” with the agreement.
The US president also acknowledged the complexity involved in putting the proposal into practice.
“Will it go through its ups and downs? It’s a very complex situation over there,” he said.
An Israeli political source said Gaza was not discussed during Netanyahu’s Washington meeting with Trump. That has raised questions about the extent of agreement between the two leaders on how the proposed roadmap should be implemented.
Hamas rejects immediate disarmament
Hamas is taking a fundamentally different position on the order in which the proposed steps should occur.
Senior Hamas official Basem Naim said the group remains committed to the roadmap agreed with mediators and representatives of Trump’s Peace Council in Cairo.
“We remain committed to the roadmap agreed with mediators and representatives of the Peace Council in Cairo,” Naim said.
However, Hamas has said Israel must first stop its attacks and fulfill its commitments under the earlier ceasefire agreement.
Ghazi Hamad, another senior Hamas official involved in the negotiations, said Hamas was prepared to accept a “difficult and painful” agreement but did not agree to immediate disarmament.
Hamas is calling for Israel to halt its attacks, withdraw its forces to earlier positions and permit increased flows of humanitarian aid and goods into Gaza. According to the group’s position, only after those measures are implemented would it consider placing its weapons under the control of the proposed National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.
What Netanyahu and Hamas disagree on
The opposing positions leave the central security issue in Trump’s Gaza plan unresolved.
Netanyahu says Hamas must disarm before Israel withdraws. Hamas, meanwhile, wants Israel to stop its attacks and begin withdrawing before it gives up control of its weapons.
This disagreement directly affects the proposed sequence of events in Trump’s roadmap and represents one of the main obstacles to its implementation.
Trump’s 15-point Gaza roadmap
The 15-point proposal calls for Hamas and other Palestinian factions to transfer Gaza’s civil administration and internal security responsibilities to a Palestinian technocratic body.
Under the plan, heavy weapons, arms depots, military sites and tunnels would be identified and placed under the control of that committee.
An international stabilization force would oversee the arrangement while separating Israeli troops from areas administered by Palestinians. Israeli forces would then withdraw in stages, with reconstruction and the restoration of public services beginning as the process moves forward.
Palestinian state remains a major point of disagreement
The roadmap also extends beyond Gaza’s immediate security arrangements. It outlines a longer-term political process centered on Palestinian self-determination and the establishment of a Palestinian state.
That objective now faces direct opposition from Netanyahu.
His statement that there will be no Palestinian state in Gaza or the West Bank while he remains prime minister places Israel’s stated position in direct conflict with the longer-term political direction outlined in Trump’s roadmap.
Regional pressure over the Gaza peace plan
The disagreements surrounding the roadmap have also prompted a coordinated response from eight Muslim-majority countries: the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Jordan, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Egypt.
The countries condemned Israel’s continuing military operations in Gaza and warned that additional action could jeopardize efforts to move forward with the next phase of the US-backed roadmap.
In a joint statement, they said Israel’s actions could “derail the political process”, lead to renewed escalation and worsen the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
The developments leave Trump’s Gaza peace plan facing competing demands from the main parties.
Israel, under Netanyahu, is insisting that Hamas be completely disarmed before an Israeli withdrawal. Hamas is demanding that Israel first halt its attacks and withdraw its forces before the group considers giving up control of its weapons.
At the same time, Netanyahu has rejected the establishment of a Palestinian state, which is part of the roadmap’s longer-term political vision.
Trump has presented the proposal as a breakthrough toward ending the war, but Netanyahu’s latest statements underscore the challenges that remain. Agreement on the broader roadmap has not resolved the fundamental disputes over Hamas’s disarmament, Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza and the future political status of the Palestinians.

sources.news_title: Trump Watch: Israel rejects Trump Gaza peace plan
sources.text:
Donald Trump matters a lot to Mzansi and the rest of the world right now. Trump is changing the way America works – and how the world’s most powerful country deals with the rest of the world.
We’ll track what he does and connect the dots to your daily life.
Israel rejects Trump Gaza peace plan
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected Donald Trump’s 15 point peace plan for Gaza.
Netanyahu said Israeli troops would not leave Gaza until Hamas had fully given up its weapons.
Trump’s peace team said last month that Hamas had agreed to disarm. Hamas said it would only hand over its heavy weapons if Israel stopped its attacks and pulled its forces out.
Netanyahu said Israel would not accept the plan as it stands. He said Hamas had to disarm properly before any Israeli withdrawal.
Hamas said it was still committed to the agreement and was ready to help carry it out.
Trump’s plan includes Hamas giving up its weapons, Israeli troops leaving Gaza and rebuilding the area.
A senior official working on Trump’s plan said talks were still happening. He said the plan remained the best way forward.
Netanyahu said he was still speaking to US officials about what happens next, but made clear that Israel did not agree with all parts of Trump’s plan.
Image source: File
Trump denies US is running low on weapons
US President Donald Trump has denied reports that America is running short of weapons during the war with Iran.
Trump said the US has “massive amounts” of weapons and that more are being made and sent where needed.
His government is facing growing questions about how many missiles are left after months of fighting.
Reports say the US has used large amounts of long-range missiles and other weapons since the war began.
Trump also threatened long jail sentences for people he believes leaked information about possible shortages.
He called the reports false and said Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was doing a good job.
Iran said the reports showed that US military supplies were becoming weaker. Its defence minister said Iran could still respond to any threat.
The exact number of US missiles is secret. But one research group estimated that America may have used a large part of some of its missile supply.
Image source: File
Trump says Iran deal is close
US President Donald Trump says a deal with Iran may be close, even though Iran says it is not holding talks with the US.
Trump said discussions were happening whether Iran admitted it or not. Iran rejected that claim.
Iran’s deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibadadi said talks were only taking place with Oman.
He said the US was ready to return to earlier promises. He did not explain exactly what those promises were.
The US and Iran signed a temporary agreement in June. Iran was meant to allow ships through the Strait of Hormuz without charge for 60 days.
In return, the US agreed to lift its naval blockade of Iranian ships.
Iran says a new agreement with Oman about the strait is close. It wants shipping routes changed because it says the old routes are no longer safe.
US officials have also said a deal to reopen the strait could be reached soon. Reports of explosions near ships off Yemen and Oman were still being investigated.
Image source: File
Armed man arrested at Trump golf club before visit
A man carrying a loaded gun has been arrested at Donald Trump’s golf club near Los Angeles.
Police said the arrest happened on Sunday, two days before Trump was due to visit the club for a Republican fundraising dinner.

Goldberg says he was shocked to see real-time details of the military operation, including names of officials and sensitive tactics. “I thought it was a prank,” he said. “But the attack happened exactly as they planned it.”
The Trump administration has confirmed the breach but is trying to downplay the damage. Hegseth even told reporters, “Nobody was texting war plans.” Goldberg hit back: “That’s a lie. He was.”
If Trump’s top officials can’t keep their own war plans private, it puts global security at risk. Countries like South Africa often work with the US on trade, security, and international cooperation. But if the US keeps making mistakes like this, it’s harder to trust them.
Image source: @POTUS
Rasool says ‘don’t replace me with a white ambassador’
Former ambassador Ebrahim Rasool has told President Cyril Ramaphosa not to choose a white replacement just to please Donald Trump.
Speaking at a homecoming rally in Cape Town on Sunday, Rasool told ANC supporters that South Africa must fix its relationship with the US but without sacrificing its values.
“We can’t think that just because America has a white president, we need a white ambassador,” he said. “We need someone who can rebuild ties, but still stand strong for what we believe in.”
Rasool was kicked out of the US last week after Trump’s government accused him of being disrespectful. Now, names like deputy minister Andries Nel and former DA leader Tony Leon are being floated as possible replacements but the presidency says there’s no rush.
Rasool also called for a new kind of diplomacy — one based on Ubuntu. “Ubuntu diplomacy is not about lying to protect your country or flattering your host,” he said. “It’s about telling the truth with respect, standing your ground, and keeping your dignity.”
The next ambassador will shape how South Africa navigates a tough relationship with Trump’s US. That choice will say a lot about whether we stand firm — or bend under pressure.
Image source: File
France wants the Statue of Liberty back
French leaders are demanding that the United States give back the Statue of Liberty — all because of Donald Trump.
French politician Raphaël Glucksmann says the statue, which was gifted to the US 140 years ago, no longer belongs there. He says Trump has “sided with tyrants” and no longer represents the values the statue stands for.
“We gave it to you as a symbol of freedom,” Glucksmann said. “But if you’ve chosen to support dictators and silence scientists, then we want our gift back.”
The Trump administration hit back hard, saying the statue is going nowhere. A White House spokesperson said France should be grateful to the US for helping them win World War II and added that “if it wasn’t for America, they’d be speaking German.”
Even Australia’s former Prime Minister jumped in, reminding everyone that France once helped America fight the British in its own war for independence.
This may sound like political theatre but it shows how Trump’s actions are damaging US relationships around the world. As America isolates itself, smaller countries like South Africa feel the knock-on effects in trade, global funding, and foreign policy influence.
Image source: File
Trump says Rasool must leave the US by Friday
South Africa’s ambassador to the US, Ebrahim Rasool, has just days to clear out his office and leave America after being declared “persona non grata” by the Trump administration.
The diplomatic bombshell dropped when Secretary of State Marco Rubio blasted Rasool as a “race-baiting politician who hates President Trump” in a social media post after the ambassador discussed white Americans becoming a minority.
Rasool’s diplomatic privileges expired Monday, and he must be out of the country by Friday.
President Ramaphosa is trying to downplay the crisis, calling it a “hiccup” and promising to engage “with deep respect” for Trump, but this comes right after Trump cut funding to South Africa over alleged “anti-white policies.”
As our top diplomat gets ready to fly home, South Africans should watch closely – when ambassadors get expelled, serious economic and political fallout usually follows.
Image source: SA Embassy
Is Trump just Musk’s babysitter now?
New photos from the White House have people asking: who’s really in charge — Donald Trump or Elon Musk?
The pictures show Trump walking next to Musk’s four-year-old son while Musk walks ahead, talking to his staff. In one photo, Trump is even seen helping the boy — nicknamed “Lil X” — onto the presidential helicopter.
Social media had a field day. “Trump finally got a real job — he’s Lil X’s nanny now,” one person joked. Another said: “Imagine being the president but spending your day babysitting a billionaire’s child.”
Some people even asked, “Does this kid live at the White House now?” One user replied: “Of course he does — he’s the real president!”
Musk posted one of the photos himself, calling it “a happy picture.” But many people noticed something else: Musk walking ahead like the boss, while Trump trails behind with the child. “It really shows who has the power,” one person wrote.
Since Trump appointed Musk to lead the Department of Government Efficiency (called DOGE), Musk has become one of the most powerful people in Washington.
Musk was born in Pretoria and now he’s influencing major decisions in the US. That could affect South Africa too, from how we use social media and tech to deals around space, green energy and trade. If Musk is the one calling the shots, his choices could impact jobs, prices, and policies here at home.
Image source: @POTUS
Putin “agrees” to Trump’s ceasefire plan but with a catch
Putin just said yes to Trump’s 30-day ceasefire plan for Ukraine, but don’t get too excited.
While thanking Trump for “regulating the conflict,” Putin added he has “a lot of questions” and any deal must “lead to long-term peace” – Putin-speak for getting what he wants.
The Russian leader couldn’t help boasting that his forces “are on the offensive everywhere” and warned Ukrainian troops they must “surrender or die.”
Experts think Putin’s agreement comes with hidden conditions and might just be playing nice with Trump, who has now restored military aid to Ukraine after Zelenskyy agreed to ceasefire talks.
Why should South Africans care? Because global conflicts affect our economy directly – from higher food prices to unstable markets. Plus, watching Trump broker deals between Russia and Ukraine shows how he handles international problems – a preview of what other countries (including ours) might face.
Image source: File
Trump’s right hand tells a story the White House won’t explain
Something strange is going on with Trump’s hand. A dark mark keeps showing up in photos – most recently during his meeting with Ireland’s leader.
The White House claims it’s just from Trump shaking too many hands. But medical experts aren’t buying it.
Dr. Anatalia Moore, a skin specialist, says normal handshakes don’t cause bruises like that, Daily Star reported.
She thinks it might be from a medical procedure where doctors put a drip in his hand.
She also points out that at 78, Trump could bruise more easily from just bumping into things, as older people often have balance issues and their bodies heal slower.
While it might just be makeup or a minor bruise, these marks are raising questions about the president’s health – something worth watching as his physical condition could affect his decisions on South Africa and other global issues.
Image source: @POTUS
Trump opens door for Afrikaner resettlement in America
It’s official – the US is now actively working to bring Afrikaner South Africans to America as refugees.
The US Embassy just confirmed they’re reviewing applications and will contact people who’ve already applied. This isn’t just Trump talking anymore – it’s becoming real policy.
Trump claims South Africa is “confiscating” white farmers’ land “without compensation” after Ramaphosa signed the Expropriation Act. Most experts say this isn’t true, but that hasn’t stopped Trump from offering “a rapid pathway to citizenship” for these farmers.
About 1,500 Afrikaners have already gathered outside the US Embassy in Pretoria to thank Trump for his support.
Meanwhile, our government refuses to get into a shouting match with Trump, with Ramaphosa’s spokesperson saying South Africa won’t engage in “counterproductive megaphone diplomacy.”
The big question now: How many farmers will actually pack up and leave? And what would that mean for our farms, food security, and race relations?
Image source: File
Trump’s market panic and what it means for South Africa
By Dylan Bettencourt
The US stock market just took a nasty dive after Trump twice dodged questions about a recession.
Why should you care? Because when America sneezes, South Africa catches a cold. Trump’s chaos affects us directly:
– When global markets panic, the Rand usually weakens
– Weaker Rand = more expensive imports = higher prices at the shops
– Foreign investors get nervous about putting money in countries like ours
– Our exports become less valuable if America’s economy slows down
Trump admitted his policies might cause economic “pain” before things get better. His own team is now rushing to calm markets, promising there won’t be a recession.
For South Africans already struggling with high prices, Trump’s unpredictable style is the last thing we need.
The big question: Will Trump back down like he did with Canada and Mexico, or stick to his disruptive plans? Either way, as one expert warned: “Good luck in this challenging time.”
Image source: File
De Klerk foundation rejects Trump’s farmer ‘rescue’ plan
By Dylan Bettencourt
The FW de Klerk Foundation has rejected Trump’s offer to give US citizenship to white South African farmers.
Their message? Trump’s plan is based on “disinformation and cheap politics” with “no basis in truth.”
Christo van der Rheede put it simply: “The challenges we face in South Africa aren’t just white people’s problems. We’re all affected by crime, unemployment and bad policies.”
The Foundation warns that Trump’s actions will hurt South Africa’s economy and farming industry.
They also connect Trump’s move to the rise of “ethnic nationalism” worldwide, suggesting right-wing groups are using this to attack South Africa’s non-racial democracy established in 1994.
Meanwhile, our government won’t engage in “megaphone diplomacy” – choosing to ignore Trump’s social media outbursts rather than dignify them with a response.
Image source: File
Health Minister says Trump ‘doesn’t’ owe us a cent’
By Dylan Bettencourt
Health Minister Aaron Motsoaledi said “Trump doesn’t owe South Africa any cent whatsoever” after the US president cut R8 billion in HIV/AIDS funding.
Instead of complaining, he called on South Africa to “stand on our own” and revealed he’s already talking to other donors like the Gates Foundation to replace Trump’s money.
EFF’s Malema had a different take, claiming the cuts are “Israel’s revenge” for South Africa’s support of Palestine. He also warned that land reform will continue “whether they like it or not.”
Motsoaledi couldn’t resist taking a jab at right-wing group Solidarity’s recent White House visit, distinguishing them from the COVID Solidarity Fund that’s helping fill funding gaps.
The bottom line for South Africans living with HIV? The political blame game won’t matter if someone doesn’t step up to save the program that employs 15,000 healthcare workers and keeps millions of patients alive.
Image source: @MYANC
Trump says ‘nobody has ever heard of’ Lesotho
Trump just took a cheap shot at our neighbor Lesotho in his Congress speech, calling it a country “nobody has ever heard of” while Republican lawmakers laughed along.
Why? He was defending his foreign aid cuts, specifically “$8 million for LGBTQI+” in Lesotho – though local LGBTQ groups say they never got this money.
Lesotho’s Foreign Minister is angry, calling the comments “shocking” and promising to send a formal protest to Washington.
The real impact? Lesotho has the world’s second-highest HIV rate, and Trump’s funding cuts threaten healthcare programs that people on both sides of the border rely on.
For South Africans, it’s perhaps a reminder of how Trump sees African nations – as jokes, not partners.
Image source: @POTUS
Zelenskyy folds after Trump cuts military aid
By Dylan Bettencourt
Trump just announced he’s got a letter from Zelenskyy saying Ukraine is “ready to come to the negotiating table” – quite the U-turn after last week’s White House showdown.
After getting his military aid cut off, Zelenskyy’s now saying he wants to “make things right” and is ready “any time and in any convenient format” to sign that minerals deal he previously walked away from.
Trump’s also claiming he’s had “serious discussions with Russia” and received “strong signals they’re ready for peace.”
For South Africans, this drama is worth watching closely. What happens when a superpower suddenly changes sides? We’re seeing countries that depend on American support scrambling to adjust.
In Trump’s world, yesterday’s allies can become today’s bargaining chips – a lesson that applies just as much to Pretoria as it does to Kyiv.
Image source: File
Trump leaves Ukraine stranded
By Dylan Bettencourt
Trump just pulled the plug on Ukraine’s military aid after publicly arguing with Zelenskyy. No more weapons, no more ammo – not even stuff that’s already on ships heading there.
It’s the same tactic he used when cutting South Africa’s HIV funding. One day you’ve got support, the next you don’t.
When Zelenskyy dared say peace might be “very, very far away,” Trump didn’t hold back: the Ukrainian president “won’t be around very long” unless he plays ball.
The message for countries like ours is crystal clear: in Trump’s world, you either give him what he wants or he’ll pull the rug out from under you – no warning, no negotiations.
So when South African ministers next fly to Washington, they’d better have more than just goodwill in their briefcases. In Trumpland, it’s deal or no deal.
Image source: File
Trump vs Zelensky fight in White House Smackdown
By Dylan Bettencourt
Trump and Ukraine’s president Zelenskyy argued live on TV and SA analyst Sandile Swana says it’s a whole new ballgame.
Gone are the days of friendly military aid. Trump’s message was crystal clear: “No minerals, no protection.” While Zelensky talked about friendship, Trump talked about business – leaving the Ukrainian leader visibly stunned.
Meanwhile, the Ukrainian Association of South Africa is urging us not to abandon Ukraine, warning that Putin won’t stop his expansion plans anytime soon.
Trump’s “my way or the highway” approach could be coming to an international relationship near you.
US ambassador quits as SA relations hit rock bottom
By Dylan Bettencourt
In the latest Trump-era shake-up, Dana Brown, America’s acting ambassador to South Africa, has suddenly resigned.
This exit happens just as relations hit rock bottom, with Trump cutting all funding to South Africa and offering refugee status to Afrikaner farmers.
The timing couldn’t be worse for South Africans. With no permanent US ambassador since January and Brown now leaving in March, our diplomatic channel to America is running on skeleton staff just when we need it most.
Meanwhile, Afrikaner lobby groups AfriForum and Solidarity flew to the White House seeking “humanitarian assistance” – a move Ramaphosa slammed as “sowing divisions.”
For ordinary South Africans, this diplomatic cold war threatens everything from healthcare funding to trade relations, showing how Trump’s personal politics directly impacts our national interests.
Image source: US Embassy
Trump axes USAID funding for HIV
By Dylan Bettencourt
Trump on Thursday pulled the plug on R8.1 billion in HIV funding, telling South African organisations to “immediately cease all activities.” He sent just letters saying the programs “aren’t aligned with Agency priorities.”
This isn’t just American politics – it’s about your friend, neighbour or family member who depends on these services. Some 8 million South Africans rely on HIV treatment programs, and these cuts threaten real lives in our communities.
While the government scrambles for a response, healthcare workers are losing jobs and vulnerable patients are left hanging. From sex workers to pregnant moms, the impact hits hardest on those who need help most.
As one health worker put it to Bhekisasa: “This isn’t just a funding cut – it’s a betrayal.”
Image source: File
Gauteng minister copies Elon Musk strategy
By Zukile Majova
The Gauteng health department is checking if all 85,642 people on its payroll are real workers who actually show up for work.
The department has already frozen the salaries of 66 workers who haven’t come forward to prove they exist.
Health MEC Nomantu Nkomo-Ralehoko says her department can’t waste money paying ghost workers when hospitals need more staff and patients need care.
“We have limited resources at our disposal and cannot afford to waste money on ghost workers while hundreds of healthcare workers are looking for employment and thousands of people require access to healthcare services,” she said.
The department’s new Ziveze (Reveal Yourself) Campaign follows a similar move by Elon Musk in America. Musk emailed US government workers asking them to prove what work they’ve done.
The billionaire head of the Trump administration’s Department of Government Efficiency said: “All federal employees will shortly receive an email requesting to understand what they got done last week. Failure to respond will be taken as a resignation.”
In Gauteng, workers must go to their HR office to prove they are real employees. Those who don’t show up risk losing their jobs and could face criminal charges.
So far, 23,789 workers still need to prove they exist.
Image source: @NkomoNomantu
Ukraine fights back against Trump’s mineral grab
By Rorisang Modiba
Trump’s got Zelenskyy flying to Washington on Friday to sign a deal over Ukraine’s precious minerals. Trump initially wanted a massive $500bn chunk of Ukraine’s resources – imagine someone trying that with our platinum!
Much like how South Africans get nervous when foreign companies eye our mineral wealth, Ukrainians weren’t having it. Zelenskyy flat-out refused to sign something “10 generations would have to repay.”
Now, they’ve settled on sharing ownership instead – sound familiar? It’s the same dance our government does with mining giants over our resources.
As global powers scramble for these battery metals and rare earths, South Africa should watch closely. This is exactly the kind of pressure our mineral-rich country could face next.
Image source: File

sources.news_title: Hamas will resist disarmament, Israeli-backed Gaza commander c
Israel Rejects Trump's Gaza Plan: Netanyahu Says No Withdrawal Until Hamas Disarms - Commonwealth Union
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a 15-point Gaza peace proposal backed by US President Donald Trump. He said Israeli troops will not leave Gaza until Hamas is fully and genuinely disarmed.
The plan was introduced by Trump’s newly formed Board of Peace. It aims to end the war through a phased agreement that includes Hamas giving up its weapons, Israeli forces withdrawing from Gaza, and the long-term rebuilding of the territory.
Hamas has stated its continued commitment to the agreement. However, the group insists that it will only hand over its heavy weapons if Israel first stops all military attacks and withdraws its forces from Gaza. Hamas has also called on international mediators to make sure every side follows the agreement.
Speaking at a cabinet meeting, Netanyahu made Israel’s position clear. He said any disarmament must be real and verifiable, not symbolic or temporary. Until that happens, Israeli forces will continue military operations to protect the country’s security.
The rejection creates another major challenge for Trump’s peace initiative. Although the proposal was announced as a breakthrough, it now faces strong resistance from both sides over the order in which key steps should happen.
Political pressure inside Israel is also shaping Netanyahu’s decision. With national elections approaching, members of his right-wing coalition are demanding a tougher approach to Gaza. Some ministers have even called for the peace plan to be abandoned completely, arguing that it gives too much ground to Hamas.
Despite the disagreement, talks between Israel and US officials are continuing. Netanyahu said Washington has presented several ideas, but Israel will only support proposals that meet its security needs.
Nickolay Mladenov, the senior diplomat helping oversee the peace process, defended the plan and urged Israel to give negotiations a chance. He said the agreement was designed to be gradual, with each stage verified before moving to the next. Under the proposal, Israeli forces would not withdraw until there was clear evidence that Hamas was disarming.
The humanitarian crisis in Gaza remains severe. The United Nations estimates that around 1.9 million people, about 90% of Gaza’s population, have been displaced since the conflict began.
The war started after the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, which killed about 1,200 people and saw 251 hostages taken. Israel’s military response has since killed more than 73,000 people in Gaza, according to the territory’s health ministry, with the UN considering those figures broadly reliable.

sources.news_title: Israel PM Netanyahu Rejects President Trump’s Gaza Roadmap
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected U.S. President Donald Trump’s proposed 15-point Gaza roadmap, amid continued U.S. pressure and a recent reduction in Israeli military operations in the territory.
Netanyahu, facing a re-election campaign ahead of the October 27 vote, is caught between far-right allies calling for tougher action against Hamas and Trump, who is pushing for progress towards ending the conflict.
Israel reportedly reduced its attacks in Gaza after Trump’s Gaza envoy, Nikolay Mladenov, met with Netanyahu on Monday. A source familiar with Israel’s position said Israeli forces would now act only against perceived immediate threats and had stopped targeted assassinations.
Mladenov said on Sunday that “negotiations over Trump’s roadmap were still continuing.”
Dispute
President Trump had announced a breakthrough in his plan last month, saying “Israel and Hamas had agreed to a framework involving an Israeli withdrawal, Hamas handing over its weapons, and the deployment of an International Stabilisation Force alongside a new Palestinian police force.”
However, disagreements have emerged over how and when the plan should be implemented.
“Israel does not accept the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said at the start of a cabinet meeting.
He added that the Israeli military “will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed … it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry.”
Mladenov said Israel would have to withdraw “sector by sector” after Hamas’s weapons had been removed and rendered unusable.
Hamas official Basem Naim said “the group remained committed to the roadmap agreed in Cairo and urged the mediators and Washington to pressure Netanyahu to implement the agreement.”
“We expect the mediators and the U.S. guarantor to press Netanyahu and his government to adhere to the roadmap and not obstruct the process for internal political and electoral reasons,” he said.
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich backed Netanyahu’s position, declaring: “We went to war with a central goal: the destruction of Hamas,” and insisting that “The military cannot withdraw even a millimetre from the Gaza Strip.”
Hamas has avoided describing its commitment as “disarmament”, saying instead that its weapons would be handed over for storage under a U.S.-backed Palestinian technocrat administration overseeing Gaza under Trump’s Board of Peace.
The group has also insisted that implementation depends on Israel fulfilling its own commitments, including withdrawing forces and ending attacks.
Since the U.S.-mediated ceasefire in October 2025, Gaza health officials say “more than 1,250 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, most of them civilians. Four Israeli soldiers have also been killed during the same period.”
Israeli forces currently control and have depopulated about two-thirds of Gaza, leaving most of the enclave’s more than two million residents concentrated in a small coastal area, many living in tents or damaged buildings.
There was no immediate public response from President Donald Trump to Netanyahu’s latest remarks, while Washington continues to support the proposed Gaza framework aimed at Hamas’ disarmament, Israeli withdrawal and the establishment of a new security and governing arrangement.
The differing positions underscore ongoing disagreements over how the plan should be implemented, with further U.S.-Israeli and regional discussions expected.
Reuters

sources.news_title: Rare Public Break: Why Netanyahu Just Rejected Trump’s 15-Point Gaza Plan Ahead of Israel's Election
sources.text:
President Donald Trump sold his Gaza peace roadmap as a breakthrough. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is now making clear that he does not accept some of its most consequential provisions.
“As long as I am Prime Minister, there will be no Palestinian state in Gaza or the West Bank,” Netanyahu said Sunday.
He also ruled out an Israeli military withdrawal from Gaza until Hamas is completely disarmed.
The comments create a striking gap between the optimism coming from Washington and the position being stated publicly by Israel’s prime minister. Trump had described the 15-point roadmap as a “major milestone” and a “great breakthrough” toward ending the war.
But the Israeli government’s position directly challenges two elements central to the proposed path forward: the timing of Israel’s withdrawal and the longer-term political future of the Palestinians.
Netanyahu draws a line on Gaza withdrawal
For Israel, the sequence is non-negotiable: Hamas must disarm first.
An Israeli official said last week there would be “no withdrawal whatsoever” from the military’s current positions unless Hamas underwent what Israel considered genuine disarmament.
Netanyahu has now reinforced that position, saying Israeli forces will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is completely disarmed.
That puts Israel at odds with the structure of Trump’s roadmap, which calls for Israeli forces to withdraw in stages as other parts of the agreement are implemented.
Trump had appeared confident after meeting Netanyahu in Washington.
“Israel helped us, and they've been very good,” Trump said, describing Israel as “very happy” with the agreement.
He also acknowledged that putting the plan into practice would not be straightforward.
“Will it go through its ups and downs? It’s a very complex situation over there,” he said.
An Israeli political source said Gaza was not discussed during Netanyahu’s Washington meeting with Trump, raising questions about how much common ground the two leaders actually have on implementation.
Hamas rejects immediate disarmament
Hamas is also demanding that the sequence of events go in the opposite direction.
Senior Hamas official Basem Naim said the group remains committed to the roadmap agreed with mediators and representatives of Trump’s Peace Council in Cairo.
“We remain committed to the roadmap agreed with mediators and representatives of the Peace Council in Cairo,” Naim said.
But Hamas says Israel must first stop its attacks and fulfill its obligations under the earlier ceasefire agreement.
Ghazi Hamad, another senior Hamas official involved in the negotiations, said the group was prepared to accept a “difficult and painful” agreement but stopped short of agreeing to immediate disarmament.
Hamas wants Israel to end attacks, withdraw its forces to earlier positions and allow increased flows of humanitarian aid and goods into Gaza. Only after those steps, the group says, would it consider placing its weapons under the control of the proposed National Committee for the Administration of Gaza.
What Trump’s Gaza plan actually proposes
The 15-point roadmap calls for Hamas and other Palestinian factions to hand over Gaza’s civil administration and internal security to a Palestinian technocratic body.
It also proposes identifying and placing heavy weapons, arms depots, military sites and tunnels under that committee’s control.
An international stabilization force would monitor the arrangement and separate Israeli troops from Palestinian-administered areas. Israeli forces would then withdraw in stages, while reconstruction and the restoration of public services begin.
Beyond Gaza’s immediate security arrangements, the roadmap points toward a longer-term political process focused on Palestinian self-determination and the establishment of a Palestinian state.
That final objective now faces an unmistakable obstacle from Netanyahu.
Regional pressure grows
The dispute has already triggered a coordinated response from eight Muslim-majority countries: the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Jordan, Indonesia, Pakistan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Egypt.
The countries condemned Israel’s continuing military operations in Gaza and warned that further action could undermine efforts to implement the next stage of the US-backed roadmap.
In a joint statement, they said Israel’s actions could “derail the political process”, trigger renewed escalation and deepen Gaza’s humanitarian crisis.
The result is a peace plan caught between two incompatible demands.
Israel wants Hamas disarmed before it withdraws. Hamas wants Israel to stop its attacks and begin withdrawing before it gives up its weapons. And Netanyahu has now ruled out the Palestinian state envisioned as part of the roadmap’s longer-term political horizon.
Trump may have called the plan a breakthrough. Netanyahu’s latest comments show that the hardest part, getting the parties to agree on what happens next, has barely begun.

sources.news_title: Israel rejects Gaza plan, deepens rift with Trump - Lagos Television
sources.text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a US-backed 15-point proposal aimed at ending the conflict in Gaza, despite the plan receiving support from Hamas and strong backing from US President Donald Trump.
Speaking during a cabinet meeting on Sunday, Netanyahu made it clear that Israel would not accept any arrangement that requires its military to withdraw from Gaza before Hamas is completely disarmed.
“Israel rejects the 15-point document,” Netanyahu said, referring to the proposal that Hamas agreed to in late July.
He maintained that the Israeli military would continue operating in Gaza until Hamas no longer posed what Israel considers a threat to its forces and citizens. According to Netanyahu, any withdrawal would only take place after what he described as the genuine disarmament of Hamas.
The Israeli leader’s position represents a significant departure from Trump’s enthusiastic support for the agreement, which the US president has described as an important opportunity to advance peace in the region.
Netanyahu, however, continued to describe Trump as a close ally, calling him “our greatest friend in the White House.” At the same time, he acknowledged that Israel and the United States do not agree on every aspect of the proposed arrangement.
“They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not,” Netanyahu said, stressing that Israel would continue to defend its position during discussions with Washington.
Political pressure at home
Netanyahu’s rejection comes as he faces growing pressure from his right-wing political allies, many of whom have strongly opposed the Gaza proposal.
The Israeli prime minister is also preparing for a closely contested election scheduled for October 27. Recent opinion polls have reportedly shown him either narrowly ahead or behind his rivals, increasing the political pressure surrounding his handling of the Gaza conflict.
The proposed agreement has reportedly been unpopular among parts of Netanyahu’s right-wing support base, while far-right members of his coalition have called on him to reject the deal entirely.
Hamas, meanwhile, has continued to support the proposal and urged the United States to pressure Netanyahu and his government to implement it.
Bassem Naim, a member of Hamas’s political bureau, called on the mediators and Washington to ensure that the proposed roadmap was not derailed by Israel’s domestic political considerations.
Hamas also reaffirmed in a statement that it remained committed to the agreement.
Disagreement over Israeli withdrawal
The proposed Gaza framework reportedly requires Hamas to hand over its weapons to an emerging Palestinian governing authority. In return, Israel would gradually withdraw its forces as the disarmament process progresses.
That sequence has been a major point of disagreement.
Following a meeting with Netanyahu last week, Trump’s Board of Peace, the body tasked with helping implement the agreement, appeared to modify its position by saying Israel would only be required to withdraw after Hamas had been completely disarmed.
The adjustment, however, failed to convince Netanyahu.
The Israeli prime minister insisted that his government was seeking what he called “real disarmament” rather than an arrangement that would leave Hamas capable of retaining its weapons.
Growing friction between Netanyahu and Trump
The disagreement over Gaza adds to a series of recent differences between Netanyahu and Trump.
Netanyahu has previously relied heavily on his close relationship with Trump, whose administration has taken several significant steps in support of Israel.
The two leaders also worked together during the conflict with Iran earlier this year. However, tensions emerged when Trump pushed for a ceasefire and a diplomatic settlement as the conflict affected US interests and contributed to rising oil prices.
Netanyahu has continued to insist that Iran must not be allowed to develop nuclear weapons.
Addressing his cabinet, he said that regardless of whether a broader agreement is reached, Israel would continue working to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons.
The Israeli government has also recently ordered new strikes in Lebanon following what it described as violations of a ceasefire involving Iran-backed Hezbollah. The developments came while US-mediated discussions between Israel and Lebanon were underway.
Gaza ceasefire remains fragile
The latest Gaza proposal represents another attempt to strengthen a ceasefire arrangement brokered by the United States.
Although the truce has reduced the scale of Israeli military activity in Gaza, fighting and other incidents have continued.
Egypt, one of the key mediators in the negotiations, has urged all parties to respect their commitments and avoid actions that could threaten the progress already made.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty reportedly discussed the situation with Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative for Gaza, and called for continued efforts to preserve the diplomatic process.
Despite Netanyahu’s rejection of the plan, Israeli military activity in Gaza appears to have declined since the proposal was announced, although operations have not stopped completely.
Gaza civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Bassal said Israeli gunfire on Sunday injured a child who was subsequently taken to hospital in Khan Yunis.
According to figures from Gaza’s health ministry, which operates under Hamas authorities and whose casualty figures are generally considered reliable by the United Nations, Israeli military operations have killed 1,258 Palestinians since the ceasefire began.
The Israeli military, meanwhile, has reported five deaths among its personnel during the same period.
The latest developments leave the future of the US-backed Gaza plan uncertain, with Hamas maintaining its commitment to the agreement while Netanyahu insists that Israel will not accept a withdrawal timetable unless Hamas is fully and genuinely disarmed.
#Israel #Gaza #Trump

sources.news_title: Israel Rejects Trump Gaza Plan: Netanyahu Vows No Withdrawal Until Hamas Disarms
sources.text:
S. President Donald Trump. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu clarified on Sunday that the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) won't withdraw from the Palestinian territory until Hamas effectively surrenders its weapons. This statement comes at a time when the Israeli military maintains control over more than half of the Gaza Strip, an area inhabited by approximately 20 lakh people. Netanyahu emphasized during a cabinet meeting that while Israel rejects the 15 point document presented by Trump, the government will continue to engage in discussions with Washington regarding future plans for Gaza. He had expressed similar sentiments last week, reinforcing his position that military pressure must continue until the group's capabilities are neutralized.
Netanyahu's Stance on Military Withdrawal
The Israeli Prime Minister's refusal to accept the deal hinges on the condition of total disarmament by Hamas.
